Chapter 7 

# A General Maximum Principle for Anticipative Stochastic Control and Applications to Insider Trading

Giulia Di Nunno, Olivier Menoukeu Pamen, Bernt Øksendal, and Frank Proske 

Abstract In this paper we suggest a general stochastic maximum principle for optimal control of anticipating stochastic differential equations driven by a Lévy-type noise. We use techniques of Malliavin calculus and forward integration. We apply our results to study a general optimal portfolio problem of an insider. In particular, we find conditions on the insider information filtration which are sufficient to give the insider an infinite wealth. We also apply the results to find the optimal consumption rate for an insider. 

Keywords Anticipative stochastic control · Maximum principle · Malliavin calculus · Insider trading · Forward integrals · Skorokhod integrals 

Mathematics Subject Classification (2010) 93E20 · 91G80 · 60G51 · 60H10 

## 7.1 Introduction

In the classical Black–Scholes model and in most problems of stochastic analysis applied to finance, one of the fundamental hypotheses is the homogeneity of information that market participants have. This homogeneity does not reflect reality. In fact, there exist many types of agents in the market that have different levels of information. In this paper, we are focusing on agents who have additional information (insiders) and show that it is important to understand how an optimal control is affected by particular pieces of such information. 

In the following, let $\{ B ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ be a Brownian motion, and $\widetilde { N } ( d z , d s ) =$ $N ( d z , d s ) - d s \nu ( d z )$ be a compensated Poisson random measure associated with a Lévy process with Lévy measure ν on the (complete) filtered probability space $( \Omega , \mathcal { F } , \mathbb { F } = \{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } , P )$ with fixed time horizon $T > 0$ . In the sequel, we assume that the Lévy measure ν fulfills 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} z ^ {2} \nu (d z) <   \infty ,
$$

where $\mathbb { R } _ { 0 } : = \mathbb { R } \backslash \{ 0 \}$ 

Here we suppose that we are given a filtration $\mathbb { G } = \{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ with 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {t} \subseteq \mathcal {G} _ {t}, \quad t \in [ 0, T ],\tag{7.1}
$$

representing the information available to the agent at time t. This information is used at decision making level yielding a G-predictable strategy or control. 

Suppose that the state process $X ( t ) = X ^ { ( u ) } ( t , \omega ) ; 0 \leq t \leq T , \omega \in \Omega$ , characterizing the agent’s wealth, is a controlled jump diffusion in R of the form 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} d ^ {-} X (t) = b (t, X (t), u (t))   d t + \sigma (t, X (t), u (t))   d ^ {-} B (t) \\ \qquad \qquad + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \theta (t, X (t), u (t), z) \widetilde {N} (d z, d ^ {-} t); \\ X (0) = x \in \mathbb {R}. \end{array} \right.\tag{7.2}
$$

Since $B ( \cdot )$ and $\widetilde { N } ( A , \cdot ) , A \subseteq \mathbb { R } _ { 0 }$ Borel, need not be semimartingales with respect to $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ , the two last integrals in (7.2) are anticipating stochastic integrals that we interpret as forward integrals. The choice of forward integration, as an anticipative extension of the Itô integration, is motivated by the possible applications to optimal portfolio problems for insiders as in Sect. 7.6 (see, e.g., [3, 6, 7]). However, the applications are not restricted to this area and include all situations of optimization problems in anticipating environments (see, e.g., [15, 20]). 

The control process 

$$
u: [ 0, T ] \times \Omega \to U
$$

is called an admissible control if (7.2) has a unique (strong) solution $X = X ^ { ( u ) }$ such that $u ( \cdot )$ is predictable with respect to the filtration $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ . We let $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathbb { G } }$ denote a given family of admissible controls assumed to be G-predictable and such that (7.2) has a strong solution. 

More specifically, the problem we are dealing with is the following. Suppose tha we are given a performance functional of the form 

$$
J (u) := E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} f (t, X (t), u (t)) d t + g (X (T)) \right], \quad u \in \mathcal {A} _ {\mathbb {G}},\tag{7.3}
$$

with 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f: [ 0, T ] \times \mathbb {R} \times U \times \varOmega \to \mathbb {R}, \\ g: \mathbb {R} \times \varOmega \to \mathbb {R}, \end{array}
$$

where $f$ is an F-adapted process for each $x \in \mathbb { R } , u \in U$ , and $g$ is an $\mathcal { F } _ { T }$ -measurable random variable for each $x \in \mathbb { R }$ satisfying 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} | f (t, X (t), u (t)) | d t + | g (X (T)) | \right] <   \infty \quad \text { for   all } u \in \mathcal {A} _ {\mathbb {G}}.
$$

The goal is to find the optimal control $u ^ { * } \in { \mathcal { A } } _ { \mathbb { G } }$ such that 

$$
\varPhi_ {\mathbb {G}} := \sup _ {u \in \mathcal {A} _ {\mathbb {G}}} J (u) = J \bigl (u ^ {*} \bigr).\tag{7.4}
$$

Special cases of this problem have been studied by many authors. See, e.g., [1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, 21] and the references therein. 

The purpose of this paper is twofold. 

First, we want to establish a general maximum principle for the optimal anticipative control problem (7.2)–(7.4), without any a priori semimartingale assumptions for the inside information filtration $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ (see Theorems 7.13 and 7.14). 

Second, we want to use these general results to investigate the following problem in insider trading: How much information does an insider need in order to generate an infinite value of $\boldsymbol { \varPhi } _ { \mathbb { G } } 2$ 

The following example by Pikovski and Karatzas in [14] illustrates the situation. Suppose that the financial market has two investments opportunities: 

1. a risk-free asset with unit price 

$$
S _ {0} (t) = 1, \quad t \in [ 0, T ],
$$

2. a risky asset with unit price 

$$
d S _ {1} (t) = S _ {1} (t) \big [ \mu d t + \sigma d B (t) \big ], \quad S (0) > 0, t \in [ 0, T ]
$$

$( \mu , \sigma > 0$ constants). If the trader chooses a portfolio $\pi ( t )$ representing the fraction of wealth to be invested in the risky asset at time t, the corresponding wealth process $X ( t ) , t \in [ 0 , T ]$ , will have the dynamics 

$$
d ^ {-} X _ {\pi} (t) = X _ {\pi} (t) \pi (t) \big [ \mu d t + \sigma d ^ {-} B (t) \big ], \quad X _ {\pi} (0) > 0.
$$

If the information flow accessible to the insider trader is given by a filtration $\mathbb { G } =$ $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ such that $\mathcal { G } _ { t } \supseteq \mathcal { F } _ { t }$ , this means that $\pi$ is required to be G-adapted (thus the Itô integration cannot be applied, and the forward integration is chosen to be used instead). Suppose that the insider wants to maximize the expected logarithmic utility of the terminal wealth, i.e., to find $\boldsymbol { \varPhi } _ { \mathbb { G } }$ and $\pi ^ { * }$ (if it exists) such that 

$$
\Phi_ {\mathbb {G}} := \max _ {\pi \in \mathcal {A} _ {\mathbb {G}}} E \bigl [ \ln \bigl (X _ {\pi} (T) \bigr) \bigr ] = E \bigl [ \ln \bigl (X _ {\pi^ {*}} (T) \bigr) \bigr ].
$$

In [14] it is proved that if 

$$
\mathcal {G} _ {t} = \mathcal {F} _ {t} \vee \sigma (B (T)), \quad t \in [ 0, T ],
$$

then $\begin{array} { r } { \varPhi _ { \mathbb { G } } = \infty , } \end{array}$ , and $\pi ^ { * }$ does not exist. 

In this paper we generalize this situation in several directions: 

(a) We include jumps in the risky asset model; 

(b) We study more general utility functions; 

(c) We study more general insider filtrations. 

These points were already partially discussed in [7] from the point of view of the existence of an optimal portfolio for a given insider. The present paper, we repeat, focuses on the study of conditions on the amount of information $\mathbb { G } = \{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ needed to obtain $\varPhi _ { \mathbb { G } } = \infty$ and the nonexistence of an optimal insider portfolio. 

The main result, which represents an anticipative stochastic maximum principle, is presented in full generality (see Theorem 7.13). However it is difficult to apply because of the appearance of some terms, which all depend on the control. We then consider the special case (see Theorem 7.14) where the coefficients of the controlled process X do not depend on X; we call such processes controlled Itô–Lévy processes. In this case, we give a condition for the existence of an optimal control. More specific results are obtained in the cases where the insider filtration is either 

(i) a D-commutablefiltration (Sect. 7.5.1 and Theorem 7.16) or 

(ii) a smoothly anticipativefiltration (Sect. 7.5.2). 

Besides the application of these results to optimal portfolio problems, we also consider applications to optimal insider consumption. In this case we show that there exists an optimal insider consumption, and in some special cases the optimal consumption can be expressed explicitly. 

The paper is structured as follows: In Sect. 7.2, we briefly recall some basic concepts of Malliavin calculus and its connection to the theory of forward integration. In Sect. 7.3, we use Malliavin calculus to obtain a maximum principle for this general non-Markovian insider information stochastic control problem. Section 7.4 considers the special case of Itô–Lévy processes. In Sect. 7.5, some specific classes of insider information are considered. Finally, in Sects. 7.6 and 7.7, we apply the results from the previous sections to study optimal insider portfolio and optimal insider consumption problems, respectively. 

## 7.2 Framework

In this section, we briefly recall some basic concepts of Malliavin calculus and its connection to the theory of forward integration. We refer to [17] or [8] for more information about Malliavin calculus. As for the theory of forward integration, the reader may consult [18, 23, 24] and [6]. 

## 7.2.1 Malliavin Calculusfor Lévy Processes

In the sequel, consider a Brownian motion $\{ B ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ on the filtered probability space 

$$
\big (\Omega^ {(B)}, \mathcal {F} ^ {(B)}, \big \{\mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {(B)} \big \} _ {0 \leq t \leq T}, P ^ {(B)} \big),
$$

where $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { ( B ) } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ is the $P ^ { ( B ) }$ -augmented filtration generated by $\{ B ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ with $\mathcal { F } ^ { ( B ) } = \mathcal { F } _ { T } ^ { ( B ) }$ . Further we assume that a Poisson random measure $N ( d t , d z )$ associated with a Lévy process is defined on the stochastic basis 

$$
\big (\Omega^ {(\widetilde {N})}, \mathcal {F} ^ {(\widetilde {N})}, \big \{\mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {(\widetilde {N})} \big \} _ {0 \leq t \leq T}, P ^ {(\widetilde {N})} \big).
$$

We denote by $\widetilde { N } ( d t , d z ) = N ( d t , d z ) - \nu ( d z )$ dt the compensated Poisson random measure, where ν is the Lévy measure of the Lévy process. See [2, 25] for more information about Lévy processes. 

The starting point of Malliavin calculus is the following observation which goes back to Itô [13]: Square-integrable functionals of $B ( t )$ and $\widetilde { N } ( d t , d z )$ enjoy the chaos representation property, that is, 

(i) If $F \in L ^ { 2 } ( \mathcal { F } ^ { ( B ) } , P ^ { ( B ) } )$ ), then 

$$
F = \sum_ {n \geq 0} I _ {n} ^ {(B)} (f _ {n})\tag{7.5}
$$

for a unique sequence of symmetric $f _ { n } \in L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda ^ { n } )$ , where λ is the Lebesgue measure, and 

$$
I _ {n} ^ {(B)} (f _ {n}) := n! \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {t _ {n}} \dots \int_ {0} ^ {t _ {2}} f _ {n} (t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {n}) d B (t _ {1}) d B (t _ {2}) \dots d B (t _ {n}), \quad n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

is the n-fold iterated stochastic integral with respect to $B ( t )$ . Here $I _ { n } ^ { ( B ) } ( f _ { 0 } ) : =$ $f _ { 0 }$ for constants $f _ { 0 }$ 

(ii) Similarly, if $G \in L ^ { 2 } ( \mathcal { F } ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) } , P ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) } )$ , then 

$$
G = \sum_ {n \geq 0} I _ {n} ^ {(\widetilde {N})} (g _ {n})\tag{7.6}
$$

for a unique sequence of kernels $g _ { n }$ in $L ^ { 2 } ( ( \lambda \times \nu ) ^ { n } )$ , which are symmetric with respect to $( t _ { 1 } , z _ { 1 } ) , \ldots , ( t _ { n } , z _ { n } )$ . Here $I _ { n } ^ { ( \bar { N } ) } ( g _ { n } )$ is defined as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I _ {n} ^ {(\widetilde {N})} (g _ {n}) := n! \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \int_ {0} ^ {t _ {n}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \ldots \left(\int_ {0} ^ {t _ {2}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} g _ {n} (t _ {1}, z _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {n}, z _ {n})\right) \\ \qquad \times \widetilde {N} (d t _ {1}, d z _ {1}) \ldots \widetilde {N} (d t _ {n}, d z _ {n}), \quad n \in \mathbb {N}. \end{array}
$$

If $F \in L ^ { 2 } ( \mathcal { F } ^ { ( B ) } , P ^ { ( B ) } )$ has chaos expansion (7.5), the Malliavin derivative $D _ { t }$ of $F$ in the direction of the Brownian motion is defined as 

$$
D _ {t} F = \sum_ {n \geq 1} n I _ {n - 1} ^ {(B)} \big (\widetilde {f} _ {n - 1} \big),\tag{7.7}
$$

where ${ \widetilde { f } } _ { n - 1 } ( t _ { 1 } , \dots , t _ { n - 1 } ) : = f _ { n } ( t _ { 1 } , \dots , t _ { n - 1 } , t )$ , provided that 

$$
\sum_ {n \geq 0} n n! \| f _ {n} \| _ {L ^ {2} (\lambda^ {n})} ^ {2} <   \infty .\tag{7.8}
$$

Similarly, for all $G \in L ^ { 2 } ( \mathcal { F } ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) } , P ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) } )$ with chaos representation (7.6) such that 

$$
\sum_ {n \geq 0} n n! \| g _ {n} \| _ {L ^ {2} ((\lambda \times \nu) ^ {n})} ^ {2} <   \infty ,\tag{7.9}
$$

the Malliavin derivative $D _ { t , z }$ of $G$ in the direction of $\widetilde { N } ( d t , d z )$ is introduced as 

$$
D _ {t, z} G := \sum_ {n \geq 1} n I _ {n - 1} ^ {(\widetilde {N})} (\widetilde {g} _ {n - 1}),\tag{7.10}
$$

where $\widetilde { g } _ { n - 1 } ( t _ { 1 } , z _ { 1 } , \dots , t _ { n - 1 } , z _ { n - 1 } ) : = g _ { n } ( t _ { 1 } , z _ { 1 } , \dots , t _ { n - 1 } , z _ { n - 1 } , t , z ) .$ 

In the following, we denote by $\mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B }$ the stochastic Sobolev space of squareintegrable Brownian functionals such that (7.8) is fulfilled. The symbol $\mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ stands for the corresponding space with respect to $\widetilde { N } ( d t , d z )$ 

We recall that the Skorokhod integral with respect to B respectively $\widetilde { N } ( \delta t , d z )$ is defined as the adjoint operator of $D _ { \cdot } : \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B } \to L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda \times P ^ { ( B ) } )$ resp. $D _ { \cdot , \cdot } : \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } } \to$ $L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda \times \nu \times P ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) } )$ . Thus, if we denote by 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} (\cdot) \delta B _ {t} \quad \text { and } \quad \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} (\cdot) \widetilde {N} (\delta t, d z)
$$

the corresponding adjoint operators, the following duality relations are satisfied: 

(i) 

$$
E _ {P ^ {(B)}} \bigg [ F \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) \delta B _ {t} \bigg ] = E _ {P ^ {(B)}} \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) D _ {t} F d t \bigg ]\tag{7.11}
$$

for all $F \in \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B }$ and all Skorokhod-integrable $\varphi \in L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda \times P ^ { ( B ) } ) \ ( \mathrm { i . e . , } \varphi$ in the domain of the adjoint operator). 

(ii) 

$$
E _ {P (\widetilde {N})} \left[ G \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \psi (t, z) \widetilde {N} (\delta t, d z) \right] = E _ {P (\widetilde {N})} \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \psi (t, z) D _ {t, z} G v (d z) d t \right]\tag{7.12}
$$

for all $G \in \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ and all Skorokhod-integrable $\psi \in L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda \times \nu \times P ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) } )$ 

In what follows, our reference stochastic basis will be 

$$
\bigl (\Omega , \mathcal {F}, \{\mathcal {F} _ {t} \} _ {0 \leq t \leq T}, P \bigr),
$$

where $\Omega = \Omega ^ { ( B ) } \times \Omega ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) } , \mathcal { F } = \mathcal { F } ^ { ( B ) } \times \mathcal { F } ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) } , \mathcal { F } _ { t } = \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { ( B ) } \times \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) } , P = P ^ { ( B ) } \times P ^ { ( \widetilde { N } ) }$ 

Later on in the paper, we will employ the duality relations (7.11) and (7.12) in connection with P. We will need the following result from [9]. 

Theorem 7.1 (Decomposition uniqueness for Skorokhod semimartingales) Let $\alpha ( t ) \in L _ { 2 } ( P )$ for all t and let $\beta 1 _ { [ 0 , t ] }$ and $\gamma 1 _ { [ 0 , t ] }$ be Skorokhod integrable for all t with respect to B and $\widetilde { N }$ , respectively. Let $\{ X ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ be a Skorokhod semimartingale oftheform 

$$
X _ {t} = \zeta + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha (s) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \beta (s) \delta B _ {s} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \gamma (s, z) \widetilde {N} (d z, \delta s).
$$

Then if 

$$
X _ {t} = 0 \quad f o r a l l 0 \leq t \leq T,
$$

we have 

$$
\zeta = 0, \quad \alpha = 0, \quad \beta = 0, \quad \gamma = 0 \quad a. e.
$$

## 7.2.2 Malliavin Calculus and Forward Integral

In this section, we briefly recall some basic concepts of Malliavin calculus and forward integrations related to this paper. We refer to [18, 23, 24] and [6] for more information about these integrals. 

## Forward Integral and Malliavin Calculus for B(·)

This section constitutes a brief review of the forward integral with respect to the Brownian motion. Let $\{ B ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ be a Brownian motion on a filtered probability space $( \varOmega , \mathcal F , \{ \mathcal F _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } , P )$ , and $T > 0$ a fixed horizon. 

Definition 7.2 Let $\phi : [ 0 , T ] \times \Omega $ R be a measurable process. The forward integral of $\phi$ with respect to $\{ B ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ is defined by 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} \phi (t, \omega) d ^ {-} B (t) = \lim _ {\epsilon \rightarrow 0} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \phi (t, \omega) \frac {B (t + \epsilon) - B (t)}{\epsilon} d t\tag{7.13}
$$

if the limit exists in probability, in which case $\phi$ is called forward integrable. 

Note that if $\phi$ is càdlàg and forward integrable, then 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} \phi (t, \omega) d ^ {-} B (t) = \lim _ {\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \sum_ {j} \phi (t _ {j}) \Delta B (t _ {j}),\tag{7.14}
$$

where $\varDelta B ( t _ { j } ) = B ( t _ { j + 1 } ) - B ( t _ { j } )$ , and the sum is taken over the points of a finite partition of [0, T]. 

Definition 7.3 Let $\mathcal { M } ^ { B }$ denote the set of stochastic processes $\phi : [ 0 , T ] \times \Omega $ R such that: 

1. $\phi \in L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda \times P ) , \phi ( t ) \in \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B }$ for almost all t and satisfies 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {T} | \phi (t) | ^ {2} d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {0} ^ {T} | D _ {u} \phi (t) | ^ {2} d u d t\right) <   \infty .
$$

We will denote by $\mathbb { L } ^ { 1 , 2 } [ 0 , T ]$ the class of such processes. 

2. $\begin{array} { r } { D _ { t + } \phi ( t ) : = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { s \to t + } D _ { s } \phi ( t ) } \end{array}$ exists in $L ^ { 1 } ( \lambda \times P )$ uniformly in $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ 

We let $\mathbb { M } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B }$ be the closure of the linear span of $\mathcal { M } ^ { B }$ with respect to the norm given by 

$$
\| \phi \| _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1, 2} ^ {B}} := \| \phi \| _ {\mathbb {L} ^ {1, 2} [ 0, T ]} + \left\| D _ {t +} \phi (t) \right\| _ {L ^ {1} (\lambda \times P)}.
$$

Then we have the relation between the forward integral and the Skorokhod integral (see [8, 15]): 

Lemma 7.4 $I f \phi \in \mathbb { M } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B }$ , then it isforward integrable, and 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} \phi (t) d ^ {-} B (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {T} \phi (t) \delta B (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {T} D _ {t +} \phi (t) d t.\tag{7.15}
$$

Moreover, 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \phi (t) d ^ {-} B (t) \right] = \mathbb {E} \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} D _ {t +} \phi (t) d t \right].\tag{7.16}
$$

Using (7.15) and the duality formula for the Skorokhod integral (see, e.g., [8]), we deduce the following result. 

Corollary 7.5 Suppose that $\phi \in \mathbb { M } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B }$ and $F \in \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { ( B ) }$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathbb {E} \bigg [ F \int_ {0} ^ {T} \phi (t) d ^ {-} B (t) \bigg ] = & \mathbb {E} \bigg [ F \int_ {0} ^ {T} \phi (t) \delta B (t) + F \int_ {0} ^ {T} D _ {t +} \phi (t) d t \bigg ] \\ = & \mathbb {E} \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \phi (t) D _ {t} F d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} F D _ {t +} \phi (t) d t \bigg ]. \end{array}\tag{7.17}
$$

Proposition 7.6 Let H be a given fixed σ-algebra, and $\varphi : [ 0 , T ] \times \Omega $ R be an H-measurable process. Set $X ( t ) = E [ B ( t ) | \mathcal { H } ]$ . Then 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) d ^ {-} B (t) \mid \mathcal {H} \right] = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) d ^ {-} X (t) \right].\tag{7.18}
$$

Proof Using uniform convergence on compacts in $L ^ { 1 } ( P )$ and the definition of forward integration in the sense of Russo–Vallois (see [23]), we observe that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t)   d ^ {-} B (t) \bigg | \mathcal {H} \bigg ] = E \bigg [ \lim _ {\epsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) \frac {B (t + \epsilon) - B (t)}{\epsilon}   d t \bigg | \mathcal {H} \bigg ] \\ \qquad = L ^ {1} (P) - \lim _ {\epsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) \frac {B (t + \epsilon) - B (t)}{\epsilon}   d t \bigg | \mathcal {H} \bigg ] \\ \qquad = \lim _ {\epsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) E \bigg [ \frac {B (t + \epsilon) - B (t)}{\epsilon} \bigg | \mathcal {H} \bigg ] d t \\ \qquad = \lim _ {\epsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) \frac {X (t + \epsilon) - X (t)}{\epsilon}   d t \\ \qquad = \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t)   d ^ {-} X (t), \quad \text { in   the   ucp   sense }, \end{array}
$$

and the result follows. 

Definition 7.7 Let $\mathbb { H } = \{ \mathcal { H } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ be a given filtration, and $\varphi : [ 0 , T ] \times \varOmega  \mathbb { R }$ be an H-adapted process. The conditionalforward integral of $\varphi$ with respect to $B ( \cdot )$ is defined by 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) E \big [ d ^ {-} B (t) \big | \mathcal {H} _ {t ^ {-}} \big ] = \lim _ {\epsilon \to 0} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \varphi (t) \frac {E [ B (t + \epsilon) - B (t) | \mathcal {H} _ {t ^ {-}} ]}{\epsilon} d t\tag{7.19}
$$

if the convergence holds uniformly on compacts in probability (i.e., ucp sense), where $\mathcal { H } _ { t ^ { - } } = \vee _ { s < t } \mathcal { H } _ { s }$ 

Remark 7.8 Note that Definition 7.7 is different from Proposition 7.6 except if $\mathcal { H } _ { t } =$ H for all t. 

## Forward Integral and Malliavin Calculus for $\widetilde { N } ( \cdot , \cdot )$

In this section, we review the forward integral with respect to the Poisson random measure $\widetilde { N }$ 

Definition 7.9 The forward integral 

$$
J (\phi) := \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \phi (t, z) \widetilde {N} \bigl (d z, d ^ {-} t \bigr),
$$

with respect to the Poisson random measure ${ \widetilde { N } } _ { \bullet }$ , of a càdlàg stochastic function $\phi ( t , z ) , t \in [ 0 , T ] , z \in \mathbb { R }$ , with $\phi ( t , z ) = \phi ( \omega , t , z ) , \omega \in \Omega$ , is defined as 

$$
J (\phi) = \lim _ {m \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \phi (t, z) 1 _ {U _ {m}} (z) \widetilde {N} (d z, d t)
$$

if the limit exists in $L ^ { 2 } ( P )$ . Here $U _ { m } , m = 1 , 2 , \ldots$ , is an increasing sequence of compact sets $U _ { m } \subseteq \mathbb { R } \backslash \{ 0 \}$ with $\nu ( U _ { m } ) < \infty$ such that $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { m \to \infty } U _ { m } = \mathbb { R } \backslash \{ 0 \}$ . The integral on the right is for each m defined ω-wise in the usual way, as limits of integrals of simple integrands. 

Definition 7.10 Let $\mathcal { M } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ denote the set of stochastic functions $\phi : [ 0 , T ] \times \mathbb { R } \times$ $\Omega \to \mathbb { R }$ in $\mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ such that: 

1. $\phi ( t , z , \omega ) = \phi _ { 1 } ( t , \omega ) \phi _ { 2 } ( t , z , \omega )$ , where $\phi _ { 1 } ( \omega , t ) \in \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ is càglàd, and $\phi _ { 2 } ( \omega , t , z )$ is adapted such that 

$$
\mathbb {E} \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \phi_ {2} ^ {2} (t, z) \nu (d z) d t \bigg ] <   \infty ,
$$

2. $D _ { t + , z } \phi : = \mathrm { l i m } _ { s  t + } D _ { s , z } \phi$ exists in $L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda \times \nu \times P )$ 

3. $\phi ( t , z ) + D _ { t + , z } \phi ( t , z )$ is Skorokhod integrable. 

We let $\mathbb { M } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ be the closure of the linear span of $\mathcal { M } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ with respect to the norm given by 

$$
\| \phi \| _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1, 2} ^ {\widetilde {N}}} := \| \phi \| _ {L ^ {2} (\lambda \times \nu \times P)} + \left\| D _ {t +, z} \phi (t, z) \right\| _ {L ^ {2} (\lambda \times \nu \times P)}.
$$

Then we have the relation between the forward integral and the Skorokhod integral (see [6, 8]): 

Lemma 7.11 $I f \phi \in \mathbb { M } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ , then it isforward integrable, and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \phi (t, z) \widetilde {N} (d z, d ^ {-} t) \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t +, z} \phi (t, z) v (d z) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} (\phi (t, z) + D _ {t +, z} \phi (t, z)) \widetilde {N} (d z, \delta t). \end{array}\tag{7.20}
$$

Moreover, 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \phi (t, z) \widetilde {N} (d z, d ^ {-} t) \right] = \mathbb {E} \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t +, z} \phi (t, z) v (d z) d t \right].\tag{7.21}
$$

Then by (7.20) and duality formula for the Skorokhod integral for Poisson process (see [8]), we have 

Corollary 7.12 Suppose that $\phi \in \mathbb { M } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ and $F \in \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} \bigg [ F \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \phi (t, z) \widetilde {N} \big (d z, d ^ {-} t \big) \bigg ] \\ = \mathbb {E} \bigg [ F \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t +, z} \phi (t, z) \nu (d z) d t \bigg ] \\ \quad + \mathbb {E} \bigg [ F \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \big (\phi (t, z) + D _ {t +, z} \phi (t, z) \big) \widetilde {N} (d z, \delta t) \bigg ] \\ = \mathbb {E} \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \phi (t, z) D _ {t, z} F \nu (d z) d t \bigg ] \\ \quad + \mathbb {E} \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} (F + D _ {t, z} F) D _ {t +, z} \phi (t, z) \nu (d z) d t \bigg ]. \end{array}\tag{7.22}
$$

## 7.3 A Stochastic Maximum Principle for Insider

We now formulate a general anticipative maximum principle for optimal control. For a presentation in the classical adapted case, see e.g. [10, 16, 21]. 

In view of the optimization problem (7.4), we require the following conditions $_ { 1 - 5 }$ on the coefficients and on the family of admissible controls $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathbb { G } }$ : 

1. The functions $b : [ 0 , T ] \times \mathbb { R } \times U \times \Omega  \mathbb { R } , \sigma : [ 0 , T ] \times \mathbb { R } \times U \times \Omega  \mathbb { R } , \theta$ $[ 0 , T ] \times \mathbb { R } \times U \times \mathbb { R } _ { 0 } \times \Omega \to \mathbb { R } , f : [ 0 , T ] \times \mathbb { R } \times U \times \Omega \to \mathbb { R }$ , and $g : \mathbb { R } \times \varOmega $ R are contained in $C ^ { 1 }$ with respect to the arguments $x \in \mathbb { R }$ and $u \in U$ for each $t \in \mathbb { R }$ and a.a. $\omega \in \varOmega$ 

2. For all $r , t \in ( 0 , T ) , t \leq r$ , and all bounded $\mathcal { G } _ { t }$ -measurable random variables $\alpha =$ $\alpha ( \omega ) , \omega \in \Omega$ , the control 

$$
\beta_ {\alpha} (s) := \alpha (\omega) \chi_ {[ t, r ]} (s), \quad 0 \leq s \leq T,\tag{7.23}

3. For all $u , \beta \in \mathcal { A } _ { \mathbb { G } }$ with $\beta$ bounded, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that

\begin{array}{l} \left\{\frac {\partial}{\partial x} f (t, X ^ {u + y \beta} (t), u (t) + y \beta (t)) \frac {d}{d y} X ^ {u + y \beta} (t) \right. \\ \left. + \frac {\partial}{\partial u} f (t, X ^ {u + y \beta} (t), u (t) + y \beta (t)) \beta (t) \right\} _ {y \in (- \delta , \delta)} \end{array}

is P-uniformly integrable.

Y (t) = Y _ {\beta} (t) = Y _ {\beta} ^ {u} (t) = \frac {d}{d y} X ^ {(u + y \beta)} (t) \bigg | _ {y = 0}

exists and follows the stochastic differential equation

\begin{array}{l} d Y _ {\beta} ^ {u} (t) = Y _ {\beta} \left(t ^ {-}\right) \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial x} b \left(t, X ^ {u} (t), u (t)\right) d t + \frac {\partial}{\partial x} \sigma \left(t, X ^ {u} (t), u (t)\right) d ^ {-} B (t) \right. \\ \left. + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \frac {\partial}{\partial x} \theta \left(t, X ^ {u} (t), u (t), z\right) \widetilde {N} \left(d z, d ^ {-} t\right) \right] \\ + \beta (t) \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial u} b \left(t, X ^ {u} (t), u (t)\right) d t + \frac {\partial}{\partial u} \sigma \left(t, X ^ {u} (t), u (t)\right) d ^ {-} B (t) \right. \\ + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \frac {\partial}{\partial u} \theta \left(t, X ^ {u} (t), u (t), z\right) \widetilde {N} \left(d z, d ^ {-} t\right) \Bigg ], \end{array} \tag {7.}\tag{7.25}

K (t) := g ^ {\prime} \bigl (X (T) \bigr) + \int_ {t} ^ {T} \frac {\partial}{\partial x} f \bigl (s, X (s), u (s) \bigr) d s,\tag{7.26}

Now let us introduce the general Hamiltonian ofan insider

## 7.4 Controlled Itô–Lévy Processes

The main result of the previous section (Theorem 7.13) is difficult to apply because of the appearance of the terms $Y ( t ) , D _ { t + } Y ( t )$ , and $D _ { t + , z } Y ( t )$ , which all depend on the control u. However, consider the special case where the coefficients do not depend on X, i.e., where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} b (t, x, u, \omega) = b (t, u, \omega), \qquad \sigma (t, x, u, \omega) = \sigma (t, u, \omega), \quad \text { and } \\ \theta (t, x, u, z, \omega) = \theta (t, u, z, \omega). \end{array}\tag{7.37}
$$

Then (7.2) gets the form 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} d ^ {-} (X) (t) = b (t, u (t), \omega)   d t + \sigma (t, u (t), \omega)   d ^ {-} B _ {t} \\ \qquad \qquad + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \theta (t, u (t), z, \omega) \widetilde {N} (d z, d ^ {-} t); \\ X (0) = x \in \mathbb {R}. \end{array} \right.\tag{7.38}
$$

We call such processes controlled Itô–Lévy processes. 

In this case, Theorem 7.13 simplifies to the following:

1. $\widehat { u } \in \mathcal { A } _ { \mathbb { G } }$ is a critical point of $J ( u )$

$$

It follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\frac {d}{d h} A _ {2} \bigg | _ {h = 0} = E \bigg [ \bigg \{K (t) \bigg (\frac {\partial b (t)}{\partial u} + D _ {t +} \frac {\partial \sigma (s)}{\partial u} + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t +, z} \frac {\partial \theta (t)}{\partial u} \nu (d z) \bigg) + \frac {\partial f (t)}{\partial u}} \\ & {\qquad + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t, z} K (t) \bigg (\frac {\partial \theta (t)}{\partial u} + D _ {t +, z} \frac {\partial \gamma (t)}{\partial u} \bigg) \nu (d z) + D _ {t} K (t) \frac {\partial \sigma (t)}{\partial u} \bigg \} \alpha \bigg ],} \\ & {\frac {d}{d h} A _ {4} \bigg | _ {h = 0} = E \bigg [ K (t) \frac {\partial \sigma (t)}{\partial u} D _ {t +} \alpha \bigg ],} \\ & {\frac {d}{d h} A _ {6} \bigg | _ {h = 0} = E \bigg [ \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \big \{K (t) + D _ {t, z} K (t) \big \} \bigg (\frac {\partial \theta (t)}{\partial u} + D _ {t +, z} \frac {\partial \gamma (t)}{\partial u} \bigg) \nu (d z) D _ {t +, z} \alpha \bigg ].} \end{array}
$$

This means that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = E \left[ \left\{K (t) \left(\frac {\partial b (t)}{\partial u} + D _ {t +} \frac {\partial \sigma (s)}{\partial u} + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t +, z} \frac {\partial \theta (t)}{\partial u} v (d z)\right) + \frac {\partial f (t)}{\partial u} \right. \right. \\ \left. + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t, z} K (t) \left(\frac {\partial \theta (t)}{\partial u} + D _ {t +, z} \frac {\partial \gamma (t)}{\partial u}\right) v (d z) + D _ {t} K (t) \frac {\partial \sigma (t)}{\partial u} \right\} \alpha \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} + K (t) \frac {\partial \sigma (t)}{\partial u} D _ {t +} \alpha + \left\{\int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \bigl \{K (t) + D _ {t, z} K (t) \bigr \} \right. \\ \times \left(\frac {\partial \theta (t)}{\partial u} + D _ {t +, z} \frac {\partial \gamma (t)}{\partial u}\right) \nu (d z) \Bigg \} D _ {t +, z} \alpha \Bigg ], \end{array}
$$

and the first part of the result follows. 

2. The converse part follows from the arguments used in the proof of Theorem 7.13. 

By this the proof is complete. 

## 7.5 Applications to Some Special Cases of Filtrations

We consider the case of an insider who has an additional information compared to the standard normally informed investor. 

• It can be the case of an insider who always has advanced information compared to the honest trader. This means that if $\mathbb { G } = \{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ and $\mathbb { F } = \{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ represent respectively the flows of informations of the insider and the honest investor, then we can write that $\mathcal { G } _ { t } \supset \mathcal { F } _ { t + \delta ( t ) }$ where $\delta ( t ) > 0 ;$ 

• It can also be the case of a trader who has at the initial date particular information about the future (initial enlargement of filtration). This means that if $\mathbb { G } = \{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ and $\mathbb { F } = \{ \mathcal { F } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ represent respectively the flows of informations of the insider and the honest investor, then we can write that $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \mathcal { F } _ { t } \vee \sigma ( L )$ where L is a random variable. 

## 7.5.1 D-commutable Filtrations

In the following, we need the notion of D-commutativity of a σ-algebra. 

Definition 7.15 A σ-algebra ${ \mathcal { A } } \subseteq { \mathcal { F } }$ is called D-commutable if for all $F \in \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } =$ $\mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B } \cap \mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { \widetilde { N } }$ , the conditional expectation $E [ F | { \mathcal { A } } ]$ belongs to $\mathbb { D } _ { 1 , 2 }$ and 

$$
D _ {t} E [ F | \mathcal {A} ] = E [ D _ {t} F | \mathcal {A} ],\tag{7.42}
$$

$$
D _ {t, z} E [ F | \mathcal {A} ] = E [ D _ {t, z} F | \mathcal {A} ].\tag{7.43}
$$

Theorem 7.16 Suppose that $\widehat { u } \in A _ { \mathbb { G } }$ is a critical point for $J ( u )$ . Assume that $\mathcal { G } _ { t }$ is D-commutable for all t. Further, require that for all t, the set of smooth G -measurable random variables is dense in $L ^ { 2 } ( { \mathcal { G } } _ { t } )$ and that $E [ M ( t ) | \mathcal { G } _ { t } ]$ and $E [ R ( t , z ) | \mathcal { G } _ { t } ]$ are Skorokhod integrable. Thenfor any $t _ { 0 } \in [ 0 , T )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ L (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) \delta B _ {t} \\ \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} E \big [ R (t, z) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) \widetilde {N} (\delta t, d z) \end{array}\tag{7.44}
$$

for all $h \in L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , T ] )$ with supp $h \subseteq [ t _ { 0 } , T ]$ 

Proof Without loss of generality, we give the proof for the Brownian motion case only. The pure jump case and mixed case follow similarly. Define $\langle X , Y \rangle = E [ X Y ]$ 

Let us fix a $t _ { 0 } \in [ 0 , T )$ . Then, by assumption, it follows that for all $\mathcal { G } _ { t _ { 0 } }$ -measurable smooth α and $h \in L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , T ] )$ with 

$$
\operatorname{supp} h \subseteq [ t _ {0}, T ], \quad t _ {0} \leq t \leq T,
$$

$$
0 = \left\langle \int_ {0} ^ {T} E [ L (t) | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ] h (t) d t, \alpha \right\rangle + \left\langle E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) \delta B _ {t} | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right], \alpha \right\rangle .
$$

On the other hand, the duality relation (7.11) implies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left\langle E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) \delta B _ {t}   \Big |   \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right], \alpha \right\rangle = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) \delta B _ {t}   E [ \alpha | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ] \right] \\ = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) \big (D _ {t}   E [ \alpha | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ] \big)   d t \right] \\ = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) E [ D _ {t} \alpha | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ]   d t \right] \\ = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ M (t) h (t)   \big |   \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] D _ {t} \alpha   d t \right] \\ = \left\langle \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ M (t)   \big |   \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) \delta B _ {t}, \alpha \right\rangle \end{array}
$$

for all $\mathcal { G } _ { t _ { 0 } }$ -measurable smooth α. So 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) \delta B _ {t} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right] = \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \left[ M (t) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right] h (t) \delta B _ {t}.
$$

Hence, by our density assumption, we obtain that 

$$
0 = \int_ {0} ^ {T} E [ L (t) | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ] h (t) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} E [ M (t) | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ] h (t) \delta B _ {t}.
$$

By this the proof is complete. 

To provide some concrete examples, let us confine ourselves to the following type of filtrations $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ . Given an increasing family of $\{ G _ { t } \} _ { t \in [ 0 , T ] }$ of Borel sets 

$G _ { t } \supset [ 0 , t ]$ , define 

{G<sub>t</sub>}<sub>0≤t≤T</sub> where 

$$
\mathcal {G} _ {t} = \mathcal {F} _ {G _ {t}} = \sigma \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {T} \chi_ {U} (s) d B (s); U \subset G _ {t}, U \text {   Borel } \right\} \vee \mathcal {N},\tag{7.45}
$$

where $\mathcal { N }$ is the collection of P-null sets. Then conditions (7.42) and (7.43) hold (see Proposition 3.12 in [8]). Examples of filtrations of type (7.45) are 

$$
\mathcal {G} _ {t} ^ {1} = \mathcal {F} _ {t + \delta (t)},
$$

$$
\mathcal {G} _ {t} ^ {2} = \mathcal {F} _ {[ 0, t ] \cup O},
$$

where O is an open set contained in [0, T]. 

It is easily seen that filtrations of type (7.45) satisfy conditions of Theorem 7.16 as well. Hence, we have the following: 

Theorem 7.17 Suppose that $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ is given by (7.45). Then $u = \widehat { u }$ is a critical pointfor J(u) ifand only if(7.44) holds. 

From this, we get the following: 

Theorem 7.18 Suppose that $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ is oftype (7.45). Then there exists a critical point $u = \widehat { u }$ for the performancefunctional J(u) in (7.3) ifand only ifthefollowing three conditions hold: 

(i) 

$$
E \big [ L (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big ] = 0,\tag{ii}
$$

$$
E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big ] = 0,\tag{iii}
$$

$$
E \big [ R (t, z) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big ] = 0,
$$

where L, M, and R are given by (7.39), (7.40), and (7.41). 

Proof This follows from the uniqueness of decomposition of Skorokhod-semimartingale processes of type (7.44) (see Theorem 3.3 in [9]). - 

Remark 7.19 Not all filtrations satisfy conditions (7.42) and (7.43). An important example is the following: Choose the σ-field H to be $\sigma ( B ( T ) )$ , where $\{ B ( t ) \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ is the Wiener process (Brownian motion) starting at 0, and $T > 0$ is fixed. Then, H is not D-commutable. In fact, let $F = B ( t _ { 0 } )$ for some $t _ { 0 } < T$ and choose s such that $t _ { 0 } < s < T$ . Then 

$$
D _ {s} E \left[ B (t _ {0}) \mid \mathcal {H} \right] = D _ {s} \left(\frac {t _ {0}}{T} B (T)\right) = \frac {t _ {0}}{T},
$$

while 

$$
E \left[ D _ {s} B (t _ {0}) \mid \mathcal {H} \right] = E [ 0 | \mathcal {H} ] = 0.
$$

A similar argument works to prove that (7.42) and (7.43) are not satisfied for $\mathcal G _ { t } = \mathcal F _ { t } \vee \sigma ( B _ { T } )$ either. It follows that the technique used in the preceding section cannot be applied to the σ-algebras of the type $\mathcal { F } _ { t } \vee \sigma ( B _ { T } )$ , and hence we need a different approach to discuss such cases. 

## 7.5.2 Smoothly Anticipative Filtrations

In this section, we consider σ-algebras which do not necessarily satisfy conditions (7.42) and (7.43). The starting point is again statement 2 of Theorem 7.14. 

Definition 7.20 We say that the filtration $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ is smoothly anticipative if for all $t _ { 0 } \in [ 0 , T ]$ , there exist a set $\mathscr { A } = \mathscr { A } _ { t _ { 0 } } \subseteq \bar { \mathbb { D } } _ { 1 , 2 } \cap L ^ { 2 } ( \mathscr { G } _ { t _ { 0 } } )$ and a measurable set $\mathcal { M } \subset [ t _ { 0 } , T ]$ such that $E [ L ( t ) | \mathcal { G } _ { t _ { 0 } } ] \cdot \chi _ { [ 0 , T ] \cap \mathcal { M } } , E [ M ( t ) | \mathcal { G } _ { t _ { 0 } } ] \cdot \chi _ { [ 0 , T ] \cap \mathcal { M } }$ , and $E [ R ( t , z ) | \mathcal { G } _ { t _ { 0 } } ] \cdot \chi _ { \lceil 0 , T \rceil \cap \mathcal { M } } , t \in [ 0 , T ] , z \in \mathbb { R } _ { 0 }$ , are Skorokhod integrable and 

(i) $D _ { t } \alpha$ and $D _ { t , z } \alpha$ are $\mathcal { G } _ { t _ { 0 } }$ -measurable for all $\alpha \in \mathcal { A } , t \in \mathcal { M }$ 

(ii) $D _ { t + } \alpha = D _ { t } \alpha$ and $D _ { t + , z } \alpha = D _ { t , z } \alpha$ for all $\alpha \in { \mathcal { A } }$ and a.a. $t , z , t \in \mathcal { M }$ 

(iii) Span A is dense in $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathcal { G } _ { t _ { 0 } } )$ 

Theorem 7.21 Suppose that $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ is smoothly anticipative. Suppose that $\widehat { u } \in { \mathcal { A } } _ { \mathbb { G } }$ is a critical point of $J ( u )$ . Then for all $h ( t ) = \chi _ { [ t _ { 0 } , s ) } ( t ) \chi _ { \mathcal { M } } ( t ) , t \in [ 0 , T ]$ (and some $s \in [ 0 , T ] )$ ), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ L (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) \delta B _ {t} \\ \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} E \big [ R (t, z) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) \widetilde {N} (\delta t, d z) \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \bigg ]. \end{array}\tag{7.46}
$$

Proof By Theorem 7.14 we know that, for every t, 

$$
E \left[ L (t) \alpha + M (t) D _ {t +} \alpha + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} R (t, z) D _ {t +, z} \alpha v (d z) \right] = 0.
$$

Let $\alpha = E [ F | \mathcal { G } _ { t _ { 0 } } ]$ for all $F \in { \mathcal { A } }$ . Further, choose $h \in L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , T ] )$ with $h ( t ) =$ $\chi _ { [ t _ { 0 } , s ) } ( t ) \chi _ { \mathcal { M } } ( t )$ . By assumption, we see that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = \bigg \langle \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ L (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) d t, \alpha \bigg \rangle + \bigg \langle E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) \delta B _ {t} \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \bigg ], \alpha \bigg \rangle \\ \qquad + \bigg \langle E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} R (t, z) h (t) \widetilde {N} (\delta t, d z) \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \bigg ], \alpha \bigg \rangle . \end{array}
$$

On the other hand, the duality relation (7.11) and (ii) imply that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left\langle E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) \delta B _ {t} \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right], \alpha \right\rangle = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) \delta B _ {t} E [ F | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ] \right] \\ \qquad = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} M (t) h (t) \big (D _ {t} E [ F | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ] \big) d t \right] \\ \qquad = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) \big (D _ {t} E [ F | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ] \big) d t \right] \\ \qquad = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) \delta B _ {t} E [ F | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} ] \right] \\ \qquad = \left\langle \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) \delta B _ {t}, \alpha \right\rangle . \end{array}
$$

In the same way, we show that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left\langle E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} R (t, z) h (t) \widetilde {N} (\delta t, d z) \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \bigg ], \alpha \right\rangle \\ = \bigg \langle \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} E \big [ R (t, z) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] h (t) \widetilde {N} (\delta t, d z), \alpha \bigg \rangle . \end{array}
$$

Then it follows from (iv) that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \left[ L (t) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right] h (t) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \left[ M (t) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right] h (t) \delta B _ {t} \right. \\ \left. + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} E \left[ R (t, z) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right] h (t) \widetilde {N} (\delta t, d z) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right] \end{array}
$$

for all $h \in L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , T ] )$ with supp $h \subseteq ( t _ { 0 } , T ]$ 

Theorem 7.22 (Brownian motion case) Assume that the conditions in Theorem 7.21 are in force and $\theta = 0$ . In addition, we require that $E [ M ( t ) | \mathcal { G } _ { t ^ { - } } ] \in \mathbb { M } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B }$ and is forward integrable with respect to $E [ d ^ { - } B ( t ) | \mathcal { G } _ { t ^ { - } } ]$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ L (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \big ] h _ {0} (t) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {T} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \big ] h _ {0} (t) E \big [ d ^ {-} B \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \big ] \\ - \int_ {0} ^ {T} D _ {t ^ {+}} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \big ] h _ {0} (t) d t \end{array}\tag{7.47}
$$

for all bounded deterministicfunctions $h _ { 0 } ( t ) , t \in [ 0 , T ]$ 

Proof We apply the preceding result to $h ( t ) = h _ { 0 } ( t ) \chi _ { [ t _ { i } , t _ { i + 1 } ] } ( t )$ , where $0 = t _ { 0 } < t _ { 1 } <$ $\cdot \cdot \cdot < t _ { i } < t _ { i + 1 } = T$ is a partition of [0, T]. From (7.46) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = \int_ {t _ {i}} ^ {t _ {i + 1}} E \big [ L (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {i}} \big ] h (t) d t + E \bigg [ \int_ {t _ {i}} ^ {t _ {i + 1}} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {i}} \big ] h (t) \delta B _ {t} \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {i}} \bigg ] \\ \qquad + E \bigg [ \int_ {t _ {i}} ^ {t _ {i + 1}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} E \big [ R (t, z) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {i}} \big ] h (t) \widetilde {N} (\delta t, d z) \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {i}} \bigg ]. \end{array}\tag{7.48}
$$

By Lemma 7.4 and by assumption, we know that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {t _ {i}} ^ {t _ {i + 1}} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {i}} \big ] h _ {0} (t) \delta B _ {t} = \int_ {t _ {i}} ^ {t _ {i + 1}} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {i}} \big ] h _ {0} (t) d ^ {-} B (t) \\ - \int_ {t _ {i}} ^ {t _ {i + 1}} D _ {t ^ {+}} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {i}} \big ] h _ {0} (t) d t. \end{array}\tag{7.49}
$$

Substituting (7.49) into (7.48), summing over all i, and taking the limit as $\varDelta t _ { i } \to 0$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} 0 = \lim_{\substack{\Delta t_{i}\to 0\\ n\to \infty}}\Bigg\{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{i + 1}}E\big[L(t)\big|\mathcal{G}_{t_{i}}\big]h_{0}(t)  dt \\ & +\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{i + 1}}E\big[M(t)\big|\mathcal{G}_{t_{i}}\big]h_{0}(t)\frac{E[B(t_{i + 1}) - B(t_{i})|\mathcal{G}_{t_{i}}]}{\Delta t_{i}}\Delta t_{i}\\ & -\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{i + 1}}D_{t^{+}}E\big[M(t)\big|\mathcal{G}_{t_{i}}\big]h_{0}(t)  dt\Bigg\} \end{aligned}
$$

in the topology of uniform convergence in probability. Hence, by Definition 7.7, we get the result. - 

Important examples of filtrations satisfying the conditions of Theorem 7.21 are based on σ-algebras that are first chaos generated (see [19]). Namely, we consider σ-algebras of the form 

$$
\sigma \left(I _ {1} (h _ {i}), i \in \mathbb {N}, h _ {i} \in L ^ {2} ([ 0, T ])\right) \vee \mathcal {N},\tag{7.50}
$$

where $\mathcal { N }$ is the collection of P-null sets. A concrete example of these σ-algebras is 

$$
\mathcal {G} _ {t} ^ {3} = \mathcal {F} _ {t} \vee \sigma (B (T)).\tag{7.51}
$$

We study the case (7.51). 

Lemma 7.23 Suppose that $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \mathcal { G } _ { t } ^ { 3 } = \mathcal { F } _ { t } \vee \sigma ( B ( T ) )$ . Then 

$$
E \left[ B (t) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right] = \frac {T - t}{T - t _ {0}} B \left(t _ {0}\right) + \frac {t - t _ {0}}{T - t _ {0}} B (T) \quad f o r a l l t > t _ {0}.
$$

In particular, 

$$
E \left[ B (t + \varepsilon) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] = B (t) + \frac {\varepsilon}{T - t} \bigl (B (T) - B (t) \bigr).
$$

Proof We have that 

$$
E \left[ B (t) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \right] = \int_ {0} ^ {t _ {0}} \varphi (t, s) d B (s) + C (t) B (T).
$$

On one hand, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} t = E \Big [ E \Big [ B (t) \Big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \Big ] B (T) \Big ] = E \Bigg [ \left(\int_ {0} ^ {t _ {0}} \varphi (t, s) d B (s)\right) B (T) \Bigg ] + C (t) T \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {t _ {0}} \varphi (t, s) d s + C (t) T. \end{array}\tag{7.52}
$$

On the other hand, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} u = E \Big [ E \big [ B (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t _ {0}} \big ] B (u) \Big ] = E \Bigg [ \left(\int_ {0} ^ {t _ {0}} \varphi (t, s)   d B (s)\right) B (u) \Bigg ] + C (t) u \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {u} \varphi (t, s)   d s + C (t) u \quad \text { for   all } u <   t. \end{array}\tag{7.53}
$$

Differentiating (7.53) with respect to u, it follows that 

$$
\varphi (t, u) + C (t) = 1.
$$

Substituting $\varphi$ by its value into (7.52), we obtain $\begin{array} { r } { C ( t ) = \frac { t - t _ { 0 } } { T - t _ { 0 } } } \end{array}$ and then $\varphi ( t , s ) =$ $\frac { T - t _ { 0 } } { T - t _ { 0 } }$ . Therefore, the result follows. - 

Corollary 7.24 Suppose that $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \mathcal { G } _ { t } ^ { 3 } = \mathcal { F } _ { t } \vee \sigma ( B ( T ) )$ ). Then 

$$
E \big [ d ^ {-} B \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \big ] = \frac {B (T) - B (t)}{T - t} d t.
$$

Combining this with Theorem 7.22, we get the following: 

Theorem 7.25 Suppose that $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \mathcal { G } _ { t } ^ { 3 } = \mathcal { F } _ { t } \vee \sigma ( B ( T ) )$ and $\theta = 0$ . Suppose that the conditions of Theorem 7.22 hold. Then $u = \widehat { u }$ is a critical point for $J ( u )$ in (7.3) if and only if 

$$
E \big [ L (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \big ] + E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \big ] \frac {B (T) - B (t)}{T - t} - D _ {t ^ {+}} E \big [ M (t) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \big ] = 0
$$

for a.a. $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ 

(7.54) 

## 7.6 Application to Optimal Insider Portfolio

Consider a financial market with two investments possibilities: 

1. A risk-free asset, where the unit price $S _ { 0 } ( t )$ at time t is given by 

$$
d S _ {0} (t) = r (t) S _ {0} (t) d t, \qquad S _ {0} (0) = 1.\tag{7.55}
$$

2. A risky asset, where the unit price $S _ { 1 } ( t )$ at time t is given by the stochastic differential equation 

$$
d S _ {1} (t) = S _ {1} \left(t ^ {-}\right) \left[ \mu (t) d t + \sigma_ {0} (t) d B ^ {-} (t) + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \gamma (t, z) \widetilde {N} \left(d ^ {-} t, d z\right) \right],\tag{7.56}
$$

$$
S _ {1} (0) > 0.
$$

Here $r ( t ) \geq 0 , \mu ( t ) , \sigma _ { 0 } ( t )$ , and $\gamma ( t , z ) \geq - 1 + \epsilon$ (for some constant $\epsilon > 0 )$ are given G-predictable, forward-integrable processes, where $\mathbb { G } = \{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ is a given filtration such that 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {t} \subset \mathcal {G} _ {t} \quad \text { for   all } t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{7.57}
$$

Suppose that a trader in this market is an insider, in the sense that she has access to the information represented by $\mathcal { G } _ { t }$ at time t. This means that if she chooses a portfolio $u ( t )$ , representing the amount she invests in the risky asset at time t, then this portfolio is a G-predictable stochastic process. 

The corresponding wealth process $X ( t ) = X ^ { ( u ) } ( t )$ will then satisfy the (forward) SDE 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d ^ {-} X (t) = \frac {X (t) - u (t)}{S _ {0} (t)} d S _ {0} (t) + \frac {u (t)}{S _ {1} (t)} d ^ {-} S _ {1} (t) \\ \qquad = X (t) r (t) d t + u (t) \bigg [ (\mu (t) - r (t)) d t + \sigma_ {0} (t) d B ^ {-} (t) \\ \qquad + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \gamma (t, z) \widetilde {N} \big (d ^ {-} t, d z \big) \bigg ], \quad t \in [ 0, T ], \end{array}\tag{7.58}
$$

$$
X (0) = x > 0.\tag{7.59}
$$

By choosing $S _ { 0 } ( \cdot )$ as a numeraire, we can, without loss of generality, assume that 

$$
r (t) = 0\tag{7.60}
$$

from now on. Then (7.58) and (7.59) simplify to 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} d ^ {-} X (t) = u (t) [ \mu (t)   d t + \sigma_ {0} (t)   d B ^ {-} (t) + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \gamma (t, z) \widetilde {N} (d ^ {-} t, d z) ], \\ X (0) = x > 0. \end{array} \right.\tag{7.61}
$$

This is a controlled Itô–Lévy process of the type discussed in Sect. 7.4, and we can apply the results of that section to the problem of the insider to maximize the expected utility of the terminal wealth, i.e., to find $\phi _ { \mathbb { G } } ( x )$ and $u ^ { * } \in \mathcal { A } _ { \mathbb { G } }$ such that 

$$
\Phi_ {\mathbb {G}} (x) = \sup _ {u \in \mathcal {A} _ {\mathbb {G}}} E \big [ U \big (X ^ {(u)} (T) \big) \big ] = E \big [ U \big (X ^ {(u ^ {*})} (T) \big) \big ],\tag{7.62}
$$

where $U : \mathbb { R } _ { + } \to \mathbb { R }$ is a given utility function, assumed to be concave, strictly increasing, and $C ^ { 1 }$ . In this case, the processes $K ( t ) , L ( t ) , M ( t )$ , and $R ( t , z )$ , given respectively by (7.26), (7.39), (7.40), and (7.41), take the form 

$$
K (t) = U ^ {\prime} \bigl (X (T) \bigr),\tag{7.63}
$$

$$
L (t) = U ^ {\prime} \bigl (X (T) \bigr) \biggl [ \mu (t) + D _ {t +} \sigma_ {0} (t) + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t +, z} \gamma (t, z) \nu (d z) \biggr ]
$$

$$
+ \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t, z} U ^ {\prime} \big (X (T) \big) \big [ \gamma (t, z) + D _ {t +, z} \gamma (t, z) \big ] \nu (d z)
$$

$$
+ D _ {t} U ^ {\prime} \big (X (T) \big) \sigma_ {0} (t),\tag{7.64}
$$

$$
M (t) = U ^ {\prime} \bigl (X (T) \bigr) \sigma_ {0} (t),\tag{7.65}
$$

$$
R (t, z) = \left\{U ^ {\prime} (X (T)) + D _ {t, z} U ^ {\prime} (X (T)) \right\} \left\{\gamma (t, z) + D _ {t +, z} \gamma (t, z) \right\}.\tag{7.66}
$$

## 7.6.1 Case $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \mathcal { F } _ { G _ { t } } , G _ { t } \supset [ \mathbf { 0 } , t ] .$ . See (7.45)

In this case, $\mathcal { G } _ { t }$ satisfies conditions (7.42) and (7.43). Therefore, Theorem 7.18 of Sect. 7.4 gives the following: 

Theorem 7.26 Suppose that $P \{ \lambda \{ t \in [ 0 , T ] ; \sigma _ { 0 } ( t ) \neq 0 \} > 0 \} > 0$ , where λ denotes the Lebesgue measure on R and that $\mathcal { G } _ { t }$ is given by (7.45). Then, there does not exist an optimal portfolio $u ^ { * } \in { \mathcal { A } } _ { \mathbb { G } }$ for the insider’s portfolio problem (7.62). 

Proof Suppose that an optimal portfolio exists. Then we have seen that in either case, the conclusion is that 

$$
E \left[ L (t) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] = E \left[ M (t) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] = E \left[ R (t, z) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] = 0
$$

for a.a. $t \in [ 0 , T ] , z \in \mathbb { R } _ { 0 }$ . In particular, 

$$
E \left[ M (t) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] = E \left[ U ^ {\prime} (X (T)) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] \sigma_ {0} (t) = 0 \quad \text { for   a.a. } t \in [ 0, T ].
$$

Since $U ^ { \prime } > 0$ , this contradicts our assumption about U. Hence, an optimal portfolio cannot exist. - 

Remark 7.27 In the case that $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \mathcal { G } _ { t } ^ { i } , i = 1 \mathrm { o r } i = 3$ , it is known that $B ( \cdot )$ is not a semimartingale with respect to $\mathbb { G } = \{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ , and hence an optimal portfolio cannot exist, by Theorem 3.8 in [3] and Theorem 15 in [7]. It follows that $S _ { 1 } ( \cdot )$ is not a G-semimartingale either, and hence we can even deduce that the market has an arbitrage for the insider in this case, by Theorem 7.2 in [5]. 

## 7.6.2 Case $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \mathcal { F } _ { t } \vee \sigma ( B ( T ) )$ . See (7.51)

In this case, $\mathcal { G } _ { t }$ is not D-commutable (see Remark 7.19). Therefore we apply results from Sect. 7.5.2. We have seen that 

$$
E \left[ d ^ {-} B \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \right] = \frac {B (T) - B (t)}{T - t} d t
$$

(Corollary 7.24). From this we have the following: 

Theorem 7.28 Assume that $\mu ( t ) = \mu _ { 0 } , \sigma _ { 0 } ( t ) = \sigma _ { 0 }$ , and $\gamma ( t , z ) = 0$ and that conditions in Theorem 7.21 hold. In addition, suppose that 

1. $E [ M ( t ) | \mathcal { G } _ { t ^ { - } } ] \in \mathbb { M } _ { 1 , 2 } ^ { B } .$ 

2. $\begin{array} { r } { \varinjlim _ { t \uparrow T } E [ | D _ { t ^ { + } } E [ M ( t ) | \mathcal { G } _ { t ^ { - } } ] | ] < \infty , } \end{array}$ 

3. $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t \uparrow T } E [ | L ( t ) | ] < \infty . } \end{array}$ 

Then, there does not exist a critical point of the performance functional $J ( u )$ in (7.3). 

Proof Assume that there is a critical point of the performance functional $J ( u )$ in (7.3). It follows from Theorems 7.14, 7.21, and 7.22 that (7.47) holds. Replacing $K ( t ) , L ( t )$ , and $M ( t )$ by their given expressions in (7.63), (7.64), and (7.65), (7.47) becomes 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 = E \left[ \mu_ {0} U ^ {\prime} (X (T)) + \sigma_ {0} D _ {t} U ^ {\prime} (X (T)) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \right] + E \left[ U ^ {\prime} (X (T)) \sigma_ {0} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \right] \frac {B (T) - B (t)}{T - t} \\ - D _ {t ^ {+}} E \left[ \sigma_ {0} U ^ {\prime} (X (T)) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t ^ {-}} \right] \quad \text { for   a.a. } t. \end{array} \tag {7.67}
$$

Taking the limit as $t \uparrow T$ , the second term in (7.67) goes to $\infty$ . Therefore, there is no critical point for the performance functional J(u) in (7.3). - 

Remark 7.29 This result is a generalization of a result in [14], where the same conclusion was obtained in the special case where 

$$
U (x) = \ln (x).
$$

## 7.7 Application to Optimal Insider Consumption

Suppose that we have a cash flow $X ( t ) = X ^ { ( u ) } ( t )$ given by 

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} d X (t) = (\mu (t) - u (t))   d t + \sigma (t)   d ^ {-} B (t) + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \theta (t, z) \widetilde {N} (d ^ {-} t, d z), \\ X (0) = x \in \mathbb {R}. \end{array} \right.\tag{7.68}
$$

Here $\mu ( t ) , \sigma ( t )$ , and $\theta ( t , z )$ are given G-predictable processes, and $u ( t ) \geq 0$ is our consumption rate, assumed to be adapted to a given insider filtration $\mathbb { G } = \{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ where $\mathcal { F } _ { t } \subset \mathcal { G } _ { t }$ for all t. Let $f ( t , u , \omega ) ; t \in [ 0 , T ] , u \in \mathbb { R } , \omega \in \Omega$ , be a given ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { T } .$ measurable utility process. Assume that $u  f ( t , u , \omega )$ is strictly increasing, concave, and $C ^ { 1 }$ for a.a. (t, ω). 

Let $g ( x , \omega ) ; x \in \mathbb { R } , \omega \in \varOmega$ , be a given $\mathcal { F } _ { T } \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e }$ e random variable for each x. Assume that $x \to g ( x , \omega )$ is concave for a.a. ω. Define the performance functional J by 

$$
J (u) = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T} f (t, u (t), \omega) d t + g (X ^ {(u)} (T), \omega) \right]; \quad u \in \mathcal {A} _ {\mathbb {G}}, u \geq 0.\tag{7.69}
$$

Note that $u  J ( u )$ is concave, so $u = \widehat { u }$ maximizes $J ( u )$ if and only if $\widehat { u }$ is a critical point of $J ( u )$ 

Theorem 7.30 (Optimal insider consumption I) $\widehat { u }$ is an optimal insider consumption ratefor the performancefunctional J in (7.69) ifand only if 

$$
E \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial u} f (t, \widehat {u} (t), \omega) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] = E \left[ g ^ {\prime} \left(X ^ {(\widehat {u})} (T), \omega\right) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right].\tag{7.70}
$$

Proof In this case, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} K (t) = g ^ {\prime} \bigl (X ^ {(u)} (T) \bigr), \\ L (t) = - g ^ {\prime} \bigl (X ^ {(u)} (T) \bigr) + \frac {\partial}{\partial u} f \bigl (t, \widehat {u} (t) \bigr), \\ M (t) = R (t, z) = 0. \end{array}
$$

Therefore, Theorem 7.14 gives $\widehat { u }$ is a critical point for $J ( u )$ if and only if 

$$
0 = E \left[ L (t) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] = E \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial u} f (t, \widehat {u} (t)) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] + E \left[ - g ^ {\prime} \left(X ^ {(\widehat {u})} (T)\right) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right].
$$

Since $X ^ { ( \widehat { u } ) } ( T )$ depends on $\widehat { u } , ( 7 . 7 0 )$ does not give the value of $\widehat { u } ( t )$ directly. However, in some special cases, $\widehat { u }$ can be found explicitly: 

Corollary 7.31 (Optimal insider consumption II) Assume that 

$$
g (x, \omega) = \lambda (\omega) x\tag{7.71}
$$

for some $\mathcal { G } _ { T }$ -measurable random variable $\lambda > 0$ 

Then the optimal consumption rate $\widehat { \boldsymbol { u } } ( t )$ is given by 

$$
E \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial u} f (t, u, \omega) \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right] _ {u = \widehat {u} (t)} = E [ \lambda | \mathcal {G} _ {t} ].\tag{7.72}
$$

Thus, we see that an optimal consumption rate exists for any given insider information filtration $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { 0 \leq t \leq T }$ . It is not necessary to be in a semimartingale setting. 

Another example in the same direction is the following: 

Theorem 7.32 (Complete future information) Suppose that we have complete future information, i.e., 

$$
\mathcal {G} _ {t} = \mathcal {F} _ {T} \quad f o r a l l t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{7.73}
$$

Suppose that we have the exponential utilities, $i . e .$ ., 

$$
f (t, u, \omega) = - K _ {1} (t, \omega) e ^ {- \alpha u}, \qquad g (x, \omega) = - K _ {2} (\omega) e ^ {- \alpha x}\tag{7.74}
$$

$f o r$ some measurable process $K _ { 1 } ( t , \omega ) > 0$ , some $\mathcal { F } _ { T }$ -measurable random variable $K _ { 2 } ( \omega ) > 0$ , and some constant $\alpha > 0$ 

Then the optimal consumptions rate $\widehat { \boldsymbol { u } } ( t )$ , if it exists, satisfies the equation 

$$
\widehat {u} (t) = \frac {1}{\alpha} \ln \left(\frac {K _ {1} (t)}{K _ {2}}\right) + X ^ {(0)} (T) - \int_ {0} ^ {T} \widehat {u} (s) d s,\tag{7.75}
$$

where 

$$
X ^ {(0)} (T) = x + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \mu (s) d s + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \sigma (s) d B (s) + \int_ {0} ^ {T} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \theta (s, z) \widetilde {N} (d s, d z)
$$

is the terminal wealth when there is no consumption. 

In particular, if $K _ { 1 } ( t ) = K _ { 1 }$ does not depend on t, then ${ \widehat { u } } ( t ) = { \widehat { u } }$ does not depend on t, and we get 

$$
\widehat {u} (t) = \widehat {u} = \frac {1}{1 + T} \left(\frac {1}{\alpha} \ln \left(\frac {K _ {1}}{K _ {2}}\right) + X ^ {(0)} (T)\right); \quad t \in [ 0, T ].\tag{7.76}
$$

Proof By (7.70) we get 

$$
- \alpha K _ {1} (t) e ^ {- \alpha \widehat {u} (t)} = - \alpha K _ {2} e ^ {- \alpha X (T)}
$$

or 

$$
\widehat {u} (t) = \frac {1}{\alpha} \ln \left(\frac {K _ {1} (t)}{K _ {2}}\right) + X (T) = \widehat {u} (t) = \frac {1}{\alpha} \ln \left(\frac {K _ {1} (t)}{K _ {2}}\right) + X ^ {(0)} (T) - \int_ {0} ^ {T} \widehat {u} (s) d s,
$$

which proves (7.75.) If $K _ { 1 } ( t ) = K _ { 1 }$ does not depend on t, then by (7.75), ${ \widehat { u } } ( t ) = u ( t )$ does not depend on t either, and (7.76) follows. - 

For related results (based on a different method) on optimal insider consumption, see [22].

Note that by the definition of Y with $Y ( s ) = Y ^ { ( \beta _ { \alpha } ) } ( s )$ and $s \geq t + h$ , the process $Y ( s )$ follows the dynamics 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d Y (s) = Y \big (s ^ {-} \big) \bigg [ \frac {\partial b}{\partial x} (s)   d s + \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial x} (s)   d ^ {-} B (s) \\ + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial x} (s, z) \widetilde {N} \big (d z, d ^ {-} s \big) \bigg ] \end{array}\tag{7.81}

for $s \geq t + h$ with initial condition $Y ( t + h )$ at time $t + h$ . By Itô’s formula for forward integral, this equation can be solved explicitly, and we get 

$$
Y (s) = Y (t + h) G (t + h, s), \quad s \geq t + h,\tag{7.82}

where, in general, for $s \geq t$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} G (t, s) := \exp \biggl (\int_ {t} ^ {s} \biggl \{\frac {\partial b}{\partial x} \bigl (r, X (r), u (r), \omega \bigr) - \frac {1}{2} \biggl (\frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial x} \biggr) ^ {2} \bigl (r, X (r), u (r), \omega \bigr) \biggr \} d r \\ \qquad + \int_ {t} ^ {s} \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial x} \bigl (r, X (r), u (r), \omega \bigr) d B ^ {-} (r) \\ \qquad + \int_ {t} ^ {s} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \biggl \{\ln \biggl (1 + \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial x} \bigl (r, X (r), u (r), \omega \bigr) \biggr) \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} - \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial x} (r, X (r), u (r), \omega) \Big \} v (d z) d t \\ + \int_ {t} ^ {s} \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \left\{\ln \left(1 + \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial x} (r, X (r ^ {-}), u (r ^ {-}), \omega)\right) \right\} \widetilde {N} (d z, d ^ {-} r) \Big). \end{array}
$$

Note that $G ( t , s )$ does not depend on h, but $Y ( s )$ does. Defining $H _ { 0 }$ as in (7.27), it follows that 

$$
A _ {1} = E \biggl [ \int_ {t} ^ {T} \frac {\partial H _ {0}}{\partial x} (s) Y (s) d s \biggr ].

Differentiating with respect to $h$ at $h = 0$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \frac {d}{d h} A _ {1} \bigg | _ {h = 0} = \frac {d}{d h} E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} \frac {\partial H _ {0}}{\partial x} (s) Y (s) d s \right] _ {h = 0} \\ + \frac {d}{d h} E \left[ \int_ {t + h} ^ {T} \frac {\partial H _ {0}}{\partial x} (s) Y (s) d s \right] _ {h = 0}. \end{array}
$$

Since $Y ( t ) = 0$ , we see that 

$$
\frac {d}{d h} E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} \frac {\partial H _ {0}}{\partial x} (s) Y (s) d s \right] _ {h = 0} = 0.
$$

Therefore, by (7.82), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d h} A _ {1} \bigg | _ {h = 0} = \frac {d}{d h} E \bigg [ \int_ {t + h} ^ {T} \frac {\partial H _ {0}}{\partial x} (s) Y (t + h) G (t + h, s) d s \bigg ] _ {h = 0} \\ \qquad = \int_ {t} ^ {T} \frac {d}{d h} E \bigg [ \frac {\partial H _ {0}}{\partial x} (s) Y (t + h) G (t + h, s) \bigg ] _ {h = 0} d s \\ \qquad = \int_ {t} ^ {T} \frac {d}{d h} E \bigg [ \frac {\partial H _ {0}}{\partial x} (s) G (t, s) Y (t + h) \bigg ] _ {h = 0} d s, \end{array}
$$

where $Y ( t + h )$ is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y (t + h) = \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} Y \big (r ^ {-} \big) \bigg [ \frac {\partial b}{\partial x} (r) d r + \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial x} (r) d ^ {-} B (r) \\ \qquad + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial x} (r, z) \widetilde {N} \big (d z, d ^ {-} r \big) \bigg ] \\ \qquad + \alpha \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} \bigg [ \frac {\partial b}{\partial u} (r) d r + \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial u} (r) d ^ {-} B (r) + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial u} (r, z) \widetilde {N} \big (d z, d ^ {-} r \big) \bigg ]. \end{array}
$$

Therefore, by the two preceding equalities, 

$$
\left. \frac {d}{d h} A _ {1} \right| _ {h = 0} = A _ {1, 1} + A _ {1, 2},
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} A _ {1, 1} = \int_ {t} ^ {T} \frac {d}{d h} E \bigg [ \frac {\partial H _ {0}}{\partial x} (s) G (t, s) \alpha \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} \bigg \{\frac {\partial b}{\partial u} (r) d r + \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial u} (r) d ^ {-} B (r) \\ \qquad + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial u} (r, z) \widetilde {N} \big (d z, d ^ {-} r \big) \bigg \} \bigg ] _ {h = 0} d s, \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} A _ {1, 2} = \int_ {t} ^ {T} \frac {d}{d h} E \bigg [ \frac {\partial H _ {0}}{\partial x} (s) G (t, s) \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} Y \big (r ^ {-} \big) \bigg \{\frac {\partial b}{\partial x} (r)   d r + \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial x} (r)   d ^ {-} B (r) \\ \qquad + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial x} (r, z) \widetilde {N} \big (d z, d ^ {-} r \big) \bigg \} \bigg ] _ {h = 0} d s. \end{array}
$$

Applying again the duality formula, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} A _ {1, 1} = \int_ {t} ^ {T} \frac {d}{d h} E \left[ \alpha \int_ {t} ^ {t + h} \left\{\frac {\partial b}{\partial u} (r) F (t, s) + \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial u} (r) D _ {r} F (t, s) \right. \right. \\ \quad \left. + F (t, s) D _ {r ^ {+}} \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial u} (r) \right. \\ \quad \left. + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \left\{\left(\frac {\partial \theta}{\partial u} (r, z) + D _ {r ^ {+}, z} \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial u} (r, z)\right) D _ {r, z} F (t, s) \right. \right. \\ \quad \left. + D _ {r ^ {+}, z} \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial u} (r, z) F (t, s) \right\} v (d z) \Bigg \} d r \Bigg ] _ {h = 0} d s \\ = \int_ {t} ^ {T} E \left[ \alpha \left\{\left(\frac {\partial b}{\partial u} (t) + D _ {t ^ {+}} \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial u} (t) + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t ^ {+}, z} \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial u} (t, z) v (d z)\right) F (t, s) \right. \right. \\ \quad \left. + \frac {\partial \sigma}{\partial u} (t) D _ {t} F (t, s) + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} \left(\frac {\partial \theta}{\partial u} (t, z) + D _ {t ^ {+}, z} \frac {\partial \theta}{\partial u} (t, z)\right) \right. \\ \quad \left. \times D _ {t, z} F (t, s) v (d z) \right\} \Bigg ] d s, \end{array}
$$

where we have put

Since $Y ( t ) = 0$ , we see that

$$

We conclude that

\left. \frac {d}{d h} A _ {1} \right| _ {h = 0} = A _ {1, 1}.\tag{7.83}

Moreover, we see that

\begin{array}{l} \frac {d}{d h} A _ {2} \bigg | _ {h = 0} = E \bigg [ \bigg \{K (t) \bigg (\frac {\partial b (t)}{\partial u} + D _ {t +} \frac {\partial \sigma (t)}{\partial u} + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t +, z} \frac {\partial \theta (t , z)}{\partial u} \nu (d z) \bigg) \\ \qquad + \frac {\partial f (t)}{\partial u} + D _ {t} K (t) \frac {\partial \sigma (t , z)}{\partial u} \\ \qquad + \int_ {\mathbb {R} _ {0}} D _ {t, z} K (t) \bigg (\frac {\partial \theta (t , z)}{\partial u} + D _ {t +, z} \frac {\partial \theta (t , z)}{\partial u} \bigg) \nu (d z) \bigg \} \alpha \bigg ], \end{array}\tag{7.84}
