Then there exists a unique solution (Y, M) to (14.7) such that Y is a bounded process. Moreover, we havefor $0 \leq t \leq T$ the estimates 

$$
S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} \underline {{Y}} _ {t} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha e ^ {\int_ {s} ^ {t} \delta_ {r} d r} U _ {s} d s \leq Y _ {t} \leq S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} \overline {{Y}} _ {t} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha e ^ {\int_ {s} ^ {t} \delta_ {r} d r} U _ {s} d s,\tag{14.8}
$$

where 

$$
\underline {{Y}} _ {t} := - \beta e ^ {- \bar {\delta} T} \log E \big [ e ^ {- \frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {\delta T} B} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big ] \quad a n d \quad \overline {{Y}} _ {t} := E [ B | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ].\tag{14.9}
$$

Proof The existence and uniqueness of a solution with Y bounded are immediate from Theorems 2.5 and 2.6 of Morlais [12]. From the definitions of $\underline { { Y } }$ and $\overline { { Y } }$ and from Itô’s formula, it is clear that there exist $\underline { { M } }$ and $\overline { { M } }$ such that 

$$
d \underline {{Y}} _ {t} = \frac {1}{2 \beta} e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} d \langle \underline {{M}} \rangle_ {t} + d \underline {{M}} _ {t}, \qquad \underline {{Y}} _ {T} = B,\tag{14.10}
$$

$$
d \overline {{Y}} _ {t} = d \overline {{M}} _ {t}, \qquad \overline {{Y}} _ {T} = B.\tag{14.11}
$$

If we first set $Y _ { t } ^ { 1 } : = S _ { t } ^ { \delta } Y _ { t }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { M _ { t } ^ { 1 } : = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } S _ { s } ^ { \delta } d M _ { s } } \end{array}$ , then the BSDE (14.7) is transformed to 

$$
d Y _ {t} ^ {1} = - \alpha S _ {t} ^ {\delta} U _ {t} d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} d \bigl <   M ^ {1} \bigr > _ {t} + d M _ {t} ^ {1}, \qquad Y _ {T} ^ {1} = \alpha^ {\prime} S _ {T} ^ {\delta} U _ {T} ^ {\prime}.\tag{14.12}
$$

If we next put $Y _ { t } ^ { 2 } : = Y _ { t } ^ { 1 } + \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \alpha S _ { s } ^ { \delta } U _ { s }$ ds and $M ^ { 2 } : = M ^ { 1 }$ , the BSDE (14.12) becomes 

$$
d Y _ {t} ^ {2} = \frac {1}{2 \beta} S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} d \bigl \langle M ^ {2} \bigr \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t} ^ {2}, \qquad Y _ {T} ^ {2} = \alpha^ {\prime} S _ {T} ^ {\delta} U _ {T} ^ {\prime} + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {T} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} U _ {s} d s = B.\tag{14.13}
$$

Because $0 \leq S _ { t } ^ { - \delta } \leq e ^ { \bar { \delta } T }$ , we deduce by comparison of (14.10), (14.13) and (14.11) that 

$$
\underline {{Y}} _ {t} \leq Y _ {t} ^ {2} \leq \overline {{Y}} _ {t}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.
$$

Returning to $Y$ by the formula $\begin{array} { r } { Y _ { t } = S _ { t } ^ { - \delta } Y _ { t } ^ { 2 } - \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \alpha e ^ { \int _ { s } ^ { t } \delta _ { r } d r } U _ { s } d s } \end{array}$ , we conclude the proof. - 

We now apply the localisation method to get the following existence result. 

Theorem 14.4 (Existence of solution) Let us suppose that 

$$
E \left[ e ^ {\frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} B _ {-}} \right] + E [ B _ {+} ] <   \infty .\tag{14.14}
$$

Then the BSDE (14.7) admits a solution $( Y , M )$ which satisfies 

$$
S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} \underline {{Y}} _ {t} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha e ^ {\int_ {s} ^ {t} \delta_ {r} d r} U _ {s} d s \leq Y _ {t} \leq S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} \overline {{Y}} _ {t} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha e ^ {\int_ {s} ^ {t} \delta_ {r} d r} U _ {s} d s\tag{14.15}
$$

for $0 \leq t \leq T$ , with $\underline { { Y } } , \overline { { Y } }$ given in (14.9). 

Proof (1) We first assume that $U _ { T } ^ { \prime }$ and U are nonnegative; then $\underline { { Y } }$ is also nonnegative. For each $n \in \mathbb { N } ,$ , we consider $U _ { t } ^ { n } : = U _ { t } \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } U _ { s } d s \leq n \} } , \ 0 \leq t \leq T$ , and $U _ { T } ^ { \prime , n } : = U _ { T } ^ { \prime } \wedge n$ . According to Proposition 14.3, the BSDE 

$$
d Y _ {t} = \left(\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t} ^ {n}\right) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \qquad Y _ {T} = \alpha^ {\prime} U _ {T} ^ {\prime , n},
$$

admits a unique solution $( Y ^ { n } , M ^ { n } )$ such that $Y ^ { n }$ is a bounded process and, by (14.8), extended from $U _ { T } ^ { \prime , n }$ and $U ^ { n }$ to $U _ { T } ^ { \prime }$ and $U$ thanks to nonnegativity, 

$$
- \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha e ^ {\int_ {s} ^ {t} \delta_ {r} d r} U _ {s} d s \leq Y _ {t} ^ {n} \leq S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} E [ B | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ].
$$

Since $U _ { T } ^ { \prime , n } \leq U _ { T } ^ { \prime , n + 1 }$ and $U ^ { n } \leq U ^ { n + 1 }$ , the sequence $( Y ^ { n } )$ is nondecreasing by a comparison result; this can be obtained similarly as in the proof of Theorem 8 in Mania/ Schweizer [11]. For $k \in \mathbb N$ , define the stopping times 

$$
\tau_ {k} := \inf \left\{t \in [ 0, T ]: \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha e ^ {\int_ {s} ^ {t} \delta_ {r} d r} U _ {s} d s + S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} E [ B | \mathcal {F} _ {t} ] \geq k \right\} \wedge T
$$

and note that $( \tau _ { k } ) _ { k \in \mathbb { N } }$ increases to $T$ stationarily. By construction, the stopped processes $Y ^ { n ; k } : = ( Y ^ { n } ) ^ { \tau _ { k } } , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , are uniformly bounded by k. Setting $M ^ { n ; k } : = ( M ^ { n } ) ^ { \tau _ { k } }$ we have 

$$
Y _ {t} ^ {n; k} = Y _ {\tau_ {k}} ^ {n} - \int_ {t} ^ {T} \mathbf {1} _ {\{s \leq \tau_ {k} \}} \left(\delta_ {s} Y _ {s} ^ {n; k} - \alpha U _ {s} ^ {n}\right) d s - \int_ {t} ^ {T} \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \left\langle M ^ {n; k} \right\rangle_ {s} - \int_ {t} ^ {T} d M _ {s} ^ {n; k}.
$$

We now take the supremum over n and apply the monotonic stability theorem (see e.g. Lemma 3.3 in Morlais [12]) to obtain, for each k, a solution $( \dot { Y } ^ { k } , M ^ { k } )$ to the BSDE 

$$
Y _ {t} ^ {k} = \xi_ {k} - \int_ {t} ^ {\tau_ {k}} \left(\delta_ {s} Y _ {s} ^ {k} - \alpha U _ {s}\right) d s - \int_ {t} ^ {\tau_ {k}} \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \left\langle M ^ {k} \right\rangle_ {s} - \int_ {t} ^ {\tau_ {k}} d M _ {s} ^ {k} \quad \text { with } \xi_ {k} := \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} Y _ {\tau_ {k}} ^ {n}.
$$

More precisely, that result shows that as $n  \infty , M _ { T } ^ { n ; k }$ converges to $M _ { T } ^ { k }$ in $L ^ { 2 }$ so that both ${ M } _ { t } ^ { n ; k }$ and $\langle M ^ { n ; k } \rangle _ { \mathrm { i } }$ converge uniformly over $t \in [ 0 , T ]$ in probability to $\boldsymbol { M } _ { t } ^ { k }$ and $\langle M ^ { k } \rangle _ { t }$ , respectively. Moreover, we have $\tau _ { k } \leq \tau _ { k + 1 }$ by construction; hence $Y _ { t \wedge \tau _ { k } } ^ { \dot { n } ; k + 1 } = Y _ { t } ^ { n ; k }$ , and so we have the localisation property 

$$
Y _ {t \wedge \tau_ {k}} ^ {k + 1} = Y _ {t} ^ {k} \quad \text { and } \quad M _ {t \wedge \tau_ {k}} ^ {k + 1} = M _ {t} ^ {k}.
$$

So if we set $\tau _ { 0 } : = 0$ and define the processes Y and M on [0, T] by 

$$
Y _ {t} := Y _ {0} ^ {1} + \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} Y _ {t} ^ {k} \mathbf {1} _ {(\tau_ {k - 1}, \tau_ {k} ]} (t) \quad \text { and } \quad M _ {t} := \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} M _ {t} ^ {k} \mathbf {1} _ {(\tau_ {k - 1}, \tau_ {k} ]} (t),
$$

the last BSDE can be rewritten as 

$$
Y _ {t} = \xi_ {k} - \int_ {t} ^ {\tau_ {k}} (\delta_ {s} Y _ {s} - \alpha U _ {s}) d s - \int_ {t} ^ {\tau_ {k}} \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {s} - \int_ {t} ^ {\tau_ {k}} d M _ {s}.
$$

Finally we observe that $P \mathrm { - a . s . , } \tau _ { k } = T$ for k large enough. This allows us to send $k  \infty$ in the previous equation and hence to prove that $( Y , M )$ is a solution to (14.7). Inequality (14.15) is satisfied by the process Y since it holds for each $Y ^ { n }$ in view of Proposition 14.3. 

(2) If $U _ { T } ^ { \prime }$ and $U$ are not necessarily nonnegative, we use a double approximation by introducing the quantities $U _ { t } ^ { n , \bar { p } } : = U _ { t } ^ { + } \bar { \mathbf { 1 } } _ { \{ \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } | U _ { s } | d s \leq n \} } - U _ { t } ^ { - } \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } | U _ { s } | d s \leq p \} }$ and $U _ { T } ^ { \prime , n , p } : = ( U _ { T } ^ { \prime } ) ^ { + } \wedge n - ( U _ { T } ^ { \prime } ) ^ { - } \wedge p$ . Condition (14.14) is used here to extend (14.8) from the truncated to the general case and to ensure that ${ \overline { { Y } } } , \underline { { Y } }$ remain well defined. In some more detail, we define $\tau _ { k }$ (with $\displaystyle | U |$ and $| B | )$ and $Y ^ { n , p ; k }$ and $M ^ { n , p ; k }$ analogously as before. Then $Y ^ { n , p ; k }$ is increasing in n and decreasing in $p _ { : }$ , and it remains bounded by k. Arguing as before, we set $Y ^ { k } : = \operatorname* { i n f } _ { p } \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } Y ^ { n , p ; k }$ to get the existence of $M ^ { k }$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { p \to \infty } \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } M _ { s \wedge \tau _ { k } } ^ { n , p ; k } = M _ { s } ^ { k } } \end{array}$ and $( Y ^ { k } , M ^ { k } )$ ) still solves the BSDE. The rest of the proof is unchanged. - 

In connection with the stochastic control problem, it will be important to know when the stochastic exponential $\textstyle { \mathcal { E } } ( - { \frac { 1 } { \beta } } M )$ is a true martingale, where M comes from the solution of the BSDE (14.7). 

Theorem 14.5 Suppose that there exists a constant $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda > 1 + \frac { e ^ { \bar { \delta } T } - 1 } { e ^ { \bar { \delta } T } } } \end{array}$ such that 

$$
E \big [ e ^ {\lambda \frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} B _ {+}} \big ] + E \big [ e ^ {\lambda \frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} B _ {-}} \big ] <   \infty .\tag{14.16}
$$

Then the stochastic exponential $\textstyle { \mathcal { E } } ( - { \frac { 1 } { \beta } } M )$ is bounded in L log $L ( P )$ and hence a (uniformly integrable) martingale on $[ 0 , T ]$ 

Proof Since (14.16) clearly implies (14.14), the existence of a solution is ensured by Theorem 14.4. For any stopping time τ with values in $[ 0 , T ]$ , the BSDE (14.7) gives 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {E} \bigg (- \frac {1}{\beta} M \bigg) _ {\tau} = \exp \bigg (- \frac {1}{\beta} \bigg (M _ {\tau} + \frac {1}{2 \beta} \langle M \rangle_ {\tau} \bigg) \bigg) \\ = \exp \bigg (- \frac {1}{\beta} \bigg (Y _ {\tau} - Y _ {0} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {s} Y _ {s}   d s + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} U _ {s}   d s \bigg) \bigg). \end{array}
$$

Hence it suffices to prove that there exists a constant $\lambda _ { 1 } > 1$ such that 

$$
E \left[ \exp \left(- \lambda_ {1} \frac {1}{\beta} \left(Y _ {\tau} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {s} Y _ {s} d s + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} U _ {s} d s\right)\right) \right] \leq C,
$$

where $C \in ( 0 , \infty )$ is a constant independent of $\tau$ . 

From the estimate (14.15) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} Y _ {\tau} + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} U _ {s}   d s - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {t} Y _ {t}   d t \geq S _ {\tau} ^ {- \delta} \underline {{Y}} _ {\tau} + \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \alpha \big (1 - e ^ {\int_ {s} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {r}   d r} \big) U _ {s}   d s \\ - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {t} \bigg (S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} \overline {{Y}} _ {t} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha e ^ {\int_ {s} ^ {t} \delta_ {r}   d r} U _ {s}   d s \bigg) d t. \end{array}
$$

But Fubini’s theorem gives $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } \delta _ { t } \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \alpha e ^ { \int _ { s } ^ { t } \delta _ { r } d r } U _ { s } d s d t = \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } \alpha ( e ^ { \int _ { s } ^ { \tau } \delta _ { r } d r } - 1 ) U _ { s } d s , } \end{array}$ and so we deduce that 

$$
Y _ {\tau} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {s} Y _ {s} d s + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} U _ {s} d s \geq S _ {\tau} ^ {- \delta} \underline {{Y}} _ {\tau} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {t} S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} \overline {{Y}} _ {t} d t.\tag{14.17}
$$

Now pick $p > 1$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda > p > 1 + \frac { e ^ { \bar { \delta } T } - 1 } { e ^ { \bar { \delta } T } } } \end{array}$ and set $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda _ { 1 } = \frac { \lambda } { p } > 1 } \end{array}$ . Using (14.17) and (14.9) and setting $\begin{array} { r } { L _ { t } ^ { * } : = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { 0 < s < t } E [ \bar { B _ { + } } | \mathcal { F } _ { s } ] } \end{array}$ , we obtain with (14.6b) that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \bigg [ \exp \bigg (- \lambda_ {1} \frac {1}{\beta} \bigg (Y _ {\tau} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {s} Y _ {s}   d s + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} U _ {s}   d s \bigg) \bigg) \bigg ] \\ \leq E \bigg [ \exp \bigg (- \lambda_ {1} \frac {1}{\beta} \bigg (S _ {\tau} ^ {- \delta} \underline {{Y}} _ {\tau} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {t} S _ {t} ^ {- \delta} \overline {{Y}} _ {t}   d t \bigg) \bigg) \bigg ] \\ \leq E \bigg [ \exp \big (\lambda_ {1} \log E \big [ e ^ {\frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} B _ {-}} | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} ] \big) \exp \bigg (\lambda_ {1} \frac {1}{\beta} L _ {T} ^ {*} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \delta_ {t} S _ {t} ^ {- \delta}   d t \bigg) \bigg ] \\ \leq E \big [ \big (E \big [ e ^ {\frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} B _ {-}} | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} ] \big) ^ {\lambda_ {1}} e ^ {\frac {\lambda_ {1}}{\beta} (e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} - 1) L _ {T} ^ {*}} \big ]. \end{array}
$$

Finally, we set $\textstyle q : = { \frac { p } { p - 1 } }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { r : = ( p - 1 ) \frac { e ^ { \bar { \delta } T } } { e ^ { \bar { \delta } T } - 1 } > 1 } \end{array}$ and use Hölder’s inequality, $\lambda _ { 1 } p = \lambda$ , Jensen’s inequality and Doob’s inequality in $L ^ { r }$ to get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \bigg [ \exp \bigg (- \lambda_ {1} \frac {1}{\beta} \bigg (Y _ {\tau} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {s} Y _ {s}   d s + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} U _ {s}   d s \bigg) \bigg) \bigg ] \\ \leq E \big [ \big (E \big [ e ^ {\frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} B _ {-}} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \big ] \big) ^ {\lambda_ {1} p} \big ] ^ {1 / p} E \big [ e ^ {\frac {\lambda_ {1} q}{\beta} (e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} - 1) L _ {T} ^ {*}} \big ] ^ {1 / q} \\ \leq C _ {r} ^ {\prime} E \big [ e ^ {\lambda \frac {1}{\beta} e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} B _ {-}} \big ] ^ {1 / p} E \big [ e ^ {\frac {\lambda_ {1} q r}{\beta} (e ^ {\bar {\delta} T} - 1) B _ {+}} \big ] ^ {\frac {1}{q r}} = C <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

because $\lambda _ { 1 } q r ( e ^ { \bar { \delta } T } - 1 ) = \lambda e ^ { \bar { \delta } T }$ 

## 14.4 The BSDE on an Infinite Horizon

In this section, we use BSDE techniques to prove the existence and uniqueness of a solution to the infinite-horizon BSDE under suitable conditions. 

Hypothesis 14.6 Throughout this section, we impose the standing assumptions 

F is a continuousfiltration, i.e. all local (P, F)-martingales 

(14.18a) 

$$
\delta \geq 0 \text {   is   uniformly   bounded   (by   } \bar {\delta}, \text {   say) }.\tag{14.18b}
$$

Again, the assumptions on $U = ( U _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ will be specified later; $U _ { T } ^ { \prime }$ does not appear here. The BSDE (14.3) under study is now 

$$
d Y _ {t} = (\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t}) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \quad \lim _ {t \to \infty} Y _ {t} = 0 \quad P \text {-a.s.},\tag{14.19}
$$

and as before, a solution of (14.19) is a pair (Y, M) satisfying (14.19), where Y is a P-semimartingale and M is a locally P-square-integrable local P-martingale null at 0. 

The first step in tackling (14.19) is to obtain a priori estimates for the finitehorizon version with terminal condition $Y _ { T } = 0$ . But in contrast to Sect. 14.3, we now need the bounds to be uniform in T, and so we need stronger assumptions on U. 

Definition 14.7 We say that a random variable X is in $D ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ if $E [ e ^ { \lambda | X | } ] < \infty$ for all $\lambda > 0 . \mathrm { A }$ progressively measurable process $U = ( U _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ is in $\boldsymbol { D } _ { 1 , T } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ for $T \in ( 0$ , ∞] if $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } | U _ { s } | d s \ } \end{array}$ is in $D ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ , and an RCLL process $Y = ( Y _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ is in $\boldsymbol { D } _ { 0 , T } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ for $T \in ( 0 , \infty ]$ if $Y _ { T } ^ { * } : = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { 0 \leq t \leq T } | Y _ { t } |$ is in $D ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ . (By convention, $Y _ { \infty } ^ { * } : = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { t \geq 0 } | Y _ { t } | . )$ 

Let us now consider the BSDE 

$$
d Y _ {t} = (\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t}) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \quad Y _ {T} = 0.\tag{14.20}
$$

Proposition 14.8 (A priori estimates) Suppose that $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } | U _ { s } |$ ds is a bounded random variable. Then there exists a unique solution $( Y , M )$ to (14.20) such that Y is a bounded process. Moreover, we have the estimate 

$$
\left. \right.\left| Y _ {t} \right| \leq \beta \log E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {t} ^ {T} \alpha \left| U _ {s} \right| d s\right) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right], \quad 0 \leq t \leq T.\tag{14.21}
$$

Proof The existence and uniqueness of a solution with Y bounded follow as for Proposition 14.3 from Theorems 2.5 and 2.6 of Morlais [12]. Applying Tanaka’s 

formula then first yields 

$$
d \left| Y _ {t} \right| = \operatorname{sign} \left(Y _ {t}\right) d Y _ {t} + d L _ {t} = \operatorname{sign} \left(Y _ {t}\right) \left(\left(\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t}\right) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}\right) + d L _ {t},
$$

where $L$ is the local time at 0 of the continuous semimartingale Y. Next, applying $\mathrm { I t } \hat { \mathrm { o } } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s }$ formula to the bounded process $\begin{array} { r } { Z _ { t } : = \exp ( \frac { 1 } { \beta } ( | Y _ { t } | + \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \bar { \alpha } | U _ { s } | d s ) ) } \end{array}$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d Z _ {t} = \frac {1}{\beta} Z _ {t} \operatorname{sign} (Y _ {t}) \bigg ((\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t})   d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta}   d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t} \bigg) \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{\beta} Z _ {t}   d L _ {t} + \frac {1}{\beta} Z _ {t} \alpha | U _ {t} |   d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta^ {2}} Z _ {t}   d \langle M \rangle_ {t} \\ \qquad \geq \frac {1}{\beta} Z _ {t}   \operatorname{sign} (Y _ {t})   d M _ {t}, \end{array}
$$

in the sense that the difference of the terms on the two sides of the inequality is an increasing process. So $Z$ is a submartingale, which gives 

$$
\left. \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \left(| Y _ {t} | + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right)\right) \leq E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {0} ^ {T} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right] \right.
$$

since $Y _ { T } = 0$ , and (14.21) follows. 

From this a priori estimate and the localisation method we obtain the existence of a solution to the infinite-horizon BSDE (14.19). 

Theorem 14.9 (Existence of solution) Let us suppose that 

$$
E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right) \right] <   \infty , \quad i. e. \quad \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right) \in L ^ {1}.\tag{14.22}
$$

Then the BSDE (14.19) admits a solution $( Y , M )$ which satisfies 

$$
\left| Y _ {t} \right| \leq \beta \log E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \alpha \left| U _ {s} \right| d s\right) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right], \quad t \geq 0.\tag{14.23}
$$

$\begin{array} { r } { I f \exp ( { \frac { 1 } { \beta } \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } \alpha | U _ { s } | d s } ) } \end{array}$ is in $L ^ { r }$ for some $r > 1$ , then so is exp $\begin{array} { r } { ( \frac { 1 } { \beta } Y _ { \infty } ^ { * } ) } \end{array}$ . If $U \in D _ { 1 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ then $Y \in D _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ 

Proof (1) We first assume that $U$ is nonnegative and set $\begin{array} { r } { U _ { t } ^ { n } : = U _ { t } \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } U _ { s } d s \leq n \} } } \end{array}$ for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . According to Proposition 14.8, the BSDE 

$$
d Y _ {t} = \left(\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t} ^ {n}\right) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \quad Y _ {n} = 0,
$$

on $[ 0 , n ]$ admits a unique solution $( Y ^ { n } , M ^ { n } )$ with $Y ^ { n }$ bounded, and by (14.21), 

$$
\left| Y _ {t} ^ {n} \right| \leq \beta \log E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right], \quad t \in [ 0, n ].
$$

If we set $Y _ { t } ^ { n } = 0$ and $M _ { t } ^ { n } = M _ { n } ^ { n }$ for $t > n$ , then $( Y ^ { n } , M ^ { n } )$ also satisfies on $[ 0 , n + 1 ]$ the BSDE 

$$
d Y _ {t} = \left(\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha \mathbf {1} _ {\{t \leq n \}} U _ {t} ^ {n}\right) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \quad Y _ {n + 1} = 0.
$$

Because U is nonnegative, $\pmb { 1 } _ { \{ t \leq n \} } U _ { t } ^ { n } \leq U _ { t } ^ { n + 1 } \ \mathrm { f o r } t \in [ 0 , n + 1 ]$ , and so the sequence $( Y ^ { n } )$ is nondecreasing by the comparison theorem. For each $k \in \mathbb N$ , we define the stopping time 

$$
\tau_ {k} := \inf \left\{t \geq 0: \beta \log E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right] \geq k \right\} \wedge k.
$$

Introducing the stopped processes $Y ^ { n ; k } : = ( Y ^ { n } ) ^ { \tau _ { k } }$ and $M ^ { n ; k } : = ( M ^ { n } ) ^ { \tau _ { k } }$ , we can argue exactly as in the proof of Theorem 14.4 to construct processes Y and M, now on $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ , satisfying for each T the BSDE 

$$
Y _ {t} = Y _ {T} - \int_ {t} ^ {T} (\delta_ {s} Y _ {s} - \alpha U _ {s}) d s - \int_ {t} ^ {T} \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {s} - \int_ {t} ^ {T} d M _ {s}.
$$

Since each $Y ^ { n }$ satisfies estimate (14.23) by Proposition 14.8, it follows from the construction that so does Y, and this implies, due to (14.22), that 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} Y _ {t} = 0 \quad P \text {-a.s.}
$$

(2) In the general case where U need not be nonnegative, we use the double approximation $\begin{array} { r } { U _ { t } ^ { n , p } : = U _ { t } ^ { + } \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } | U _ { s } | d s \leq n \} } \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ t \leq n \} } - U _ { t } ^ { - } \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } | U _ { s } | d s \leq p \} } \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ t \leq p \} } , t \geq 0 } \end{array}$ , and denote by $( Y ^ { n , p } , M ^ { n , p } )$ the solution to 

$$
d Y _ {t} = \left(\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t} ^ {n, p}\right) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \quad Y _ {n \vee p} = 0.
$$

Then the proof goes like for Theorem 14.4, using that $Y ^ { n , p }$ increases in n and decreases in $p .$ 

(3) The integrability assertions about Y follow from (14.23) and Doob’s inequality. - 

To get a uniqueness result for the infinite-horizon BSDE (14.19), we need a stronger assumption. 

Theorem 14.10 (Uniqueness of solution) Suppose that U is in $D _ { 1 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ . Then the BSDE (14.19) admits a unique solution $( Y , M )$ with $Y \in D _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ 

Proof The existence is clear from Theorem 14.9. For uniqueness, let $( Y , M )$ and $( Y ^ { \prime } , M ^ { \prime } )$ be two such solutions and note that the martingale part is always unique by the uniqueness of the canonical decomposition of a special semimartingale. Fix $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ and set $\hat { Y } : = Y - \theta Y ^ { \prime }$ and $\hat { M } : = M - \theta M ^ { \prime }$ . Then 

$$
d \hat {Y} _ {t} = (\delta_ {t} \hat {Y} _ {t} - \alpha (1 - \theta) U _ {t}) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d (\langle M \rangle_ {t} - \theta \langle M ^ {\prime} \rangle_ {t}) + d \hat {M} _ {t}.\tag{14.24}
$$

Noting that convexity gives 

$$
d \langle M \rangle_ {t} = d \left\langle \theta M ^ {\prime} + (1 - \theta) \frac {\hat {M}}{1 - \theta} \right\rangle_ {t} \leq \theta d \langle M ^ {\prime} \rangle_ {t} + \frac {1}{1 - \theta} d \langle \hat {M} \rangle_ {t},\tag{14.25}
$$

we rewrite (14.24) as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d \hat {Y} _ {t} = \left(\delta_ {t} \hat {Y} _ {t} - \alpha (1 - \theta) U _ {t}\right) d t + d \hat {M} _ {t} \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \bigg (\langle M \rangle_ {t} - \theta \langle M ^ {\prime} \rangle_ {t} - \frac {1}{1 - \theta} \langle \hat {M} \rangle_ {t} \bigg) + \frac {1}{2 \beta (1 - \theta)} d \langle \hat {M} \rangle_ {t}. \end{array}\tag{14.26}
$$

Now Tanaka’s formula yields $\begin{array} { r } { d \hat { Y } _ { t } ^ { - } = - \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ \hat { Y } _ { t } \leq 0 \} } d \hat { Y } _ { t } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } d \hat { L } _ { t } } \end{array}$ , where $\hat { L }$ is the local time at 0 of the process $\hat { Y }$ . Applying next Itô’s formula to the process 

$$
Z _ {t} := \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta (1 - \theta)} \left(\hat {Y} _ {t} ^ {-} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \alpha (1 - \theta) | U _ {s} | d s\right)\right), \quad t \geq 0,
$$

we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d Z _ {t} = \frac {1}{\beta (1 - \theta)} Z _ {t} \bigg (- \mathbf {1} _ {\{\hat {Y} _ {t} \leq 0 \}} d \hat {Y} _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} d \hat {L} _ {t} + \alpha (1 - \theta) | U _ {t} | d t \bigg) \\ \quad + \frac {1}{2 \beta^ {2} (1 - \theta) ^ {2}} Z _ {t} \mathbf {1} _ {\{\hat {Y} _ {t} \leq 0 \}} d \langle \hat {M} \rangle_ {t} \\ \geq - \frac {1}{\beta (1 - \theta)} Z _ {t} \mathbf {1} _ {\{\hat {Y} _ {t} \leq 0 \}} d \hat {M} _ {t}, \end{array}
$$

where the last inequality uses (14.26) and (14.25). Thus $Z$ is a local submartingale, and so there exists an increasing sequence of stopping times $\tau _ { n } ~ \nearrow$ ∞ such that 

$$
\left. \right. \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta (1 - \theta)} \hat {Y} _ {t \wedge \tau_ {n}} ^ {-}\right) \leq E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta (1 - \theta)} \hat {Y} _ {T \wedge \tau_ {n}} ^ {-} + \frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {t \wedge \tau_ {n}} ^ {T \wedge \tau_ {n}} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right].
$$

Because $\hat { Y } \in D _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } } , U \in D _ { 1 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t \to \infty } \hat { Y } _ { t } = 0 } \end{array}$ , we obtain for $n  \infty$ and $T \to \infty$ that 

$$
\exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta (1 - \theta)} \hat {Y} _ {t} ^ {-}\right) \leq E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right],
$$

which is equivalent to 

$$
\left. \right.\left(Y _ {t} - \theta Y _ {t} ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {-} = \hat {Y} _ {t} ^ {-} \leq \beta (1 - \theta) \log E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right].
$$

Letting $\theta  1$ , we deduce that $Y _ { t } \geq Y _ { t } ^ { \prime }$ , and since a symmetrical argument gives the reverse inequality, the proof is complete. - 

As in Sect. 14.3, we again want to know when the stochastic exponential $\textstyle { \mathcal { E } } ( - { \frac { 1 } { \beta } } M )$ is a true martingale, where M now comes from the solution of the BSDE (14.19). However, we only expect to obtain this here on the open interval $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ , and the proof below shows why $T = \infty$ causes a difficulty. 

Theorem 14.11 Suppose that U is in $D _ { 1 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ and denote by $( Y , M )$ the solution to (14.19)from Theorem 14.9. Thenfor everyfinite T and every $r < \infty$ , the stochastic exponential $( \mathcal E ( - \frac { 1 } { \beta } M ) _ { t } ) _ { 0 \le t \le T }$ is bounded in $L ^ { r }$ , and so $\mathcal { E } ( - \frac { 1 } { \beta } M )$ is a martingale on $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ 

Proof Fix $T \in ( 0 , \infty )$ and let $\tau$ be a stopping time with values in $[ 0 , T ]$ . As in the proof of Theorem 14.5, the BSDE (14.19) gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {E} \bigg (- \frac {1}{\beta} M \bigg) _ {\tau} = \exp \bigg (- \frac {1}{\beta} \bigg (Y _ {\tau} - Y _ {0} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \delta_ {s} Y _ {s} d s + \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} U _ {s} d s \bigg) \bigg) \\ \qquad \leq \exp \bigg (\frac {1}{\beta} Y _ {0} \bigg) \exp \bigg (\frac {1}{\beta} Y _ {T} ^ {*} (1 + \bar {\delta} T) + \frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s \bigg), \end{array}
$$

and the conclusion follows from Theorem 14.9 because $Y \in D _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ 

## 14.5 The Stochastic Control Problem on an Infinite Horizon

In this section, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a solution to the infinitehorizon stochastic control problem. 

Let us first give a precise formulation. We recall from Sect. 14.2 the underlying filtered probability space $( \varOmega , \mathcal { F } , \mathbb { F } , P )$ with $\mathbb { F } = ( \mathcal { F } _ { t } ) _ { 0 \leq t \leq \infty }$ , the parameters $\alpha \ge 0$ $\beta > 0$ and the processes $\delta = ( \delta _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ and $U = ( U _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ . We denote by $\mathcal { Q }$ the set of all probability measures $Q { \stackrel { \mathrm { l o c } } { \ll } } P$ and by $Z ^ { Q } = ( Z _ { t } ^ { Q } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ an RCLL version of the density process of $Q$ with respect to $P$ . Since $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ is trivial, we have 

$$
\left\{Z ^ {\mathcal {Q}} \mid \mathcal {Q} \in \mathcal {Q} \right\}
$$

<sub>⊆</sub> <sub>all RCLL P-martingales</sub> $Z = ( Z _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ with $Z \ge 0$ and $Z _ { 0 } = 1 \} = : \mathcal { Z }$ 

Now define for any $t \geq 0$ and $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } }$ , in analogy to (14.4) and (14.5), 

$$
\tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) := \alpha \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \frac {S _ {s} ^ {\delta}}{S _ {t} ^ {\delta}} \frac {Z _ {s}}{Z _ {t}} U _ {s} d s,
$$

$$
\tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) := \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} \frac {S _ {s} ^ {\delta}}{S _ {t} ^ {\delta}} \frac {Z _ {s}}{Z _ {t}} \log \frac {Z _ {s}}{Z _ {t}} d s
$$

and the cost functional 

$$
\tilde {c} _ {\infty} (Z) := \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z).
$$

The stochastic control problem studied here is to minimise the functional 

$$
Z \mapsto \Gamma_ {\infty} (Z) := E _ {P} \big [ \tilde {c} _ {\infty} (Z) \big ]
$$

over a subset $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ of $\mathcal { Z }$ , defined below. Note that by the minimum principle for supermartingales, $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } }$ remains 0 if it ever hits $0 ;$ so both summands of $\widetilde { c } _ { \infty } ( Z )$ are well defined. 

Hypothesis 14.12 Throughout this section, we impose the standing assumptions 

There exists some $T _ { 0 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ such that for all $\gamma > 0$ 

$$
E _ {P} \left[ \exp \left(\gamma \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} | U _ {s} | d s\right) \right] + E _ {P} \left[ \int_ {T _ {0}} ^ {\infty} \exp (\gamma | U _ {s} |) \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}} d s \right] <   \infty .\tag{14.27a}
$$

$0 < \underline { { \delta } } \le \delta _ { t } \le \bar { \delta } < \infty$ , uniformly in $( t , \omega )$ , for constants $\underline { { \delta } } , \bar { \delta } .$ 

(14.27b) 

The first condition in (14.27a) says that $U$ is in $\boldsymbol { D } _ { 1 , T _ { 0 } } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ ; we remark that the indicator function in the second term fixes an obvious oversight in (4.4) of Bordigoni [1]. Condition (14.27b) is natural for an infinite-horizon problem. Note that we do not assume here that $\mathbb { F }$ is a continuous filtration. 

Definition 14.13 $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ denotes the set of all martingales $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } }$ satisfying $E _ { P } [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z ) ] < \infty$ 

Our stochastic control problem is slightly more general than the one studied in Chap. 4 of Bordigoni [1] since we do not insist on working on the canonical (Skorokhod) path space. The presentation here is linked to Bordigoni [1] and to the slightly different formulation in Sect. 14.2 as follows. For any $Q$ with $Z ^ { Q } \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ , we have under (14.27a), for any $t \geq 0$ 

$$
E _ {P} \left[ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z ^ {Q}) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right] = E _ {P} \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} \frac {S _ {s} ^ {\delta}}{S _ {t} ^ {\delta}} \frac {Z _ {s} ^ {Q}}{Z _ {t} ^ {Q}} \log \frac {Z _ {s} ^ {Q}}{Z _ {t} ^ {Q}} d s \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right] = E _ {Q} \left[ \mathcal {R} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Q) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right],
$$

$$
E _ {P} \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z ^ {Q}) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big ] = E _ {P} \bigg [ \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \frac {S _ {s} ^ {\delta}}{S _ {t} ^ {\delta}} \frac {Z _ {s} ^ {Q}}{Z _ {t} ^ {Q}} U _ {s} d s \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg ] = E _ {Q} \big [ \mathcal {U} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big ];
$$

this is proved in Lemma 4.6 and Remark 4.10 of Bordigoni [1], essentially by using Bayes’ rule. In particular, this shows that 

$$
\Gamma_ {\infty} \big (Z ^ {Q} \big) := E _ {P} \big [ \tilde {c} _ {\infty} \big (Z ^ {Q} \big) \big ] = E _ {Q} \big [ c _ {\infty} (Q) \big ] =: \Gamma_ {\infty} (Q).
$$

Expressing everything under P and working with martingales $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ turns out to be a bit more flexible than working with probability measures $Q { \stackrel { \mathrm { l o c } } { \ll } } P$ . From now on, all expectations without subscript are under P. 

Remark 14.14 Under (14.27b), $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { t } ^ { \infty } \delta _ { s } S _ { s } ^ { \delta } d s = S _ { t } ^ { \delta } } \end{array}$ for every $t \geq 0$ , and hence also 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} \frac {S _ {s} ^ {\delta}}{S _ {t} ^ {\delta}} \frac {Z _ {s}}{Z _ {t}} d s \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right] = 1 \quad \text {   for   every   } t \geq 0 \text {   and   any   } Z \in \mathcal {Z}.
$$

We start with some auxiliary estimates. These are true for any $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } }$ , with the understanding that we set $E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z ) ] = + \infty$ for $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } } \setminus { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ 

Lemma 14.15 For every $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } }$ and every $T \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , 

$$
E \left[ Z _ {T} \log Z _ {T} \right] \leq \frac {1}{\underline {{\delta}}} e ^ {\bar {\delta} (T + 1)} \left(E \left[ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \right] + e ^ {- 1}\right).
$$

Proof Since $t \mapsto E [ Z _ { t } \log Z _ { t } ]$ is increasing and $z \log z \geq - e ^ { - 1 }$ , Fubini and (14.27b) give 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E [ Z _ {T} \log Z _ {T} ] \leq E \left[ \int_ {T} ^ {T + 1} \frac {\delta_ {s}}{\underline {{\delta}}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} e ^ {\bar {\delta} s} \left(Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s} + e ^ {- 1}\right) d s \right] \\ \leq \frac {1}{\underline {{\delta}}} e ^ {\bar {\delta} (T + 1)} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \left(Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s} + e ^ {- 1}\right) d s \right] \\ = \frac {1}{\underline {{\delta}}} e ^ {\bar {\delta} (T + 1)} \left(E \left[ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \right] + e ^ {- 1}\right) \end{array}
$$

by Remark 14.14. 

Proposition 14.16 There is a constant $C < \infty$ such thatfor every $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } }$ 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} | U _ {s} | d s \right] \leq C \left(1 + E \left[ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \right]\right) \leq C \left(1 + \Gamma_ {\infty} (Z)\right).\tag{14.28}
$$

Proof This is a simplified version of the proofs for Lemma 4.9 and Proposition 4.11 in Bordigoni [1]. In the sequel, we use several times the elementary inequality $x y \le e ^ { x } + y$ log y for $x \in \mathbb { R } , y \geq 0$ , typically applied to $\boldsymbol { x y } = \gamma \boldsymbol { x } \frac { 1 } { \gamma } \boldsymbol { y }$ . Starting with $\widetilde { c } _ { \infty } ( Z )$ , we split $\tilde { \mathcal { U } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z )$ into an integral from 0 to $T _ { 0 }$ and another from $T _ { 0 }$ to $\infty$ to write first 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} | U _ {s} | d s \bigg ] \leq E \bigg [ Z _ {T _ {0}} \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} | U _ {s} | d s \bigg ] \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq E \bigg [ \exp \bigg (\gamma \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} | U _ {s} | d s \bigg) \bigg ] + \frac {1}{\gamma} E \big [ Z _ {T _ {0}} \big (\log Z _ {T _ {0}} + | \log \gamma | \big) \big ]. \end{array}\tag{14.29}
$$

Next, we have due to $S ^ { \delta } \leq 1$ and Remark 14.14 that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \left[ \int_ {T _ {0}} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} | U _ {s} | d s \right] \\ \leq E \left[ \int_ {T _ {0}} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\gamma | U _ {s} |} \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}} d s \right] + E \left[ \int_ {T _ {0}} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{\gamma} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} \log \left(\frac {1}{\gamma} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s}\right) \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}} d s \right] \\ \leq E \left[ \int_ {T _ {0}} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\gamma | U _ {s} |} \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}} d s \right] + \frac {1}{\gamma} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\delta_ {s}}{\underline {{\delta}}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} (Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s} + e ^ {- 1}) d s \right] \\ + \frac {1}{\gamma} | \log \gamma | E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\delta_ {s}}{\underline {{\delta}}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} d s \right] \\ = E \left[ \int_ {T _ {0}} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\gamma | U _ {s} |} \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}} d s \right] + \frac {1}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}} \left(E [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) ] + e ^ {- 1} + | \log \gamma |\right). \end{array} \tag {14}\tag{14.30}
$$

Combining (14.29) with Lemma 14.15 and (14.30) gives the left inequality in (14.28) in the form 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} | U _ {s} | d s \right] \leq C + E \left[ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \right] \frac {1}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}} \left(e ^ {\bar {\delta} \left(T _ {0} + 1\right)} + 1\right),\tag{14.31}
$$

where the constant C depends on γ and also on U via (14.27a). By definition, then, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Gamma_ {\infty} (Z) = E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big ] + \beta E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big ] \\ \qquad \geq - \alpha E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} | U _ {s} | d s \bigg ] + \beta E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big ] \\ \qquad \geq - \alpha C + E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big ] \bigg (\beta - \frac {\alpha}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}} \big (1 + e ^ {\bar {\delta} (T _ {0} + 1)} \big) \bigg), \end{array}
$$

and so the right inequality in (14.28) follows by taking $\gamma$ large enough and choosing a new constant appropriately. - 

The above argument also shows that ${ \cal T } _ { \infty } ( Z ) \le C ( 1 + E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z ) ] )$ for all $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } }$ , with a suitable constant. Another direct consequence is the following result that will be used later. 

Corollary 14.17 For every $T \geq T _ { 0 }$ , every $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } }$ and every $\gamma > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \bigg [ \int_ {T} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} U _ {s}   d s \bigg ] \leq E \bigg [ \int_ {T} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\gamma | U _ {s} |} \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}}   d s \bigg ] \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}} \big (E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big ] + e ^ {- 1} + | \log \gamma | \big). \end{array}
$$

With these preparations, we are ready to prove the existence and uniqueness of a solution to our stochastic control problem. 

Theorem 14.18 Under Hypothesis 14.12, there exists a unique $Z ^ { * } \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ that minimises the costfunctional $Z \mapsto { \cal { I } } _ { \infty } ( Z )$ over all $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ 

Proof This again follows closely the arguments in Bordigoni [1]; see there the proof of Theorem 4.15. Since we optimise over $Z$ instead of $Q .$ , we need not work on path space and can simplify some arguments. 

First of all, the uniqueness is clear because $Z \mapsto {  { \Gamma } } _ { \infty } ( Z )$ is strictly convex like $z \mapsto z \log z$ . The existence is proved in several steps. 

(1) Since $Z \equiv 1$ is in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ and $E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( 1 ) ] = 0$ , (14.27a) and Proposition 14.16 imply that $- \infty < \operatorname* { i n f } _ { Z \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f } } { I _ { \infty } ( Z ) } < \infty$ . So we can take a sequence $( Z ^ { n } ) _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ such that $T _ { \infty } ( Z ^ { n } )$ decreases to in $\mathrm { f } _ { Z \in \mathcal { Z } _ { f } } \ : T _ { \infty } ( Z )$ as $n  \infty$ . Combining the well-known Komlós-type result in Lemma A1.1 in Delbaen/Schachermayer [7] with a diagonalisation argument produces a sequence $( \bar { Z } ^ { n } ) _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ with $\bar { Z } ^ { n } \in \mathrm { c o n v } ( Z ^ { n } , Z ^ { n + 1 } , \ldots )$ for all n and such that with probability 1, 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \bar {Z} _ {r} ^ {n} =: \bar {Z} _ {r} ^ {\infty} \quad \text { exists   in } [ 0, \infty ] \text { for   all } r \in \mathbb {Q} ^ {+}.
$$

Since each ${ \bar { Z } } ^ { n }$ is like the $Z ^ { n }$ a martingale $\geq 0$ with expectation 1, Fatou’s lemma yields that each $\bar { Z } _ { r } ^ { \infty }$ is integrable and $( { \bar { Z } } _ { r } ^ { \infty } ) _ { r \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { + } }$ is a supermartingale. By a standard argument (see Dellacherie/Meyer [8], Theorem VI.2), we can therefore extend $( \bar { Z } _ { r } ^ { \infty } ) _ { r \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { + } }$ to a process $Z ^ { * } = ( Z _ { t } ^ { * } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ with RCLL trajectories and such that $Z ^ { * }$ is a supermartingale $\geq 0$ (now over $\left[ 0 , \infty \right)$ instead of $\mathbb { Q } ^ { + } )$ . In fact, we can take $\begin{array} { r } { Z _ { t } ^ { * } : = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { r \searrow t , r \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { + } } \bar { Z } _ { r } ^ { \infty } } \end{array}$ 

(2) In order to show that $Z ^ { * }$ is even a martingale and in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ , we first use Lemma 14.15 to obtain for each $r \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { + }$ that 

$$
\sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} E \big [ \bar {Z} _ {r} ^ {n} \log \bar {Z} _ {r} ^ {n} \big ] \leq \frac {1}{\underline {{\delta}}} e ^ {\bar {\delta} (r + 1)} \Big (\sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} \big (\bar {Z} ^ {n} \big) \big ] + e ^ {- 1} \Big) <   \infty ,
$$

because by Proposition 14.16 and the convexity of $Z \mapsto {  { \cal { T } } } _ { \infty } ( Z )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} \big (\bar {Z} ^ {n} \big) \big ] \leq C \big (1 + \Gamma_ {\infty} \big (\bar {Z} ^ {n} \big) \big) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qend{array}
$$

So $( \bar { Z } _ { r } ^ { n } ) _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is uniformly integrable for each $r \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { + }$ , and this implies 

$$
E \big [ \bar {Z} _ {r} ^ {\infty} \big ] = \lim _ {n \to \infty} E \big [ \bar {Z} _ {r} ^ {n} \big ] = 1 \quad \text { for   all } r \in \mathbb {Q} ^ {+},
$$

which means that the supermartingale $\bar { Z } ^ { \infty }$ is a martingale $( \mathrm { o v e r } \mathbb { Q } ^ { + } )$ ). Using Doob’s maximal inequality and the fact that $( \bar { Z } _ { m } ^ { n } ) _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ converges to $Z _ { m } ^ { * }$ in $L ^ { 1 }$ for every $m \in \mathbb { N }$ next shows that with probability 1, $( { \bar { Z } } ^ { n } ) _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ converges to $Z ^ { * }$ uniformly on compact subsets of $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ , and the same uniform integrability argument as above then yields that also $Z ^ { * }$ is a martingale (over $\left[ 0 , \infty \right) )$ , hence in $\mathcal { Z }$ . Finally, Fatou’s lemma, Remark 14.14 and Proposition 14.16 give 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z ^ {*}) \big ] = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} ^ {*} \log Z _ {s} ^ {*} d s \right] \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (\bar {Z} ^ {n}) \big ] \leq \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} C (1 + \Gamma_ {\infty} (\bar {Z} ^ {n})) <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

so that $Z ^ { * }$ is in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ . 

(3) To show that $Z ^ { * }$ is optimal, we want to prove that $Z \mapsto { \Gamma _ { \infty } ( Z ) }$ is lower semicontinuous along the sequence $( \bar { Z } ^ { n } ) _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ , because we then get by convexity 

$$
\Gamma_ {\infty} \big (Z ^ {*} \big) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \Gamma_ {\infty} \big (\bar {Z} ^ {n} \big) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \Gamma_ {\infty} \big (Z ^ {n} \big) = \inf _ {Z \in \mathcal {Z} _ {f}} \Gamma_ {\infty} (Z).
$$

We have just seen in step (2) that $\begin{array} { r } { E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z ^ { * } ) ] \leq \operatorname* { l i m } \operatorname* { i n f } _ { n  \infty } E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( \bar { Z } ^ { n } ) ] } \end{array}$ , so that it only remains to prove the analogous inequality for the part with $\tilde { \mathcal { U } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z )$ Now $U \in D _ { 1 , T _ { 0 } } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ by (14.27a), and so we can use the finite-horizon results in Bordigoni/Matoussi/Schweizer [2] to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} ^ {*} U _ {s}   d s \right] = E \left[ Z _ {T _ {0}} ^ {*} \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} U _ {s}   d s \right] \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E \left[ \bar {Z} _ {T _ {0}} ^ {n} \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} U _ {s}   d s \right] = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n} U _ {s}   d s \right]; \end{array}
$$

see step (4) in the proof of Theorem 9 in Bordigoni/Matoussi/Schweizer [2]. We then split the remaining integral from $T _ { 0 }$ to ∞ into one integral from $T _ { 0 }$ to $T \geq T _ { 0 }$ and another from $T$ to ∞. The integral over the finite interval $( T _ { 0 } , T ]$ is again treated as above, using that (14.27a) also gives $U \in D _ { 1 , T } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ by Jensen’s inequality. Finally, Corollary 14.17 gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \left[ \int_ {T} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n} U _ {s} d s \right] \leq E \left[ \int_ {T} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\gamma | U _ {s} |} \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}} d s \right] \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}} \left(\sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} E \left[ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (\bar {Z} ^ {n}) \right] + e ^ {- 1} + | \log \gamma |\right) \end{array}
$$

for all $\gamma > 0$ and all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , and the same estimate holds for $Z ^ { * }$ instead of ${ \bar { Z } } ^ { n }$ as well. Choosing first $\gamma$ large to make the second summand above small and then, using (14.27a), T large to get the first summand small as well, we deduce that 

$$
\lim _ {T \rightarrow \infty} \sup \left\{E \left[ \int_ {T} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} U _ {s} d s \right]: Z = Z ^ {*} \text {   or   } Z = \bar {Z} ^ {n} \text {   for   some   } n \in \mathbb {N} \right\} = 0,
$$

and so we obtain after putting everything together that 

$$
E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} ^ {*} U _ {s}   d s \right] \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n} U _ {s}   d s \right].
$$

This completes the proof. 

As in the finite-horizon case treated in Bordigoni/Matoussi/Schweizer [2], one can show that the optimal $Z ^ { * }$ from Theorem 14.18 is strictly positive. If there exists $Q ^ { * }$ with density process $Z ^ { * }$ (e.g. as in Bordigoni [1] if one works on path space), this translates into saying that $Q ^ { * } { \overset { \underset { \mathrm { l o c } } { } } { \approx } } P$ . The proof of positivity can be found in Bordigoni [1], Theorem 4.18, and largely parallels that of Theorem 12 in Bordigoni/ Matoussi/Schweizer [2]. 

Also as in Bordigoni/Matoussi/Schweizer [2], one can show that the martingale optimality principle holds in our setting; see Proposition 4.19 and Corollary 4.20 in Bordigoni [1] for details of this standard argument. As a consequence, the optimal $Z ^ { * }$ from Theorem 14.18 is also conditionally optimal at any time t or even stopping time τ. To properly formulate this, we denote by $V = ( V _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ an RCLL version of the process 

$$
V _ {t} := \underset {Z \in \mathcal {Z} _ {f}} {\text { ess   inf }} E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big ] =: \underset {Z \in \mathcal {Z} _ {f}} {\text { ess   inf }} J _ {t} (Z), \quad t \geq 0.\tag{14.32}
$$

Then conditional optimality says that 

$$
V _ {t} = J _ {t} \left(Z ^ {*}\right) \quad P \text {-a.s. for all t\geq 0},
$$

and we now use this to describe the behaviour of $V _ { t }$ as $t \to \infty$ 

Proposition 14.19 Under Hypothesis 14.12, 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} V _ {t} = 0 \quad P \text {-a.s.}
$$

Proof This is analogous to the proof of Lemma 4.22 in Bordigoni [1]. Since $Z \equiv 1$ is in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f } , S ^ { \delta }$ is decreasing and $E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { t , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z ) | \mathcal { F } _ { t } ] \geq 0$ , we have 

$$
V _ {t} = J _ {t} \left(Z ^ {*}\right) \leq J _ {t} (1) \leq \alpha E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} | U _ {s} | d s \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right],
$$

which yields lim su $\operatorname { p } _ { t \to \infty } V _ { t } \leq 0$ due to (14.27a). To get a lower bound for $V _ { t }$ , we use analogous arguments as in the proof of Proposition 14.16 to first obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left| E \bigg [ \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \frac {S _ {s} ^ {\delta}}{S _ {t} ^ {\delta}} \frac {Z _ {s} ^ {*}}{Z _ {t} ^ {*}} U _ {s}   d s \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg ] \right| \leq E \bigg [ \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\gamma | U _ {s} |} \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}}   d s \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg ] \\ + \frac {1}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}} \big (E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z ^ {*}) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big ] + e ^ {- 1} + | \log \gamma | \big). \end{array}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V _ {t} = J _ {t} \big (Z ^ {*} \big) \geq - \alpha E \left[ \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\gamma | U _ {s} |} \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}} d s \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} \right] \\ - \frac {\alpha}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}} \big (e ^ {- 1} + | \log \gamma | \big) + \left(\beta - \frac {\alpha}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}}\right) E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} \big (Z ^ {*} \big) | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big ], \end{array}
$$

and taking $\gamma$ so large that $\beta - \textstyle { \frac { \alpha } { \gamma \underline { { \delta } } } } \geq 0$ , we get from $E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { t , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z ^ { * } ) | \mathcal { F } _ { t } ] \geq 0$ and (14.27a) that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {t \to \infty} V _ {t} \geq - \frac {\alpha}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}} \big (e ^ {- 1} + | \log \gamma | \big) \quad P \text {-a.s.}
$$

Since $\gamma$ is arbitrary, we conclude that lim in $\operatorname { f } _ { t \to \infty } V _ { t } \geq 0 ~ P { \cdot } \mathrm { a } . s$ ., which completes the proof. - 

All results in this section so far hold for a general filtration. If F is continuous, one can in addition show as in Bordigoni/Matoussi/Schweizer [2] that V obeys the dynamics 

$$
d V _ {t} = (\delta_ {t} V _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t}) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}
$$

for some (continuous) local martingale M; see Theorem 4.27 in Bordigoni [1] for a detailed proof. Together with Proposition 14.19, this explains where the infinitehorizon BSDE (14.3) comes from. Since the above derivation uses no essential new ideas in comparison with Bordigoni/Matoussi/Schweizer [2], we refrain from giving more details. 

## 14.6 Solving the Stochastic Control Problem via the BSDE

Our goal in this section is to use the results on the infinite-horizon BSDE (14.19) for a characterisation of the dynamic value process V for the stochastic control problem from Sect. 14.5. As just mentioned, we could have shown that V solves (14.19), but this is not enough: The uniqueness result in Theorem 14.10 only holds for solutions (Y, M) with $Y \in D _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ , and we do not know at this point how to argue directly that V from the control problem is in $\boldsymbol { D } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ . The BSDE techniques developed so far will enable us to prove this. To that end, we now show how one can construct from a (particular) solution to the BSDE (14.19) a (and actually the, by uniqueness) solution for the infinite-horizon stochastic control problem. 

## Hypothesis 14.20 Throughout this section, we impose the standing assumptions

F is a continuousfiltration, i.e. all local (P, F)-martingales 

are continuous. 

(14.33a) 

$$
0 <   \underline {{\delta}} \leq \delta_ {t} \leq \bar {\delta} <   \infty , \text {   uniformly   in   } (t, \omega), \text {   for   constants   } \underline {{\delta}}, \bar {\delta}.\tag{14.33b}
$$

Conditions on U will be specified below, when we successively treat three cases. Our arguments rely substantially on the finite-horizon results proved in Bordigoni/Matoussi/Schweizer [2], so that we very briefly recall these here. Fix $T < \infty$ and consider on [0, T] the BSDE 

$$
d Y _ {t} = (\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t}) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \qquad Y _ {T} = \alpha^ {\prime} U _ {T} ^ {\prime}.\tag{14.34}
$$

Recall from (14.4) and (14.5) the definitions of $\mathcal { U } _ { t , T } ^ { \delta }$ and $\mathcal { R } _ { t , T } ^ { \delta }$ , and assume that U (as a process on [0, T]) is in $\boldsymbol { D } _ { 1 , T } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ and $U _ { T } ^ { \prime }$ is in $D ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ . Then Theorem 17 of Bordigoni/Matoussi/Schweizer [2] states that (14.34) has a unique solution $( Y , M )$ in $D _ { 0 , T } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } } \times \mathcal { M } _ { 0 , \mathrm { l o c } } ( P )$ , that $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { Z } : = \mathcal { E } ( - \frac { 1 } { \beta } M ) } \end{array}$ is a martingale on $[ 0 , T ]$ with $E [ \bar { Z } _ { T }$ log $\bar { Z } _ { T } ] < \infty$ , and that for any martingale $Z \ge 0$ on $[ 0 , T ]$ with $Z _ { 0 } = 1$ and $E [ Z _ { T }$ log $Z _ { T } ] < \infty$ , we have for any stopping time $\tau \leq T$ that 

$$
Y _ {\tau} = E \bigg [ \frac {\bar {Z} _ {T}}{\bar {Z} _ {\tau}} \mathcal {U} _ {\tau , T} ^ {\delta} + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {\tau , T} ^ {\delta} (\bar {Z}) \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \bigg ] \leq E \bigg [ \frac {Z _ {T}}{Z _ {\tau}} \mathcal {U} _ {\tau , T} ^ {\delta} + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {\tau , T} ^ {\delta} (Z) \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \bigg ].
$$

(This reformulates the statement that the dynamic value process of the finite-horizon stochastic control problem is the unique solution of (14.34).) For $\tau \equiv 0$ , this reduces to 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y _ {0} \leq E \bigg [ Z _ {T} \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {T} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} U _ {s}   d s + Z _ {T}   \alpha^ {\prime} S _ {T} ^ {\delta} U _ {T} ^ {\prime} \bigg ] \\ \quad + \beta E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s}   d s + S _ {T} ^ {\delta} Z _ {T} \log Z _ {T} \bigg ], \end{array}\tag{14.35}
$$

with equality for $Z = { \bar { Z } }$ 

## 14.6.1 The Bounded Case

Let us now first study the case where $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } | U _ { s } |$ ds is bounded. This is of course a restrictive assumption, but it allows fairly simple arguments and provides a basic building block. We shall see that the proofs in more general cases follow the same scheme. 

Proposition 14.21 Suppose that $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } | U _ { s } |$ ds is a bounded random variable. For any solution $( Y , M )$ to the infinite-horizon BSDE (14.19) with Y bounded, we then have, for any $t \geq 0$ 

$$
Y _ {t} = \underset {Z \in \mathcal {Z} _ {f}} {\text { ess   inf }} E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big ].
$$

Proof Without loss of generality, we prove the result for $t = 0$ 

(1) Let us start by arguing that for any $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ , we have 

$$
Y _ {0} \leq E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big ].\tag{14.36}
$$

We first note that the nonnegative function $g ( s ) : = E [ \delta _ { s } S _ { s } ^ { \delta } ( Z _ { s } \log Z _ { s } + e ^ { - 1 } ) ]$ satisfies, by Remark 14.14 and Fubini, 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} g (s) d s = E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \left(Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s} + e ^ {- 1}\right) d s \right] = E \left[ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \right] + e ^ {- 1} <   \infty .
$$

This implies that there exists a sequence of deterministic times $T _ { n } ~ { \nearrow }$ ∞ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} E \big [ S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta} \big (Z _ {T _ {n}} \log Z _ {T _ {n}} + e ^ {- 1} \big) \big ] \leq \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\underline {{\delta}}} g (T _ {n}) = 0
$$

and therefore also 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} E \big [ S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta} Z _ {T _ {n}} \log Z _ {T _ {n}} \big ] = 0,\tag{14.37}
$$

since $S _ { T _ { n } } ^ { \delta } \leq e ^ { - \underline { { { \delta } } } T _ { n } } \to 0$ . Moreover, because Y is bounded and $Z \ge 0$ is a martingale, we have 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \left| E \left[ S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta} Z _ {T _ {n}} Y _ {T _ {n}} \right]\right| \leq \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} e ^ {- \underline {{\delta}} T _ {n}} \| Y \| _ {\infty} E [ Z _ {T _ {n}} ] = 0.\tag{14.38}
$$

Now Y is bounded, hence in $D _ { 0 , T _ { n } } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ , and satisfies the finite-horizon BSDE (14.34) with final value $\alpha ^ { \prime } U _ { T _ { n } } ^ { \prime } : = Y _ { T _ { n } }$ . Moreover, $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ verifies $E [ Z _ { T _ { n } } \log Z _ { T _ { n } } ] < \infty$ due to Lemma 14.15, and so the finite-horizon results tell us that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y _ {0} \leq E \left[ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {n}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} U _ {s} d s + S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta} Z _ {T _ {n}} Y _ {T _ {n}} \right] \\ \quad + \beta E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {n}} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s} d s + S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta} Z _ {T _ {n}} \log Z _ {T _ {n}} \right]. \end{array}\tag{14.39}
$$

On the right-hand side, the second and the fourth summands tend to 0 as $n \to \infty$ by (14.38) and (14.37), respectively. Next, Fatou’s lemma yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} | U _ {s} | d s \right] & \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E \left[ Z _ {T _ {n}} \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {n}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} | U _ {s} | d s \right] \\ & \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E \left[ Z _ {T _ {n}} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} | U _ {s} | d s \right] <   \infty \end{array}
$$

since $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } | U _ { s } | d s$ is bounded and $Z \ge 0$ is a martingale. By the dominated convergence theorem, we thus deduce that the first summand in (14.39) converges to $\begin{array} { r } { E [ \tilde { \alpha } \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } S _ { s } ^ { \delta } Z _ { s } U _ { s } d s ] = E [ \tilde { U } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z ) ] } \end{array}$ as $n \to \infty$ . Finally, 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {T _ {n}} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s} d s = \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {n}} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \left(Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s} + e ^ {- 1}\right) d s - e ^ {- 1} \left(1 - S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta}\right)
$$

implies via monotone integration and by using $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } \delta _ { s } S _ { s } ^ { \delta } d s = 1 } \end{array}$ that the third summand in (14.39) converges to $\beta E [ \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } \delta _ { s } S _ { s } ^ { \delta } Z _ { s }$ log $Z _ { s } d s ] = \beta E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z ) ]$ as $n \to \infty$ . Putting everything together gives (14.36). 

(2) Now define $\begin{array} { r } { \dot { \bar { Z } } : = \mathcal { \bar { E } } ( - \overline { { \frac { 1 } { \beta } } } M ) } \end{array}$ . Since $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } | U _ { s } |$ ds is bounded, U is in $D _ { 1 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ and since $( Y , M )$ solves (14.19), Theorem 14.11 tells us that $\bar { Z }$ is a martingale on $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ , so that $\bar { Z } \in \mathcal { Z }$ . We want to prove that $\bar { Z }$ is even in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ . To that end, we apply the finite-horizon results to write 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y _ {0} = E \bigg [ \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {n}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} U _ {s}   d s + S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} Y _ {T _ {n}} \bigg ] \\ \qquad + \beta E \bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {n}} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} \log \bar {Z} _ {s}   d s + S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} \log \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} \bigg ]. \end{array}
$$

Using Fatou’s lemma and $z \log z \geq - e ^ { - 1 }$ therefore gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \beta E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (\bar {Z}) \big ] \\ = \beta E \Bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} \log \bar {Z} _ {s} d s \Bigg ] \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \beta E \Bigg [ \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {n}} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} \log \bar {Z} _ {s} d s \Bigg ] \\ = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \Big (Y _ {0} - \beta E \big [ S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} \log \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} \big ] - E \Bigg [ \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {n}} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} U _ {s} d s + S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} Y _ {T _ {n}} \Bigg ] \Bigg) \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \Big (Y _ {0} + \beta e ^ {- 1} + \alpha \left\| \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} | U _ {s} | d s \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty}} E [ \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} ] + \| Y _ {\infty} ^ {*} \| _ {L ^ {\infty}} E [ \bar {Z} _ {T _ {n}} ] \Big) <   \infty \end{array}
$$

because Y and $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } | U _ { s } |$ ds are bounded and $\bar { Z } \ge 0$ is a martingale. Hence $\bar { Z }$ is indeed in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ 

(3) Since $\bar { Z }$ is in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ by step (2) and satisfies (14.35) with equality, the same argument as in step (1) shows that the inequality in (14.36) becomes an equality for $Z = { \bar { Z } }$ . Hence $\bar { Z }$ attains the infimum, and the proof is complete. - 

## 14.6.2 The Positive Case

We now turn to the case where U is nonnegative and satisfies some integrability condition. Note that $U \geq 0$ is a fairly natural assumption. Indeed, if we think of a full-fledged robust control problem for utility maximisation, then $U _ { t }$ typically represents the utility $\mathbf { U } ( c _ { t } )$ from consumption at time t, where we still optimise over c in a second step. As a consumption rate, $c _ { t } \geq 0 ;$ so ${ \cal U } _ { t } = { \bf U } ( c _ { t } ) \geq 0$ for any nonnegative utility function U on $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ , like e.g. the power utility $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { U } ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { \gamma } x ^ { \gamma } } \end{array}$ for $\gamma \in ( 0 , 1 )$ 

Theorem 14.22 Suppose that $U \geq 0$ and U is in $D _ { 1 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ . For the solution $( Y , M )$ to (14.19)from Theorem 14.9, we then have,for any $t \geq 0$ 

$$
Y _ {t} = \underset {Z \in \mathcal {Z} _ {f}} {\text { ess   inf }} E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z)   \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big ].
$$

Proof Without loss of generality, we again argue for $t = 0$ . The overall structure of the proof is like for Proposition 14.21, but we first need to recall the construction of $( Y , M )$ . For each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , set $U _ { t } ^ { n } : = U _ { t } \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } U _ { s } d s \leq n \} }$ and denote by $( Y ^ { n } , M ^ { n } )$ with $Y ^ { n }$ bounded the solution to the BSDE 

$$
d Y _ {t} = \left(\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t} ^ {n}\right) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \qquad Y _ {n} = 0,
$$

on $[ 0 , n ]$ . Extending $( Y ^ { n } , M ^ { n } )$ to $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ by setting $Y _ { t } ^ { n } = 0 , M _ { t } ^ { n } = M _ { n } ^ { n }$ for $t > n$ , we then get on $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ a solution $( Y ^ { n } , M ^ { n } )$ to the BSDE 

$$
d Y _ {t} = \left(\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha \mathbf {1} _ {\{t \leq n \}} U _ {t} ^ {n}\right) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \quad \lim _ {t \rightarrow \infty} Y _ {t} = 0,\tag{14.40}
$$

and $Y _ { t } = \mathcal { I } - \mathrm { l i m } _ { n  \infty } Y _ { t } ^ { n }$ for all $t \geq 0$ . We first prove that, for any $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ 

$$
Y _ {0} \leq E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big ].\tag{14.41}
$$

Indeed, applying Proposition 14.21 to the process $( \mathbf { 1 } _ { \{ t \leq n \} } U _ { t } ^ { n } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ and the solution to (14.40) gives 

$$
Y _ {0} ^ {n} \leq E \left[ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} \mathbf {1} _ {\{s \leq n \}} U _ {s} ^ {n} d s + \beta \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s} d s \right],
$$

and (14.41) follows by monotone integration since $U \geq 0$ 

Now set $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { Z } : = \mathcal { E } ( - \frac { 1 } { \beta } M ) } \end{array}$ , so that $\bar { Z } \in \mathcal { Z }$ by Theorem 14.11; this uses the integrability assumption on $U$ . To prove that $\bar { Z }$ is even in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ , we first note that by Proposition 14.21 and its proof, we have equality in (14.41) for the choice $\begin{array} { r } { \dot { Z } = \bar { Z } ^ { \bar { n } } : = \mathcal { E } ( - \frac { 1 } { \beta } M ^ { n } ) } \end{array}$ , so that 

$$
Y _ {0} ^ {n} = E \bigg [ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n} \mathbf {1} _ {\{s \leq n \}} U _ {s} ^ {n} d s + \beta \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n} \log \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n} d s \bigg ].
$$

But by construction, $( Y _ { 0 } ^ { n } ) _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ increases to $Y _ { 0 }$ , and $( M ^ { n } ) _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ and $( \langle M ^ { n } \rangle ) _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ converge to $M$ and $\langle M \rangle$ locally uniformly in probability, so that also $\bar { Z } ^ { n } \to \bar { Z }$ locally uniformly in probability as $n \to \infty$ . Hence Fatou’s lemma yields 

$$
Y _ {0} \geq E \left[ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} U _ {s} d s + \beta \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} \log \bar {Z} _ {s} d s \right] = E \left[ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (\bar {Z}) + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (\bar {Z}) \right],
$$

and so $\bar { Z } \in \mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ because $U \geq 0$ . Since (14.41) gives the converse inequality, we actually have equality in (14.41) for $Z = { \bar { Z } }$ , and this completes the proof. - 

## 14.6.3 The General Case

Finally, we study a situation where U can be real-valued. Then we need slightly stronger integrability assumptions. 

Theorem 14.23 Suppose that U is in $D _ { 1 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ and that U also satisfies (14.27a), i.e. there exists some $T _ { 0 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ such that,for all $\gamma > 0$ 

$$
E _ {P} \left[ \exp \left(\gamma \int_ {0} ^ {T _ {0}} | U _ {s} | d s\right) \right] + E _ {P} \left[ \int_ {T _ {0}} ^ {\infty} \exp (\gamma | U _ {s} |) \mathbf {1} _ {\{U _ {s} \neq 0 \}} d s \right] <   \infty .
$$

For the solution (Y, M) to (14.19)from Theorem 14.9, we then have,for any $t \geq 0$ 

$$
Y _ {t} = \underset {Z \in \mathcal {Z} _ {f}} {\text { ess   inf }} E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {t, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big ].
$$

Proof As already in the last proof, we argue for $t = 0$ without loss of generality and again first recall from the proof of Theorem 14.9 the construction of $( Y , M )$ . For $n , p \in \mathbb { N }$ , set 

$$
U _ {t} ^ {n, p} := U _ {t} ^ {+} \mathbf {1} _ {\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} | U _ {s} | d s \leq n \}} \mathbf {1} _ {\{t \leq n \}} - U _ {t} ^ {-} \mathbf {1} _ {\{\int_ {0} ^ {t} | U _ {s} | d s \leq p \}} \mathbf {1} _ {\{t \leq p \}}
$$

and denote by $( Y ^ { n , p } , M ^ { n , p } )$ with $Y ^ { n , p }$ bounded the solution to the BSDE 

$$
d Y _ {t} = (\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha U _ {t}) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \qquad Y _ {n \vee p} = 0,
$$

on $[ 0 , n \lor p ]$ . We extend $( Y ^ { n , p } , M ^ { n , p } )$ to $\left[ 0 , \infty \right)$ by setting $Y _ { t } ^ { n , p } = 0$ and $M _ { t } ^ { n , p } = M _ { n \vee p } ^ { n , p }$ for $t > n \vee p$ to get on $[ 0 , \infty )$ a solution to the BSDE 

$$
d Y _ {t} = \left(\delta_ {t} Y _ {t} - \alpha \mathbf {1} _ {\{t \leq n \vee p \}} U _ {t} ^ {n, p}\right) d t + \frac {1}{2 \beta} d \langle M \rangle_ {t} + d M _ {t}, \quad \lim _ {t \rightarrow \infty} Y _ {t} = 0.\tag{14.42}
$$

Then $\begin{array} { r } { Y _ { t } = \mathcal { I } \cdot \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \searrow \subset \supset \neg \operatorname* { l i m } _ { p \to \infty } Y _ { t } ^ { n , p } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { M _ { t } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \operatorname* { l i m } _ { p \to \infty } M _ { t } ^ { n , p } } \end{array}$ . We proceed on a familiar path. 

(1) First we prove that, for any $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ 

$$
Y _ {0} \leq E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) + \beta \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (Z) \big ].\tag{14.43}
$$

Like in Sect. 14.6.2, using Proposition 14.21 gives 

$$
Y _ {0} ^ {n, p} \leq E \left[ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} \mathbf {1} _ {\{s \leq n \vee p \}} U _ {s} ^ {n, p} d s + \beta \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} Z _ {s} \log Z _ {s} d s \right],
$$

and (14.43) follows by letting $p  \infty$ and then $n  \infty$ , provided that we can use dominated convergence. But this is ensured by the first estimate in Proposition 14.16; indeed, (14.27a) yields $\begin{array} { r } { E [ \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } S _ { s } ^ { \delta } Z _ { s } | U _ { s } | d s ] < \infty } \end{array}$ for $Z \in { \mathcal { Z } } _ { f }$ 

(2) Thanks to the first integrability assumption on $U$ , Theorem 14.11 implies that the process $\bar { Z } : = \mathcal { E } ( - \textstyle \frac 1 \beta \bar { M } )$ is in $\mathcal { Z }$ . To show that it is even in $\mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ , we use Proposition 14.21 for $\bar { Z } ^ { n , p } : = \mathcal { E } ( - \textstyle \frac { 1 } { \beta } M ^ { n , p } )$ to get 

$$
Y _ {0} ^ {n, p} = E \left[ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n, p} \mathbf {1} _ {\{s \leq n \vee p \}} U _ {s} ^ {n, p} d s + \beta \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \delta_ {s} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n, p} \log \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n, p} d s \right].\tag{14.44}
$$

But (14.31) in the proof of Proposition 14.16 gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| E \bigg [ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n, p} \mathbf {1} _ {\{s \leq n \lor p \}} U _ {s} ^ {n, p} d s \bigg ] \right| \leq E \bigg [ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n, p} | U _ {s} | d s \bigg ] \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad C _ {\gamma , U} + E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (\bar {Z} ^ {n, p}) \big ] \frac {1}{\gamma \underline {{\delta}}} (e ^ {\bar {\delta} (T _ {0} + 1)} + 1), \end{array}
$$

where the constant $C _ { \gamma , U }$ depends on $\gamma$ and $U$ via (14.27a), but not on n and $p .$ Plugging this estimate with a minus sign into (14.44) and taking γ big enough yields 

$$
\sup _ {n, p \in \mathbb {N}} E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {R}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} \big (\bar {Z} ^ {n, p} \big) \big ] \leq C \Big (1 + \sup _ {n, p \in \mathbb {N}} Y _ {0} ^ {n, p} \Big) <   \infty ,\tag{14.45}
$$

because applying the a priori estimate (14.23) from Theorem 14.9 to (14.42) tells us that 

$$
\left| Y _ {0} ^ {n, p} \right| \leq \beta \log E \left[ \exp \left(\frac {1}{\beta} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \alpha | U _ {s} | d s\right) \right] <   \infty
$$

for all n and $p _ { : }$ , by using the definition of $U ^ { n , p }$ . As $n  \infty$ and $p  \infty$ , we have locally uniformly in probability $M ^ { n , p }  M$ and $\langle M ^ { n , p } \rangle \to \langle M \rangle$ , hence also $\bar { Z } ^ { n , p } \to \bar { Z }$ , and so $\bar { Z } \in \mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ because $E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( \bar { Z } ) ] < \infty$ by Fatou’s lemma and (14.45). 

(3) To prove that we have equality in (14.43) for $Z = { \bar { Z } }$ , we start from the equality in (14.44). As $n  \infty$ and $p  \infty , Y _ { 0 } ^ { n , p }$ tends to $Y _ { 0 }$ , and we have lim in $\mathrm { f } _ { n  \infty }$ lim in $\begin{array} { r } { \mathfrak { f } _ { p  \infty } E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( \bar { Z } ^ { n , p } ) ] \geq E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( \bar { Z } ) ] } \end{array}$ by Fatou’s lemma. Because $Z \mapsto E [ \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( Z ) ]$ is bounded along the sequence $( \bar { Z } ^ { n , p } ) _ { n , p \in \mathbb { N } }$ by (14.45), almost the same argument as in step 3) of the proof of Theorem 14.18 gives 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \underset {n \to \infty} {\text { lim   inf }} \underset {p \to \infty} {\text { lim   inf }} E \left[ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} ^ {n, p} \mathbf {1} _ {\{s \leq n \vee p \}} U _ {s} ^ {n, p} d s \right] \geq E \left[ \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} S _ {s} ^ {\delta} \bar {Z} _ {s} U _ {s} d s \right] \\ = E \big [ \tilde {\mathcal {U}} _ {0, \infty} ^ {\delta} (\bar {Z}) \big ]. \end{array}
$$

Note that this exploits the integrability assumption (14.27a). Therefore (14.44) implies that $Y _ { 0 } \ge E [ \tilde { \mathcal { U } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( \bar { Z } ) + \beta \tilde { \mathcal { R } } _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \delta } ( \bar { Z } ) ]$ , and so we must have equality due to (14.43) since $\bar { Z } \in \mathcal { Z } _ { f }$ . This completes the proof. - 

## 14.6.4 Consequencesfor the Stochastic Control Problem

As in (14.32), denote by $V = ( V _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ the dynamic value process of the infinitehorizon stochastic control problem. We already mentioned at the end of Sect. 14.5 that if F is continuous, then V satisfies the infinite-horizon BSDE (14.19). For the proof, we referred to Bordigoni [1]; let us just note here that the required assumptions are Hypothesis 14.12 plus continuity of F, i.e. Hypothesis 14.20 plus (14.27a). Under a slightly stronger condition, we can now even prove a BSDE characterisation for V. 

Theorem 14.24 Assume Hypothesis 14.20 and that U is in $D _ { 1 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ . If in addition either $U \geq 0$ or U satisfies (14.27a), then V is the first component of the unique solution in $D _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } } \times \mathcal { M } _ { 0 , \mathrm { l o c } } ( P )$ to the infinite-horizon BSDE (14.19). In particular, $V \in D _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ 

Proof By Theorem 14.10 (14.19) has a unique solution (Y, M) with $Y \in D _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ ; and by the definition of V in (14.32) and either Theorem 14.22 or Theorem 14.23, Y coincides with V. - 

## Remark 14.25

(1) The second case of Theorem 14.24 is the infinite-horizon analogue to the finitehorizon Theorem 17 in Bordigoni/Matoussi/Schweizer [2], with assumptions and conclusions almost exactly parallel. The only difference lies in the conditions on U: In (14.27a), we need $U \in D _ { 1 , T _ { 0 } } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ , but also an exponential moment control over U on the infinite time interval $[ T _ { 0 } , \infty )$ . See Remark 4.28 in Bordigoni [1] for a more detailed comment on this point. The result for $U \geq 0$ has no precedent. 

(2) Our approach for $T = \infty$ here is different from Bordigoni [1] in that we show for the solution of the BSDE (14.19) that it satisfies the defining property (14.32) of the value process V. As a bonus, we are able to deduce that V is indeed in $D _ { 0 , \infty } ^ { \mathrm { e x p } }$ ; this was conjectured, but not proved, in Bordigoni [1].
