(a) The solution to ODEs (16.11) and (16.12) is an invertible matrix, and by $Q ( s , t )$ we denote the inverse of $P ( s , t )$ . The inverse matrix $Q ( s , t )$ is a solution of the 

following (random) ODE: 

$$
\frac {\partial Q (s , t)}{\partial t} = - \Lambda_ {t} Q (s, t) d t, \qquad Q (s, s) = \mathbb {I}.
$$

(b) The conditional transition matrices $( P ( t , u ) ) _ { 0 \leq t \leq u }$ satisfy the Chapman– Kolmogorov equations, i.e., for $0 \leq u \leq t$ , we have 

$$
P (0, u) = P (0, t) P (t, u).
$$

If C has an intensity matrix Λ, then $P ( 0 , t )$ is invertible, which implies that we can write 

$$
P (t, u) = Q (0, t) P (0, u).\tag{16.13}
$$

(c) If $C$ is an F-DS Markov chain, then $\mathbb { F }$ is immersed in $\mathbb { F } \vee \mathbb { F } ^ { C }$ , i.e., every $\mathbb { F } _ { - }$ martingale is an $\mathbb { F } \vee \mathbb { F } ^ { C }$ -martingale (for proof, see [16, Proposition 3.4]). 

Theorem 16.26 Let $( \varLambda ( t ) ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ be an arbitrary $\mathbb { F } .$ -adapted matrix-valued stochastic process which satisfies conditions (16.9) and (16.10). Then there exists an F-DS Markov chain with intensity $( \varLambda ( t ) ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ 

Further, the following theorem will be crucial: 

Theorem 16.27 $L e t \widetilde { \mathbb { G } } = ( \widetilde { \mathcal { G } } _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 } .$ , where $\widetilde { \mathcal { G } } _ { t } : = \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } \vee \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { C }$ . Suppose that $( C _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ is a K-valued stochastic process and $( \varLambda ( t ) ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ is a matrix-valued process satisfying (16.9) and (16.10). Thefollowing conditions are equivalent: 

1. The process C is an F-DS Markov chain with an intensity Λ. 

2. The process M defined by 

$$
M _ {t} := H _ {t} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Lambda_ {u} ^ {\top} H _ {u} d u,\tag{16.14}
$$

where $H _ { t } ^ { i } = \mathbb { 1 } _ { \{ C _ { t } = i \} }$ , and $H _ { t } : = ( H _ { t } ^ { 1 } , \ldots , H _ { t } ^ { K } ) ^ { \top }$ is a G<sup></sup>-local martingale. 3. The process L defined by 

$$
L _ {t} := Q ^ {\top} (0, t) H _ {t} = H _ {0} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} Q ^ {\top} (0, u) d M _ {u}\tag{16.15}
$$

is a $\widetilde { \mathbb { G } } .$ -local martingale. 

Remark 16.28 In a view of the above characterization, the class of F-DS Markov chains can be described as the class of processes that behave like time-inhomogeneous Markov chains when conditioned on $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty }$ . The word behave should be understood by means of a behavior of $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty }$ -conditional transition probabilities. 

We say that a given random time $\rho$ avoids F-stopping times if $\mathbb { P } ( \rho = \sigma ) = 0$ for every F-stopping time $\sigma$ 

Proposition 16.29 Let C be an F-DS Markov chain with an intensity, $\tau _ { 0 } = 0$ , and let 

$$
\tau_ {k} := \inf \{t > \tau_ {k - 1}: C _ {t} \neq C _ {\tau_ {k - 1}} \}.\tag{16.16}
$$

For $k \geq 1$ , the stopping time $\tau _ { k }$ avoids F-stopping times, provided that $\tau _ { k } < \infty a . s .$ 

## 16.4 Valuation of Defaultable Rating-Sensitive Claims with Ratings Given by a Doubly Stochastic Markov Chain

## 16.4.1 Description of Claims

We consider an arbitrage-free market with finite horizon on which defaultable instruments are also traded. We denote by $\mathbb { F }$ the reference filtration corresponding to observation of the market without credit rating, i.e., a filtration corresponding to the interest rate risk and other market factors that drive the credit risk. C is a credit rating process which takes values in the set of rating classes ${ \mathcal { K } } = \{ 1 , \ldots , K \}$ with the unique absorbing state $K$ . If $K = 2$ , then it is understood that there are only two states, nondefault and default. We assume that the process C is càdlàg. Let $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \mathcal { F } _ { t } \vee \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { C }$ . By a defaultable rating-sensitive claim we mean a classical one broadened by a migration process. 

Definition 16.30 By a defaultable rating-sensitive claim maturing at $T$ we mean a quintuple $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ , where $\begin{array} { r } { X = ( \breve { X } ^ { 1 } , \dots , X ^ { K - 1 } ) ^ { \top } \mathrm { ~ i s ~ a ~ } ( K - 1 ) } \end{array}$ -dimensional vector of F -measurable random variables, $A = ( A ^ { 1 } , \ldots , A ^ { \dot { K } - 1 } ) ^ { \top }$ is a $( K - 1 ) \ –$ dimensional vector-valued F-progressively measurable stochastic process of finite variation, $Z$ is an F-predictable $K \times K$ -dimensional matrix-valued process with zero on the diagonal, $C$ is a càdlàg process with values in $\kappa .$ and $\tau$ is a positive random variable defined by 

$$
\tau := \inf \{t \geq 0: C _ {t} = K \}.
$$

In this definition, X describes the promised payoff which is contingent on rating at maturity $T$ , i.e., the payoff is equal to $X ^ { i }$ , provided that $\{ C _ { T } = i \}$ ; the process A models the process of promised dividends which can depend on current credit rating; the processes $Z ^ { i , j }$ describe the payments at times when the rating changes from i to $j ;$ in particular, $Z ^ { j , K }$ specifies the recovery payment at the default time $\tau .$ provided that before the default time, we are in the state $j ;$ ; and $C$ is the credit rating process. This definition of claim is very general and covers many different types of claims. 

Remark 16.31 If we put $X ^ { i } = Y$ for each i, where Y is $\mathcal { F } _ { T } \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e }$ , bounded random variable, then the promised payment depends only on the default time: 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} X ^ {i} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {T} = i \}} = Y \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {T} = i \}} = Y \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {T} \neq K \}} = Y \mathbb {1} _ {\{\tau > T \}}.
$$

Remark 16.32 Since 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \int_ {\left[ \left. 0, t \wedge T \right] \right]} Z _ {u} ^ {i, K} d H _ {u} ^ {i, K} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} Z _ {\tau} ^ {i, K} \mathbb {1} _ {\{0 <   \tau \leq t \wedge T, C _ {\tau -} = i \}} = Z _ {\tau} ^ {C _ {\tau -}, K} \mathbb {1} _ {\{0 <   \tau \leq t \wedge T \}},
$$

the recovery process allows recovery depending on the rating of the bond before the default time τ. 

Now, we define the dividend process which describes the cash flows from the claim in the interval [0, T]. 

Definition 16.33 The dividend process $D = ( D _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ of the claim $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ maturing at T equals, for $t \geq 0$ 

$$
D _ {t} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \bigg (X ^ {i} H _ {T} ^ {i} \mathbb {1} _ {[   [ T, + \infty ]   [} (t) + \int_ {\left[   [ 0, t \wedge T ]   ] \right.} H _ {u} ^ {i} d A _ {u} ^ {i} + \sum_ {j \neq i \in \mathcal {K}} \int_ {\left[   [ 0, t \wedge T ]   ] \right.} Z _ {u} ^ {i, j} d H _ {u} ^ {i, j} \bigg).\tag{16.17}
$$

Remark 16.34 For fixed i, if at time t the rating process changes from state i to state j, then the promised dividend $A _ { t } ^ { i } - A _ { t - } ^ { i }$ is not passed over to the holder of the claim, and if the rating process changes from some j to i, then the promised dividend $A _ { t } ^ { i } - A _ { t - } ^ { i }$ is passed over to the holder of the claim. 

Example 16.35 Consider a defaultable bond with fractional recovery of par value. In this case, the bond’s holder receives at maturity time T its face value (say 1 unit of cash), provided that default did not occur before or at T. If the default occurred before or at time $T$ , the recovery $\delta _ { C _ { \tau - } }$ is paid at the default time τ to the bond holder. $\mathrm { \bf S o }$ , the recovery payment depends on the predefault rating $C _ { \tau - } .$ , and it is assumed that the recovery $\delta _ { i } \in [ 0 , 1 )$ is a fixed number for each $i \in \mathcal { K } \backslash K$ . By taking 

$$
X ^ {i} = 1, \quad A ^ {i} = 0, \quad Z ^ {i, K} = \delta_ {i} \quad \text { for } i = 1, \ldots , K - 1, \qquad Z ^ {i, j} = 0 \quad \text { for } j \neq K,
$$

we see that a defaultable bond is a claim in the sense of our definition. The dividend process for such a claim equals 

$$
D _ {t} = \mathbb {1} _ {\{\tau > T \}} \mathbb {1} _ {[ [ T, + \infty ] [} (t) + \delta_ {C _ {\tau -}} \mathbb {1} _ {\{0 <   \tau \leq t \wedge T \}}.
$$

Example 16.36 Another example is a defaultable credit-sensitive note. It is a corporate bond with coupons linked to the rating of corporation. The coupons of this note are paid at prespecified coupon dates $0 < T _ { 1 } < T _ { 2 } < \cdot \cdot \cdot < T _ { n }$ if default does not arise and the value of the coupon is contingent on rating corporate at the coupon date. If a default occurred before or at time $T$ , the recovery $\delta _ { C _ { \tau - } }$ is paid at the default time τ to the bond holders. It is assumed that $\delta _ { i } \in [ 0 , 1 )$ is fixed for each $i \in \mathcal { K } \backslash K$ So 

$$
X ^ {i} = 1, \quad Z ^ {i, K} = \delta_ {i} \quad \mathrm{for} i \leq K - 1, \qquad Z ^ {i, j} = 0 \quad \mathrm{for} j \neq K,
$$

$$
A _ {t} ^ {i} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \mathbb {1} _ {\{t \geq T _ {j} \}} d _ {i, j},
$$

where $d _ { i , j }$ are fixed constants chosen in advance, and the dividend process of this note is given by 

$$
D _ {t} = \mathbb {1} _ {\{\tau > T \}} \mathbb {1} _ {[ [ T, + \infty ] [ (t)} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \int_ {[ [ 0, t \wedge T ] ]} \delta_ {i} d H _ {u} ^ {i, K} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \int_ {[ [ 0, t \wedge T ] ]} H _ {u} ^ {i} d A _ {u} ^ {i}.
$$

Example 16.37 We can consider modification of the example above with $A _ { t } ^ { i } = d _ { i } t$ which corresponds to continuous payments at the rate $d _ { i }$ , provided that at time t the rating is equal to i. The dividend process of this note is given by 

$$
D _ {t} = \mathbb {1} _ {\{\tau > T \}} \mathbb {1} _ {[ [ T, + \infty ] [ (t) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \int_ {\left\| 0, t \wedge T \right\|} \delta_ {i} d H _ {u} ^ {i, K} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \int_ {\left\| 0, t \wedge T \right\|} H _ {u} ^ {i} d _ {i} d u.}
$$

## 16.4.2 Pricing ofRating-Sensitive Claims

Now, we consider the problem of pricing of rating-sensitive claims. We put ourselves in an arbitrage-free framework, which means that we assume existence of a spot martingale measure $\mathbb { Q }$ for the underlying market. We fix $\mathbb { Q }$ in what follows. As usual, the spot martingale measure $\mathbb { Q }$ is a measure related to the choice of the saving account B as a numéraire. Then the price process discounted by B of any tradable security (nondividend paying) is a martingale under $\mathbb { Q }$ . We assume that the dynamics of saving account B is given by 

$$
d B _ {t} = r _ {t} B _ {t} d t, \qquad B _ {0} = 1,
$$

where r is a nonnegative F-progressively measurable stochastic process. So $B ^ { - 1 }$ is a discount factor. In what follows, we assume that the process C of rating migration is an F-DS Markov chain under $\mathbb { Q }$ with intensity process Λ which satisfies the following integrability condition: 

$$
\mathbb {E} _ {\mathbb {Q}} \left(\int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \sum_ {i \in \mathcal {K}} \left| \lambda_ {i, i} (s) \right| d s\right) <   \infty .\tag{16.18}
$$

In this subsection, conditional expectations are calculated under spot martingale measure $\mathbb { Q } ;$ ; hence, for short, we shall write E instead of $\mathbb { E } _ { \mathbb { Q } }$ 

The main theorem of this subsection gives a convenient form of the ex-dividend price process S of a defaultable rating-sensitive claim. It generalizes the results of Bielecki et al. [8] obtained for $K = 2$ 

Theorem 16.38 Let $( X , A , Z , \tau , C )$ be a defaultable rating-sensitive claim with $X$ $Z ,$ , A bounded. For $t < T$ , the value ofex-dividend price is given by theformula 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S _ {t} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} = \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K - 1} B _ {t} \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {X ^ {j} p _ {i , j} (t , T)}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} B _ {u} ^ {- 1} p _ {i, j} (t, u) d A _ {u} ^ {j} \right. \\ \left. + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \frac {Z _ {u} ^ {j , k}}{B _ {u}} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, k} (u) d u \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right). \end{array} \tag {1}\tag{16.19}
$$

In the proof of theorem, we need the following lemmas which generalize results of Bielecki et al. [4, Corollary 5.1.1, Propositions 5.1.1, and 5.1.2] to the case of multiple ratings. In the proofs, we will use the immersion property of filtrations connected with F-DS Markov chains. 

Lemma 16.39 Let X be a bounded $\mathcal { F } _ { T }$ -measurable random variable, and $j \in \mathcal { K } \backslash$ K. Then 

$$
\mathbb {E} (X \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {T} = j \}} | \mathcal {G} _ {t}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \bigl (X p _ {i, j} (t, T) \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigr).
$$

Proof This is an easy consequence of the definition of an F-DS Markov chain and the immersion property (see [16, Proposition 3.4]). Indeed, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} (X \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {T} = j \}} | \mathcal {G} _ {t}) = \mathbb {E} \big (X \mathbb {E} \big (\mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {T} = j \}} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {\infty} \vee \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {C} \big) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big) \\ \qquad = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \big (X p _ {i, j} (t, T) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big) \\ \qquad = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \big (X p _ {i, j} (t, T) \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big). \end{array}
$$

Lemma 16.40 Let Z be a bounded F-predictable stochasticprocess, and $j \in \mathcal { K } \backslash K$ Under condition (16.18),for $k \neq j$ , we have 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} Z _ {u} d H _ {u} ^ {j, k} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t}\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = 1 \}} \mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} Z _ {u} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, k} (u) d u \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right).\tag{16.20}
$$

Proof Fix $k \neq j \in \mathcal { K }$ . Because 

$$
\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} Z _ {u}   d H _ {u} ^ {j, k} = \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} Z _ {u}   d M _ {u} ^ {j, k} + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} Z _ {u} H _ {u} ^ {j} \lambda_ {j, k} (u)   d u,
$$

and $M ^ { j , k }$ is a martingale and $Z$ a bounded process, we have 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} Z _ {u} d H _ {u} ^ {j, k} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t}\right) = \mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} Z _ {u} H _ {u} ^ {j} \lambda_ {j, k} (u) d u \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t}\right) = I.
$$

Using the conditional version of Fubini’s theorem (see, e.g., Applebaum [2, p. 12]), the definition of an F-DS Markov chain, hypothesis H, and taking $\widetilde { \mathcal { G } } _ { t } : = \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } \setminus \mathcal { F } _ { t } ^ { \tilde { C } }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I = \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \mathbb {E} \big (Z _ {u} H _ {u} ^ {j} \lambda_ {j, k} (u) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big) d u = \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \mathbb {E} \big (\mathbb {E} \big (Z _ {u} H _ {u} ^ {j} \lambda_ {j, k} (u) \big | \widetilde {\mathcal {G}} _ {t} \big) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big) d u \\ = \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \mathbb {E} \Bigg (Z _ {u} \lambda_ {j, k} (u) \Bigg (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \Bigg) \Bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \Bigg) d u \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \mathbb {E} \big (Z _ {u} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, k} (u) \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big) d u \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \Bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} Z _ {u} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, k} (u) d u \Bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \Bigg), \end{array}
$$

and this completes the proof. 

Lemma 16.41 Let A be an F-predictable bounded stochastic process offinite variation. Under condition (16.18),for any $j \in \mathcal { K } \setminus K$ , we have 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} H _ {u} ^ {j} d A _ {u} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t}\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} p _ {i, j} (t, u) d A _ {u} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right).
$$

Proof We follow the idea from Bielecki and Rutkowski’s book [4], in which the case with two states (default and no default) is considered. Fix t. Define $\widetilde { A } _ { u } \mathrel { \mathop : } = A _ { u } - A _ { t }$ for $u \in [ t , v ]$ . Obviously, this is an $\mathbb { F } .$ -predictable bounded process of finite variation, and $\widetilde { A } _ { t } = 0$ . The integrals with respect to A and $\widetilde { A }$ are equal, and therefore, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} H _ {u} ^ {j} d A _ {u} \Big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg) = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} H _ {u} ^ {j} d \widetilde {A} _ {u} \Big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg) \\ \qquad = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\widetilde {A} _ {v} H _ {v} ^ {j} - \widetilde {A} _ {t} H _ {t} ^ {j} - \int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \widetilde {A} _ {u -} d H _ {u} ^ {j} \Big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg) \\ \qquad = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\widetilde {A} _ {v} H _ {v} ^ {j} - \int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \widetilde {A} _ {u -} d H _ {u} ^ {j} \Big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg) = I _ {1} + I _ {2}, \end{array}
$$

where 

$$
I _ {1} := \mathbb {E} \big (\widetilde {A} _ {v} H _ {v} ^ {j} \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big), \qquad I _ {2} := \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \widetilde {A} _ {u -} d H _ {u} ^ {j} \Big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg).
$$

Since $\widetilde { A } _ { v }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty }$ -measurable, it follows that 

$$
I _ {1} = \mathbb {E} \big (\widetilde {A} _ {v} \mathbb {E} \big (H _ {v} ^ {j} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {\infty} \vee \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {C} \big) \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \big (\widetilde {A} _ {v} p _ {i, j} (t, v) \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big).
$$

Now we calculate $I _ { 2 }$ . By boundedness of ${ \widetilde { A } } ,$ , using martingale property of $M ^ { j }$ , the conditional Fubini theorem, hypothesis H, and the Kolmogorov forward equation (16.12), we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I _ {2} = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \widetilde {A} _ {u -} d M _ {u} ^ {j} + \int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \widetilde {A} _ {u -} \lambda_ {C _ {u}, j} (u)   d u \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg) \\ = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \widetilde {A} _ {u -} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K - 1} H _ {u} ^ {k} \lambda_ {k, j} (u)   d u \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg) = \int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\widetilde {A} _ {u -} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K - 1} H _ {u} ^ {k} \lambda_ {k, j} (u) \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg)   d u \\ = \int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\widetilde {A} _ {u -} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {E} \big (H _ {u} ^ {k} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {\infty} \vee \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {C} \big) \lambda_ {k, j} (u) \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg)   d u \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\widetilde {A} _ {u -} \bigg (\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K - 1} p _ {i, k} (t, u) \lambda_ {k, j} (u) \bigg) \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg)   d u \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \widetilde {A} _ {u -} \bigg (\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K - 1} p _ {i, k} (t, u) \lambda_ {k, j} (u) \bigg)   d u \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg) \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \widetilde {A} _ {u -} d p _ {i, j} (t, u) \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg). \end{array}
$$

Hence, 

$$
I _ {1} + I _ {2} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\widetilde {A} _ {v} p _ {i, j} (t, v) - \int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} \widetilde {A} _ {u -} d p _ {i, j} (t, u) \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg),
$$

and by integration by parts, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I _ {1} + I _ {2} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\widetilde {A} _ {t} p _ {i, j} (t, t) + \int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} p _ {i, j} (t, u)   d \widetilde {A} _ {u} \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg) \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, v \rrbracket} p _ {i, j} (t, u)   d A _ {u} \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg). \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 16.38 The theorem follows immediately from (16.17) and the above lemmas applied to $\begin{array} { r } { \widetilde { X } : = \frac { X } { B _ { T } } , d \widetilde { A } _ { u } : = \frac { 1 } { B _ { u } } d A _ { u } , \widetilde { Z } _ { u } : = \frac { \check { Z } _ { u } } { B _ { u } } } \end{array}$ . Of course, Assumption INT-1 is satisfied. - 

Remark 16.42 In Theorem 16.38, we have assumed that X, A, Z are bounded. This assumption can be relaxed, e.g., one can assume weaker conditions: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} \big (B _ {T} ^ {- 1} \big | X ^ {i} \big | \big) <   \infty , \quad \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\left[   \left[ 0, T \right] \right]} \big | A _ {u} ^ {i} \big | ^ {2} \big | \lambda_ {C _ {u}, i} (u) \big | d u \bigg) <   \infty \quad \forall i \in \mathcal {K} \setminus K, \\ \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\left[   \left[ 0, T \right] \right]} \big | Z _ {u} ^ {i, j} \big | ^ {2} H _ {u -} ^ {i} \lambda_ {i, j} (u) d u \bigg) <   \infty \quad \forall i \neq j, i, j \in \mathcal {K} \setminus K. \end{array}\tag{16.21}
$$

Under these assumptions, the results of Lemmas 16.39–16.41 remain valid. Moreover, these conditions imply that INT-1 is satisfied, so the ex-dividend price is well defined. Indeed, it is easily seen that Assumption INT-1 for a dividend process D of a defaultable rating-sensitive claim $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ is equivalent to 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} \big (B _ {T} ^ {- 1} \big | X ^ {i} \big | \big) <   \infty , \quad \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} H _ {u} ^ {i} B _ {u} ^ {- 1} d \big | A ^ {i} \big | _ {u} \bigg) <   \infty \quad \forall i \in \mathcal {K} \setminus K, \\ \mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \big | Z _ {u} ^ {i, j} \big | B _ {u} ^ {- 1} H _ {u -} ^ {i} d H _ {u} ^ {j} \bigg) <   \infty \quad \forall i \neq j,   i, j \in \mathcal {K} \setminus K, \end{array}
$$

and (16.21) imply these conditions. 

## 16.4.3 Examples ofPricing of Selected Instruments

In a series of propositions, we now give examples of application of general Theorem 16.38. All these results are stated under the assumption that the migration process C is an F-DS Markov chain with intensity process $( \varLambda _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ . Whenever we apply results based on Lemma 16.40, we assume that $( \varLambda _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ satisfies condition (16.18). 

## Defaultable Bond with Fractional Recovery of Par Value

This simple example of a rating-sensitive claim is described in Example 16.35. We only stress that the recovery payment is contingent on the predefault rating, i.e., on $C _ { \tau - }$ 

Proposition 16.43 The ex-dividend price $D ^ { \delta }$ of a defaultable bond with fractional recovery ofpar value hasfor $t < T$ , on the set $\{ C _ { t } = i \}$ , theform 

$$
D ^ {\delta} (t, T) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K - 1} B _ {t} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {p _ {i , j} (t , T)}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \frac {\delta_ {j}}{B _ {u}} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, K} (u) d u \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg).
$$

## Credit Sensitive Note (CNS)-Resetting at Coupon Payment Date

Recall that CSN are, generally speaking, corporate coupon bonds that pay coupons which are sensitive to credit rating of a firm assigned by some rating agency (see Example 16.36). Coupons are usually greater if the rating is worse. 

Proposition 16.44 The ex-dividend price of a Credit Sensitive Note with coupons resetting at coupon payment date is,for $t < T$ , equal to 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S _ {t} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} = \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {E} \bigg (e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r _ {u} d u} p _ {i, j} (t, T) + \sum_ {k: t <   T _ {k}} e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T _ {k}} r _ {u} d u} d _ {j, k} p _ {i, j} (t, T _ {k}) \\ \qquad + \delta_ {j} \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {u} r _ {v} d v} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, K} (u) d u \Bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg). \end{array}
$$

Remark 16.45 Specifying d by $d _ { j , k } = s _ { U } ( j - i _ { U } ) ^ { + }$ where $s _ { U }$ is constant, one can include a rating-triggering step-up feature to coupon payments. If the rating crosses level $i _ { U }$ (step-up), then the coupon will increase proportionally. The socalled Rating-Triggered Step-Up Bonds were issued by some European telecom companies, e.g., Deutsche Telecom, France Telecom; for details, see Lando and Mortensen [20]. 

## Credit Sensitive Note—Continuous Coupon Payments

One can consider CSN with coupons that are paid continuously in time at rate $d _ { C _ { t } }$ depending on rating state at t (see Example 16.37). This is a mathematical idealization of the previous case, rather than a real-life example, but it might be seen as approximation of discrete payments considered in the previous subsection. 

Proposition 16.46 The ex-dividend price ofthe Credit Sensitive Note with continuous coupon payments is,for $t \leq T$ , equal to 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S _ {t} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} = \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {E} \bigg (e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T} r _ {u} d u} p _ {i, j} (t, T) + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} d _ {j} e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {u} r _ {v} d v} p _ {i, j} (t, u) d u \\ \qquad + \delta_ {j} \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {u} r _ {v} d v} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, K} (u) d u \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg). \end{array}
$$

## Credit Default Swap

Credit Default Swap is an agreement between two parties, protection buyer and protection seller. This agreement has two legs: 

Premium Leg: The protection buyer agrees to pay a fixed amount κ (CDS spread) at fixed times $\mathcal { T } = \{ T _ { 1 } < T _ { 2 } < \cdot \cdot \cdot < T _ { n } \}$ . He pays $\kappa \varDelta _ { k }$ at time $T _ { k }$ (where $\varDelta \ v { k } : =$ $T _ { k } - T _ { k - 1 } )$ , provided that no default has occurred before or at $T _ { k }$ . Then for $t < T _ { n }$ the value of the premium leg is equal to 

$$
V _ {P} (t) = B _ {t} \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {\kappa}{B _ {\tau}} (\tau - T _ {\beta (\tau) - 1}) \mathbb {1} _ {\{t <   \tau \leq T _ {n} \}} + \sum_ {k = \beta (t)} ^ {n} \frac {\kappa \Delta_ {k}}{B _ {T _ {k}}} \mathbb {1} _ {\{\tau > T _ {k} \}} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t}\right),
$$

where $\beta ( t ) : = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ j : T _ { j } \geq t \}$ 

Default leg: The protection seller agrees to cover all losses on the reference bond, provided that the loss occurs before the protection horizon $T _ { n }$ . For $t < T _ { n }$ , the value of this default leg is equal to 

$$
V _ {D} (t) = B _ {t} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {1 - \delta_ {C _ {\tau -}}}{B _ {\tau}} \mathbb {1} _ {\{t <   \tau \leq T _ {n} \}} \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg).
$$

If we know the value of the spread, i.e., κ, then the CDS value at time t is the difference between the premium leg and the default leg, 

$$
\operatorname{CDS} (t, \mathcal {T}, \kappa) = V _ {P} (t) - V _ {D} (t).
$$

A market CDS spread (fair spread) $\kappa = \kappa ( t , \mathcal { T } )$ is agreed at contract’s inception (at some time $t < T _ { 1 } )$ in such a way that the value of the contract is 0, $\mathrm { i . e . , C D S } ( t , \mathcal { T } , \kappa ) = 0$ . The next theorem, which is an easy consequence of Theorem 16.38, provides formulas for the value of both legs expressed through the conditional transition probability process P and intensity process Λ, so we can calculate CDS(t, T, κ). 

Theorem 16.47 Assume that C is an $\mathbb { F } { - } D S$ Markov chain with intensity matrix process $( \varLambda _ { u } ) _ { u \geq 0 }$ and conditional transition probability process $P ( s , t )$ . The value of the default leg ofCDS,for $t < T _ { n }$ , is equal to 

$$
V _ {D} (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \left(\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K - 1} (1 - \delta_ {j}) \int_ {t} ^ {T _ {n}} \mathbb {E} \left(e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {u} r _ {v} d v} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, K} (u) | \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right) d u\right).
$$

The value ofthe premium leg ofCDS is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V _ {P} (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {t} = i \}} \Bigg (\sum_ {k = \beta (t)} ^ {n} \mathbb {E} \big (e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {T _ {k}} r _ {u} d u} \big (1 - p _ {i, K} (t, T _ {k}) \big) \varDelta_ {k} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big) \\ \qquad + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K - 1} \int_ {t} ^ {T _ {n}} (u - T _ {\beta (u) - 1}) \mathbb {E} \big (e ^ {- \int_ {t} ^ {u} r _ {u} d u} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, K} (u) \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big) d u \Bigg). \end{array}
$$

In the case of the model given in Example 16.22, one can obtain a more explicit formula for values of the default leg and the premium leg of the CDS (see Sect. 4.2 in [15]). 

## 16.5 Hedging of Rating-Sensitive Claims

Considering the problem of hedging requires a detailed description of the market. Especially, we have to specify instruments which we use in hedging. We assume that on the market, we can put money into a saving account and trade in n nondividend paying default free assets with price Y. Let $\overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = } \overset { \mathbf { \check { F } } } { = }$ , C be a rating migration process, and R be an ex-dividend price process of a $( K - 1 )$ )-dimensional vector of rating-sensitive claims. To construct a hedging strategy for a given payment stream D, according to Lemma 16.17, it is convenient to have some form of martingale representation of discounted cash flows accumulated till maturity T, i.e., a martingale representation of 

$$
\int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} d D _ {u}.
$$

In what follows, we find such representation. We assume throughout the rest of the paper that the following hypotheses hold: 

Assumption 16.48 There exists a martingale measure $\mathbb { Q }$ for the market consisting with the saving account and the default free assets with price process Y, i.e., a measure such that $\mathbb { Q } \sim \mathbb { P }$ and $Y ^ { * } = Y / B$ is an F-martingale. Moreover, we assume that the market is F-complete in the sense that every square-integrable $\mathcal { F } _ { T }$ -measurable random variable is attainable. 

Assumption 16.49 There exists an equivalent martingale measure for the extended market, i.e., a probability measure $\mathbb { Q } ^ { * } \sim \mathbb { P }$ such that $( Y ^ { * } , R ^ { c * } )$ is a $\mathbb { G } = \mathbb { F } ^ { B , Y , C } .$ martingale. 

Assumption 16.50 The rating migration process C is an F-doubly stochastic Markov chain under $\mathbb { Q } ^ { * }$ with intensity matrix process Λ and absorbing state K. 

Remark 16.51 For $\mathbb { Q }$ and any $\mathbb { Q } ^ { * }$ satisfying the above assumptions, there holds 

$$
\mathbb {Q} ^ {*} | _ {\mathcal {F} _ {T}} = \mathbb {Q} | _ {\mathcal {F} _ {T}}.
$$

Remark 16.52 Let C be an F-DS Markov chain under a probability measure P. The process $C$ does not have to be an F-DS Markov chain under an equivalent probability measure $\mathbb { Q } .$ . However, there is a large class of equivalent probability measures under which C is an F-DS Markov chain (see [16]). 

Remark 16.53 Obviously, processes obtained from M and L by removing the last Kth coordinate are also G-local martingales. The last row of Λ contains only zeros since the state K is an absorbing state of C, and so 

$$
\widetilde {M} _ {t} := \widetilde {H} _ {t} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \widetilde {\Lambda} _ {u} ^ {\top} \widetilde {H} _ {u} d u,\tag{16.22}
$$

wheredenotes the matrix (vector) with the last row and last column (last coordinate) deleted. The same remark concerns L: 

$$
\widetilde {L} _ {t} := \widetilde {Q} ^ {\top} (0, t) \widetilde {H} _ {t} = \widetilde {H} _ {0} + \int_ {\left[ \left[ 0, t \right] \right]} \widetilde {Q} ^ {\top} (0, u) d \widetilde {M} _ {u},\tag{16.23}
$$

where $\widetilde { Q } ( 0 , u )$ denotes the matrix $Q ( 0 , u )$ with the last row and last column deleted. However, for simplicity, we abuse notation and in what follows write M, L, Q, Λ for $\widetilde { M } , \widetilde { L } , \widetilde { Q } , \widetilde { A }$ . We insist here on working with these “reduced” versions of matrices/vectors since they are in some sense “minimal.” The reduced form models of credit risk can be considered as two-state rating models, and martingale representation theorems are also given with “reduced” versions of vectors/matrices (see Blanchet-Scaillet [9]). Martingales which correspond to M and L are in this case given by 

$$
M _ {t} ^ {\prime} = \mathbb {1} _ {\{\tau \leq t \}} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mathbb {1} _ {\{\tau > u \}} \lambda_ {u} d u, \qquad L _ {t} ^ {\prime} = e ^ {\int_ {0} ^ {t} \lambda_ {u} d u} \mathbb {1} _ {\{\tau > t \}}.
$$

In the following, all conditional expectations are calculated under the martingale measure $\mathbb { Q } ^ { * }$ ; hence, for short, we shall write E instead of $\mathbb { E } _ { \mathbb { Q } ^ { * } }$ . We divide our results into two subsections. 

In the first part, for simplicity of exposition, we assume that the rating-sensitive claims are of a very special form, namely, they are $T$ maturing defaultable claims with only terminal payoffs at time $T$ of the form $\mathbb { 1 } _ { \{ C _ { T = i \} } }$ . The vector of prices is denoted by 

$$
R (t, T) = \left(R _ {1} (t, T), \dots , R _ {K - 1} (t, T)\right) ^ {\top},\tag{16.24}
$$

and according to our convention, $R ^ { c }$ denotes its cumulative price, so we have $R _ { i } ^ { c } ( T , T ) = \mathbb { 1 } _ { \{ C _ { T } = i \} }$ , whereas $R _ { i } ( T , T ) = 0$ (see Remark 16.5). We show how to deal with hedging of rating-sensitive claims by using rating digital options. In the subsequent subsection, we will show that similar results can be derived for more complex primary instruments with a little effort. 

## 16.5.1 Hedging with Rating Digital Options

Our main aim in this subsection is to show that general rating-sensitive claims can be replicated by trading in some default free assets and a system of $K - 1$ special rating-sensitive claims, namely the rating digital options. We will proceed in two steps. First, we provide a replication strategy for very simple rating-sensitive claims, i.e., $( X , 0 , 0 , C , \tau )$ , and in the second step, we show how to deal with the case of a general rating-sensitive claim $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ . Although from the result of the second step we can easily obtain a replication strategy for simple rating-sensitive claims, we believe that this makes the presentation of the results more transparent. We want to apply Lemma 16.17, so we need to know the dynamics of the discounted cumulative prices $R ^ { c * }$ of the primary assets (which are rating-sensitive claims) under the martingale measure $\mathbb { Q } ^ { * }$ . Secondly, we find a representation of the martingale $S ^ { c * }$ given by formula (16.3) as a stochastic integral with respect to some martingale and then translate it into a stochastic integral with respect to discounted primary assets as in (16.7) of Lemma 16.17. The proposition below gives the dynamics of the vector-valued process $R ^ { c * }$ which represents the discounted cumulative price of rating digital options (see Remark 16.2): 

$$
R _ {j} ^ {c *} (t, T) := \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {\mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {T} = j \}}}{B _ {T}} \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg),
$$

where R is given by (16.24). 

Proposition 16.54 Assume that rating digital options with the price R are tradable assets. Then we have the following representation for the vector $R ^ { c }$ of cumulative prices of T-maturing rating digital options: 

$$
R ^ {c} (t, T) = \widehat {R} (t, T) ^ {\top} H _ {t},
$$

where 

$$
\widehat {R} (t, T) := B _ {t} \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {P (t , T)}{B _ {T}} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right).\tag{16.25}
$$

Moreover, $R ^ { c * } ( t , T ) : = R ^ { c } ( t , T ) B _ { t } ^ { - 1 }$ has thefollowing dynamics: 

$$
d R ^ {c *} (t, T) = \left(B _ {t} ^ {- 1} \widehat {R} (t -, T)\right) ^ {\top} d M _ {t} + \left(H _ {t} ^ {\top} Q (0, t) d m _ {t}\right) ^ {\top},
$$

where $M _ { t }$ is defined by (16.22), and $m _ { t }$ is a matrix-valued martingale defined by the formula 

$$
[ m _ {t} ] _ {i, j} := \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {p _ {i , j} (0 , T)}{B _ {T}} \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg).\tag{16.26}
$$

Proof For the jth coordinate of $R ^ { c } ( t , T )$ , we have 

$$
\frac {R _ {j} ^ {c} (t , T)}{B _ {t}} = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {\mathbb {1} _ {\{C _ {T} = j \}}}{B _ {T}} \bigg | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \bigg) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} H _ {t} ^ {i} \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {p _ {i , j} (t , T)}{B _ {T}} \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg),
$$

where the second equality follows from the fact that $C$ is assumed to be an F-DS stochastic Markov chain. So, in the matrix-vector notation, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c}\frac {R ^ {c} (t , T)}{B _ {t}} = \left(\mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (t , T)}{B _ {T}} \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right)\left. \right) ^ {\top} H _ {t} = \bigg (Q (0, t) \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (0 , T)}{B _ {T}} \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg) \bigg) ^ {\top} H _ {t}\\= \left(\mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (0 , T)}{B _ {T}} \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right) \bigg) ^ {\top} L _ {t} = m _ {t} ^ {\top} L _ {t}.\end{array}
$$

By integration by parts it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d R ^ {c *} (t, T) = m _ {t -} ^ {\top} Q ^ {\top} (0, t)   d M _ {t} + \left(d m _ {t} ^ {\top}\right) Q ^ {\top} (0, t) H _ {t -} + \varDelta m _ {t} ^ {\top} Q ^ {\top} (0, t) \varDelta H _ {t} \\ = \left(Q (0, t) m _ {t -}\right) ^ {\top} d M _ {t} + \left(H _ {t -} ^ {\top} Q (0, t)   d m _ {t}\right) ^ {\top}, \end{array}
$$

where the last equality follows from Proposition 16.29. 

## Remark 16.55

(a) We have derived formulas for cumulative prices of rating digital options. Since these instruments have only terminal payment at the maturity time $T$ , the exdividend price process R is different from the cumulative price process $R ^ { c }$ only at maturity time (see Remark 16.5). 

(b) Elements of the matrix $\widehat { R }$ are conditional cumulative prices of rating digital options $R , \mathrm { i . e . , } [ \widehat { R } ( t , T ) ] _ { i , j }$ is the price of the digital option on the jth rating on the set $\{ C _ { t } = i \}$ 

Lemma 16.56 For $p _ { i , j } ( 0 , T ) / B _ { T }$ which is an ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { T }$ measurable random variable, $i , j \in \mathcal { K } \backslash K$ , there exist F-predictable stochastic processes $\mu ^ { l , i , j } , l = 1 , \dots , n$ , such that thefollowing representation holds: 

$$
\frac {p _ {i , j} (0 , T)}{B _ {T}} = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {p _ {i , j} (0 , T)}{B _ {T}} \bigg) + \int_ {\left\| 0, T \right\|} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \mu_ {t} ^ {l, i, j} d Y _ {t} ^ {l *}.
$$

Ifwe denote by $\mu _ { t } ^ { ( l ) }$ the matrix $[ \mu _ { t } ^ { ( l ) } ] _ { i , j } : = \mu _ { t } ^ { l , i , j }$ , then the above representation can be written in thefollowing matrixform: 

$$
\frac {P (0 , T)}{B _ {T}} = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (0 , T)}{B _ {T}} \bigg) + \int_ {\left[ 0, T \right]} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \mu_ {t} ^ {(l)}   d Y _ {t} ^ {l *}.\tag{16.27}
$$

Proof The random variable $p _ { i , j } ( 0 , T ) / B _ { T }$ is bounded, hence it is square integrable, and therefore the assertion follows by Assumption 16.48. - 

Lemma 16.56 gives the representation of matrix-valued martingale $( m _ { t } ) _ { t \in [ [ 0 , T ] ] }$ defined by formula $( 1 6 . 2 6 )$ . The following proposition gives a representation of the martingale $\mathbb { E } ( X ^ { \top } H _ { T } / B _ { T } | { \mathcal G } _ { t } )$ in terms of stochastic integrals with respect to the martingales $( m _ { t } ^ { X } ) _ { t \in [ [ 0 , T ] ] }$ and $( M _ { t } ) _ { t \geq 0 }$ 

Proposition 16.57 Let $T > 0$ , and $X = ( X ^ { 1 } , \ldots , X ^ { K - 1 } ) ^ { \top }$ be a vector of $\mathcal { F } _ { T }$ measurable random variables such that $\frac { X ^ { \top } H _ { T } } { B _ { T } }$ is square integrable. Then the Gmartingale defined by 

$$
X ^ {c *} (t, T) := \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {X ^ {\top} H _ {T}}{B _ {T}} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t}\right), \quad t \in [ 0, T ],\tag{16.28}
$$

has the representation 

$$
X ^ {c *} (t, T) = B _ {t} ^ {- 1} \widehat {X} (t, T) ^ {\top} H _ {t},
$$

where ${ \widehat { X } } ( t , T )$ is defined by 

$$
\widehat {X} (t, T) := B _ {t} \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {P (t , T) X}{B _ {T}} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right).\tag{16.29}
$$

Moreover, the martingale $X ^ { c * }$ has the following representation via stochastic integrals w.r.t. M and $m ^ { \check { X } }$ : 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X ^ {c *} (t, T) = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (0 , T) X}{B _ {T}} \bigg) ^ {\top} H _ {0} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \left(B _ {t} ^ {- 1} \widehat {X} (u -, T)\right) ^ {\top} d M _ {u} \\ \qquad + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} H _ {u -} ^ {\top} Q (0, u)   d m _ {u} ^ {X}, \end{array}\tag{16.30}
$$

where $m ^ { X }$ is the vector-valued F-martingale given by 

$$
m _ {t} ^ {X} := \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (0 , T) X}{B _ {T}} \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg).
$$

Proof The proof is analogous to the proof of Proposition 16.54. 

Remark 16.58 

(a) The coordinates of the vector $\widehat { X }$ are conditional cumulative prices of the claim $( X , 0 , 0 , C , \tau )$ , i.e., $[ \widehat { X } ( t , T ) ] _ { i }$ is the price of the digital option on the set $\{ C _ { t } = i \}$ , provided that $t < T$ 

(b) The stochastic integrals in formula (16.30) are stopped at $\tau .$ . The fact that the first integral is stopped at $\tau$ is obvious and follows from the fact that M is stopped at τ. The second integral is also stopped at τ, since e Ht− $H _ { t - }$ is constant and equal to zero after $\tau$ 

Corollary 16.59 Assume that $X / B _ { T }$ is an $\mathbb { R } ^ { K - 1 }$ -valued vector ofsquare-integrable random variables. Then there exist F-predictable stochastic processes $\mu ^ { X , l }$ (with values in $\mathbb { R } ^ { K - 1 } )$ such that 

$$
m _ {T} ^ {X} = m _ {0} ^ {X} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \mu_ {t} ^ {X, l} d Y _ {t} ^ {l, *}.\tag{16.31}
$$

Proof Note that $P ( 0 , T ) ^ { \top } X / B _ { T }$ is a square-integrable random variable, and therefore Assumption 16.48 implies the desired representation. - 

Representation (16.31) is a generalization of Lemma 16.56 and gives a representation of the martingale $( m _ { t } ^ { X } ) _ { t \in [ 0 , T ] }$ 

The theorem below yields a replication strategy for the claim $( X , 0 , 0 , C , \tau )$ maturing at $T > 0$ 

Theorem 16.60 Let $( X , 0 , 0 , C , \tau )$ be a rating-sensitive claim such that $X B _ { T } ^ { - 1 }$ is square integrable. Assume thatfor each $t , \widehat { X } ( t , T ) \in \operatorname { I m } ( \widehat { R } ( t , T ) )$ , where $\widehat { R }$ is given by (16.25), and $\widehat { X } \ b y \ ( 1 6 . 2 9 )$ . Then the portfolio $( \psi , \varphi , \gamma )$ with the initial capital $\begin{array} { r } { V _ { 0 } ( \phi ) = \mathbb { E } ( \frac { P ( 0 , T ) X } { B _ { T } } ) ^ { \top } H _ { 0 } } \end{array}$ is a D-financing portfolio that replicates the claim $( X , 0 , 0 , C , \tau )$ , provided that $\gamma$ is given as a minimum norm solution to the following system oflinear equations: 

$$
\widehat {R} (t -, T) \gamma_ {t} = \widehat {X} (t -, T),\tag{16.32}
$$

and $\psi$ , ϕ are defined by 

$$
\varphi_ {t} ^ {l} = H _ {t -} ^ {\top} Q (0, t) \big (\mu_ {t} ^ {X, l} - \mu_ {t} ^ {(l)} \gamma_ {t} \big),
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \psi_ {t} = V _ {0} (\phi) + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {u} ^ {l} d Y _ {u} ^ {l *} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \gamma_ {t} ^ {\top} d R ^ {c *} (u, T) \\ - \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {t} ^ {l} Y _ {t} ^ {l, *} - \gamma_ {t} ^ {\top} R ^ {*} (t, T) - \frac {X ^ {\top} H _ {T}}{B _ {T}} 1 _ {\llbracket T, \infty \rrbracket (t)} \end{array}\tag{16.33}
$$

with $\mu ^ { X , l }$ given by (16.31) and $\mu _ { t } ^ { ( l ) }$ by (16.27). 

Proof We have to show that there exists a D-financing portfolio for the dividend process $D _ { t } : = X ^ { \top } H _ { T } \boldsymbol { 1 } _ { [ T , + \infty [ } ( t )$ . From Proposition 16.57 and (16.31) it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X ^ {c *} (t, T) = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (0 , T) X}{B _ {T}} \bigg) ^ {\top} H _ {0} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \left(B _ {u} ^ {- 1} \widehat {X} (u -, T)\right) ^ {\top} d M _ {u} \\ \qquad + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} H _ {u -} ^ {\top} Q (0, u -) \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \mu_ {u} ^ {X, l} d Y _ {u} ^ {l, *}. \end{array}
$$

Now, if we find G-predictable processes $\varphi$ and $\gamma$ such that 

$$
X ^ {c *} (t, T) = V _ {0} ^ {*} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {u} ^ {l} d Y _ {u} ^ {l, *} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \gamma_ {u} ^ {\top} d R ^ {c *} (u, T) =: I,\tag{16.34}
$$

then, by Lemma 16.17, we can choose $\psi$ in such a way that $( \psi , \varphi , \gamma )$ is a $D \cdot$ financing portfolio that replicates $D$ . Proposition 16.54 implies that the RHS of (16.34) has the form 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I = V _ {0} ^ {*} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {u} ^ {l} d Y _ {u} ^ {l, *} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \gamma_ {u} ^ {\top} \big (B _ {u} ^ {- 1} \widehat {R} (u -, T) \big) ^ {\top} d M _ {u} \\ \qquad + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \big (H _ {u} ^ {\top} Q (0, u) d m _ {u} \gamma_ {u} \big) ^ {\top}, \end{array}
$$

and Lemma 16.56 gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I = V _ {0} ^ {*} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \gamma_ {u} ^ {\top} \big (B _ {u} ^ {- 1} \widehat {R} (u -, T) \big) ^ {\top} d M _ {u} \\ \qquad + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \big (\varphi_ {u} ^ {l} + \widetilde {H} _ {u} ^ {\top} Q (0, u) \mu_ {u} ^ {(l)} \gamma_ {u} \big) d Y _ {u} ^ {l *}. \end{array}
$$

If $\begin{array} { r } { V _ { 0 } = \mathbb { E } ( \frac { P ( 0 , T ) X } { B _ { T } } ) ^ { \top } H _ { 0 } } \end{array}$ and $\varphi , \gamma$ are G-predictable processes satisfying 

$$
\left(\widehat {X} (u -, T)\right) ^ {\top} = \gamma_ {u} ^ {\top} \left(\widehat {R} (u -, T)\right) ^ {\top},\tag{16.35}
$$

$$
H _ {u -} ^ {\top} Q (0, u -) \mu_ {u} ^ {X, l} = \big (\varphi_ {u} ^ {l} + H _ {u -} ^ {\top} Q (0, u -) \mu_ {u} ^ {(l)} \gamma_ {u} \big),\tag{16.36}
$$

then (16.34) holds. Note that the system of linear equations (16.35) is equivalent to (16.32); moreover, the solution to the second system (16.36) is obviously given by (16.33). The component $\varphi$ is clearly G-predictable, and taking $\gamma$ to be a minimum norm solution to (16.32) gives a G-predictable solution to (16.32). This finishes the proof. - 

Now we pass to general rating-sensitive claims. We present the way of hedging general rating-sensitive claims using digital options and default-free assets. We start by introducing matrix notation which will be very convenient in the subsequent calculations. 

Notation 16.61 We will use the following notation: 

$$
\check {Z} _ {t} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c c} - Z _ {t} ^ {1, K} & Z _ {t} ^ {1, 2} - Z _ {t} ^ {1, K} & \ldots & Z _ {t} ^ {1, K - 1} - Z _ {t} ^ {1, K} \\ Z _ {t} ^ {2, 1} - Z _ {t} ^ {2, K} & - Z _ {t} ^ {2, K} & \ldots & Z _ {t} ^ {2, K - 1} - Z _ {t} ^ {2, K} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ Z _ {t} ^ {K - 1, 1} - Z _ {t} ^ {K - 1, K} & Z _ {t} ^ {K - 1, 2} - Z _ {t} ^ {K - 1, K} & \ldots & - Z _ {t} ^ {K - 1, K} \end{array} \right],
$$

$$
(Z \Lambda) _ {t} ^ {j} := \left[ Z _ {t} \Lambda_ {t} ^ {\top} \right] _ {j, j} = \sum_ {k = 1, k \neq j} ^ {K} Z _ {t} ^ {j, k} \lambda_ {j, k} (t) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \check {Z} _ {t} ^ {j, k} \lambda_ {j, k} (t) =: (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {t} ^ {j}.
$$

Using our notation, we can represent the vector of ex-dividend price of the ratingsensitive claim (X, A, Z, C, τ) described in Theorem 16.38 in the compact form 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {S _ {t}}{B _ {t}} = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (t , T) X}{B _ {T}} \mathbb {1} _ {\{t <   T \}} + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (t , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} \\ \qquad + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (t , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg) ^ {\top} H _ {t}. \end{array}\tag{16.37}
$$

As we have seen in the case of claims of the form $( X , 0 , 0 , C , \tau )$ , the crucial point in finding a replication strategy is a suitable martingale representation theorem for $X ^ { c * }$ , i.e., for the cumulative price process of the claim $( X , 0 , 0 , C , \tau )$ . For a general rating-sensitive claim $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ , we will present a similar version of a martingale representation for $S ^ { c * }$ 

The following martingale representation theorem allows us to separate hedging of default risk, associated with jumps due to rating changes, and spread risk, associated with uncertainty as to the predefault value of the claim. 

Theorem 16.62 Let $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ be an arbitrary rating-sensitive claim satisfying Assumption INT-1. Then 

$$
\frac {S _ {t} ^ {c}}{B _ {t}} = S _ {0} ^ {c} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \alpha_ {u} ^ {\top} d m _ {u} ^ {S} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \beta_ {u} ^ {\top} d M _ {u},\tag{16.38}
$$

where M is given by (16.22), $m ^ { S }$ is an F-martingale given by 

$$
m _ {t} ^ {S} := \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (0 , T) X}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigg),\tag{16.39}
$$

and $\alpha , \beta$ are G-predictable stochastic processes defined by 

$$
\alpha_ {t} = Q ^ {\top} (0, t) H _ {t -}, \quad \beta_ {t} = \frac {\widehat {S} (t -, T) + \check {Z} _ {t} ^ {\top} H _ {t -}}{B _ {t}},\tag{16.40}
$$

with 

$$
\widehat {S} (t, T) := B _ {t} \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {P (t , T) X}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {[ [ t, T ] ]} \frac {P (t , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} + \int_ {[ [ t, T ] ]} \frac {P (t , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right)
$$

and $S _ { 0 } ^ { c } = ( m _ { 0 } ^ { S } ) ^ { \top } H _ { 0 }$ 

(16.41) 

Proof The processes $m ^ { S }$ and $\widehat { S }$ are well defined by Assumption INT-1. It is enough to prove the theorem for the claim of the form $( 0 , A , Z , C , \tau )$ . Indeed, having a general rating-sensitive claim $( X , { \widehat { A } } , Z , C , \tau )$ , observe that by letting $A _ { t } = \widehat { A } _ { t } +$ $X \mathbb { 1 } _ { [ [ T , \infty [ [ t ) }$ we can restrict to the case of $( 0 , A , Z , C , \tau )$ . For such a claim, we have 

$$
\frac {S _ {t} ^ {c}}{B _ {t}} = \mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} d D _ {u} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t}\right) = I _ {t} ^ {(1)} + I _ {t} ^ {(2)},
$$

where 

$$
I _ {t} ^ {(1)} := \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} d D _ {u} \quad \text { and } \quad I _ {t} ^ {(2)} := \mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} d D _ {u} \Big | \mathcal {G} _ {t}\right).
$$

Using (16.22) and the fact that 

$$
\int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} \left(Z _ {u} ^ {\top} \widehat {H} _ {u -}\right) ^ {\top} d \widehat {H} _ {u} = \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} \left(\check {Z} _ {u} ^ {\top} H _ {u -}\right) ^ {\top} d H _ {u},
$$

where $\widehat { H } _ { t } : = ( H _ { t } ^ { 1 } , \ldots , H _ { t } ^ { K } ) ^ { \top }$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I _ {t} ^ {(1)} = \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} H _ {u} ^ {\top} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} \big (Z _ {u} ^ {\top} \widehat {H} _ {u -} \big) ^ {\top} d \widehat {H} _ {u} \\ = \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} H _ {u} ^ {\top} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} \big (\check {Z} _ {u} ^ {\top} H _ {u -} \big) ^ {\top} d M _ {u} \\ \quad + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} \big (\check {Z} _ {u} ^ {\top} H _ {u -} \big) ^ {\top} \varLambda_ {u} ^ {\top} H _ {u -} d u \\ = \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} H _ {u} ^ {\top} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} \big (\check {Z} _ {u} ^ {\top} H _ {u -} \big) ^ {\top} dM _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \varLambda) _ {u} ^ {\top} H _ {u -} d u, \end{array}

\begin{array}{l} I _ {t} ^ {(2)} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} H _ {t} ^ {i} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K - 1} \mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} B _ {u} ^ {- 1} p _ {i, j} (t, u) d A _ {u} ^ {j} \right. \\ \left. + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \frac {Z _ {u} ^ {j , k}}{B _ {u}} p _ {i, j} (t, u) \lambda_ {j, k} (u) d u \Bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right). \end{array}
$$

Using Notation 16.61, we can write $I ^ { ( 2 ) }$ in the form 

$$
\begin{array}{l}I _ {t} ^ {(2)} = \left(\mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (t , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (t , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right)\left. \right) ^ {\top} H _ {t}\\= \left(\mathbb {E} \bigg (\int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket t, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right)\left. \right) ^ {\top} Q ^ {\top} (0, t) H _ {t}\\= \left(m _ {t} - \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} - \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u\right) ^ {\top} L _ {t},\end{array}
$$

where $L _ { t } = Q ^ { \top } ( 0 , t ) H _ { t }$ (so L is given by (16.23)), and m is defined by 

$$
m _ {t} := \mathbb {E} \left(\int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right).\tag{16.42}
$$

Hence, 

$$
d I _ {t} ^ {(2)} = \left(m _ {t -} - \int_ {\mathbb {I} 0, t [   [} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} - \int_ {\mathbb {I} 0, t [   [} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u\right) ^ {\top} d L _ {t}
$$

$$
+ \left(d m _ {t} - \frac {P (0 , t)}{B _ {t}} d A _ {t} - \frac {P (0 , t)}{B _ {t}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {t} d t\right) ^ {\top} L _ {t -}
$$

since the continuous martingale part of L is zero. Thus, by the continuity of $Q ( 0 , \cdot )$ and (16.23) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d I _ {t} ^ {(2)} = \bigg (Q (0, t) \bigg (m _ {t -} - \int_ {\mathbb {I} 0, t [   [} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} - \int_ {\mathbb {I} 0, t [   [} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \bigg) \bigg) ^ {\top} d M _ {t} \\ \qquad + \bigg (Q (0, t) d m _ {t} - Q (0, t) \frac {P (0 , t)}{B _ {t}} d A _ {t} - Q (0, t) \frac {P (0 , t)}{B _ {t}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {t} d t \bigg) ^ {\top} H _ {t -} \\ \qquad = \bigg (Q (0, t) \bigg (m _ {t -} - \int_ {\mathbb {I} 0, t [   [} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} - \int_ {\mathbb {I} 0, t [   [} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Delta) _ {u} d u \bigg) \bigg) ^ {\top} d M _ {t} \\ \qquad + \bigg (Q (0, t) d m _ {t} - \frac {1}{B _ {t}} d A _ {t} - \frac {1}{B _ {t}} (\check {Z} \Delta) _ {t} d t \bigg) ^ {\top} H _ {t -}. \end{array}
$$

Finally, since $I _ { 0 } ^ { ( 2 ) } = S _ { 0 } ^ { c }$ , we have

\begin{array}{l}\frac {S _ {t} ^ {c}}{B _ {t}} = S _ {0} ^ {c} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} H _ {u -} ^ {\top} Q (0, u) d m _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} \left(\check {Z} _ {u} ^ {\top} H _ {u -}\right) ^ {\top} d M _ {u}\\\quad + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \left(Q (0, u) \left(m _ {u -} - \int_ {\llbracket 0, u \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , v)}{B _ {v}} d A _ {v} \right. \right.\\\quad \left. - \int_ {\llbracket 0, u \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , v)}{B _ {v}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {v} d v\right)\left. \right) ^ {\top} d M _ {u}\end{array}

with $S _ { 0 } ^ { c } = m _ { 0 } ^ { \top } H _ { 0 }$ . Hence, to obtain representation (16.38), it is enough to observe that (16.42) implies 

$$
Q (0, t) \bigg (m _ {t} - \int_ {\mathbb {I} 0, t [   [} \frac {P (0 , v)}{B _ {v}} d A _ {v} - \int_ {\mathbb {I} 0, t ]   ]} \frac {P (0 , v)}{B _ {v}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {v} d v \bigg) = \frac {\widehat {S} (t , T)}{B _ {t}}.
$$

The process $\beta$ is G-predictable since $\frac { \widehat { S } ( t - , T ) } { B _ { t } }$ and $Z$ are G-predictable processes by definition. - 

Remark 16.63 We note that, in general, the components of the vector $\widehat { S } ( t , T )$ defined in Theorem 16.62 do not represent the ex-dividend price of claim $( X , A , Z$ $C , \tau )$ given by (16.37) on the sets $\{ C _ { t - } = i \}$ . There are two differences. The first is that $\widehat { S } ( t , T )$ includes possible payment of promised dividend at time t. The second is at time T, when the ex-dividend price is by definition equal to zero. 

Now we introduce another assumption on rating sensitive claims. 

Assumption INT-2 We assume that a defaultable rating-sensitive claim satisfies 

$$
\mathbb {E} \left(\left| \frac {P (0 , T) X}{B _ {T}} \right| ^ {2} + \left| \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} \right| ^ {2} + \left| \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \right| ^ {2}\right) <   \infty .
$$

As an immediate consequence of Assumption 16.48, we obtain: 

Remark 16.64 If a claim $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ satisfies INT-2, then there exist $( K - 1 ) \ –$ dimensional F-predictable stochastic processes $\mu ^ { S , l } , l = 1 , \dots , n$ , such that $m ^ { S }$ given by (16.39) has the representation 

$$
m _ {T} ^ {S} = m _ {0} ^ {S} + \int_ {\left\| 0, T \right\|} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \mu_ {t} ^ {S, l} d Y _ {t} ^ {l *},\tag{16.43}
$$

where 

$$
m _ {0} ^ {S} := \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (0 , T) X}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \bigg).
$$

The following theorem yields replication strategy for the general rating-sensitive claims. 

Theorem 16.65 Let $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ be an arbitrary rating-sensitive claim satisfying Assumption INT-2. Assume that,for each t, 

$$
\bigl (\widehat {S} (t -, T) + \check {Z} _ {t} ^ {\top} H _ {t -} \bigr) \in \operatorname{Im} \bigl (\widehat {R} (t -, T) \bigr),
$$

where $\widehat { R }$ is given by (16.25), and ${ \widehat { S } } \ b y$ (16.41). Then the portfolio $( \psi , \varphi , \gamma )$ with the initial capital 

$$
V _ {0} (\phi) = \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {P (0 , T) X}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u\right) ^ {\top} H _ {0}
$$

is a D-financing portfolio which replicates claim $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ , provided that γ is given as a minimum norm solution to thefollowing system oflinear equations: 

$$
\widehat {R} (t -, T) \gamma_ {t} = \widehat {S} (t -, T) + \check {Z} _ {t} ^ {\top} H _ {t -},
$$

and ϕ, ψ are defined by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \varphi_ {t} ^ {l} = H _ {t -} ^ {\top} Q (0, t) \big (\mu_ {t} ^ {S, l} - \mu_ {t} ^ {(l)} \gamma_ {t} \big), \\ \psi_ {t} = V _ {0} (\phi) + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {u} ^ {l} d Y _ {u} ^ {l *} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \gamma_ {t} ^ {\top} d R ^ {c *} (u, T) - \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {t} ^ {l} Y _ {t} ^ {l} - \gamma_ {t} ^ {\top} R (t, T) \\ - \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}} d D _ {u} \end{array}
$$

with $\mu ^ { S , l }$ given by (16.43) and $\mu ^ { ( l ) }$ by (16.27). 

Proof For the proof, it is sufficient to repeat the arguments from Theorem 16.60 and use Theorem 16.62. - 

## 16.5.2 Hedging with General Rating-Sensitive Claims

In the previous subsection, we have solved problem of replication of general ratingsensitive claims by trading in default-free assets and in the system of digital rating options. This result is unsatisfactory for practitioners since we have used in a replication the digital rating options which are not traded on the real market. In this subsection, we give a generalization of the previous results by allowing to trade in an arbitrary (to some extent) system of tradable general rating-sensitive claims. We point out that this system includes defaultable bonds, Credit Sensitive Notes, CDS, etc. 

Now we will consider the case where an investor can trade in m general ratingsensitive claims, where $m \geq K - 1$ . In the other words, we consider the case where, on the market, we can trade in general rating-sensitive claims $( X ^ { ( i ) } , A ^ { ( i ) } , Z ^ { ( i ) } , C , \tau )$ $i = 1 , \ldots , m$ , and we are interested in providing sufficient conditions for the existence of replication strategy for an arbitrary claim $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ . Before we proceed further, we introduce another convenient matrix notation. 

Notation 16.66 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbf {X} := \big [ X ^ {(1)}, \ldots , X ^ {(m)} \big ], \qquad \mathbf {A} _ {t} := \big [ A _ {t} ^ {(1)}, \ldots , A _ {t} ^ {(m)} \big ], \\ [ \check {\mathbf {Z}} \mathbf {H} ] _ {t} := \big [ \big (\check {Z} _ {t} ^ {(1)} \big) ^ {\top} H _ {t -}, \ldots , \big (\check {Z} _ {t} ^ {(m)} \big) ^ {\top} H _ {t -} \big ], \\ [ \check {\mathbf {Z}} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ] _ {t} := \big [ \big (\check {Z} ^ {(1)} \varLambda \big) _ {t}, \ldots , \big (\check {Z} ^ {(m)} \varLambda \big) _ {t} \big ]. \end{array}
$$

In the next proposition, we give the dynamics of the discounted cumulative prices of a system of $m \geq K - 1$ rating-sensitive claims. We will use the same idea and proceed as before. 

Proposition 16.67 Assume that a system of m traded general rating-sensitive claims $( ( X ^ { ( i ) } , A ^ { ( i ) } , Z ^ { ( i ) } , C , \tau ) ) _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ satisfies Assumption INT-1. Then the discounted cumulative price process $R ^ { c * }$ ofthese claims has the dynamics 

$$
\frac {R ^ {c} (t , T)}{B _ {t}} = R ^ {c} (0, T) + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \left(\alpha_ {u} ^ {\top} d \mathbf {m} _ {u}\right) ^ {\top} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \boldsymbol {\Theta} _ {u} ^ {\top} d M _ {u},\tag{16.44}
$$

where m is an F-martingale with values in the space of matrices of dimension $( K - 1 ) \times m$ , given by 

$$
\mathbf {m} _ {t} := \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {P (0 , T) \mathbf {X}}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d \mathbf {A} _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} [ \check {\mathbf {Z}} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ] _ {u} d u \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right),\tag{16.45}
$$

and $\alpha , \beta$ are G-predictable stochastic processes defined by 

$$
\alpha_ {t} = Q ^ {\top} (0, t) H _ {t -}, \qquad \mathbf {\Theta} _ {t} = \frac {\widehat {\mathbf {R}} (t - , T) + [ \check {\mathbf {Z}} \mathbf {H} ] _ {t}}{B _ {t}},\tag{16.46}
$$

with $R ^ { c } ( 0 , T ) = { \bf m } _ { 0 } ^ { \top } H _ { 0 }$ and 

$$
\widehat {\mathbf {R}} (t, T) := B _ {t} \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {P (t , T) \mathbf {X}}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {[ [ t, T ] ]} \frac {P (t , u)}{B _ {u}} d \mathbf {A} _ {u} + \int_ {[ ] t, T ] ]} \frac {P (t , u)}{B _ {u}} [ \check {\mathbf {Z}} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ] _ {u} d u \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right).\tag{16.47}
$$

Proof The thesis follows immediately from the martingale representation, Theorem 16.62. - 

Remark 16.68 Assume that the claims $( X ^ { ( i ) } , A ^ { ( i ) } , Z ^ { ( i ) } , C , \tau ) , i = 1 , \ldots , m$ , satisfy Assumption INT-2 for every i. Then Assumption 16.48 implies that m given by (16.45) has the following representation 

$$
\mathbf {m} _ {T} = \mathbf {m} _ {0} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \mu_ {t} ^ {(l)} d Y _ {t} ^ {l *},\tag{16.48}
$$

where $\mu ^ { ( l ) } , l = 1 , \dots , n$ , are F-predictable stochastic processes with values in matrices of dimension $( K - 1 ) \times m$ and 

$$
\mathbf {m} _ {0} := \mathbb {E} \left(\frac {P (0 , T) \mathbf {X}}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d \mathbf {A} _ {u} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, T \rrbracket} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} [ \check {\mathbf {Z}} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ] _ {u} d u\right).
$$

Now we present the theorem which gives sufficient conditions for a replication of a general rating-sensitive claim. 

Proposition 16.69 $L e t \left( { \cal X } , { \cal A } , { \cal Z } , { \cal C } , \tau \right)$ be an arbitrary rating-sensitive claim satisfying Assumption INT-2. Assume that,for each t, 

$$
\widehat {S} (t -, T) + \check {Z} _ {t} ^ {\top} H _ {t -} \in \operatorname{Im} \left(\widehat {\mathbf {R}} (t -, T) + [ \check {\mathbf {Z}} \mathbf {H} ] _ {t}\right),
$$

where $\widehat { \mathbf { R } }$ is given by (16.47) and $\widehat { S }$ by (16.41). Then the portfolio $( \psi , \varphi , \gamma )$ with initial capital 

$$
V _ {0} (\phi) = \mathbb {E} \bigg (\frac {P (0 , T) X}{B _ {T}} + \int_ {\left\| 0, T \right\|} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} d A _ {u} + \int_ {\left\| 0, T \right\|} \frac {P (0 , u)}{B _ {u}} (\check {Z} \Lambda) _ {u} d u \bigg) ^ {\top} H _ {0}
$$

is a D-financing portfolio that replicates claim (X, A, Z, C, τ), provided that $\gamma$ is given as a minimum norm solution to thefollowing system oflinear equations: 

$$
\left(\widehat {\mathbf {R}} (t -, T) + [ \check {\mathbf {Z}} \mathbf {H} ] _ {t}\right) \gamma_ {t} = \widehat {S} (t -, T) + \check {Z} _ {t} ^ {\top} H _ {t -},
$$

and $\varphi$ , ψ are defined by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \varphi_ {t} ^ {l} = H _ {t -} ^ {\top} Q (0, t) \big (\mu_ {t} ^ {S, l} - \mu_ {t} ^ {(l)} \gamma_ {t} \big), \\ \psi_ {t} = V _ {0} (\phi) + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {u} ^ {l}   d Y _ {u} ^ {l *} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \gamma_ {u} ^ {\top}   d R ^ {c *} (u, T) \\ \qquad - \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {t} ^ {l} Y _ {t} ^ {l} - \gamma_ {t} ^ {\top} R (t, T) - \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \frac {1}{B _ {u}}   d D _ {u}, \end{array}\tag{16.49}
$$

where $\mu ^ { ( l ) }$ are F-predictable stochastic processes that appear in representation (16.48), and $\mu ^ { S , l }$ are given in representation (16.43). 

Proof According to Lemma 16.17, we are looking for process $( \varphi , \gamma )$ such that 

$$
S _ {t} ^ {c *} = V _ {0} (\phi) + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {u} ^ {l} d Y _ {u} ^ {l *} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \gamma_ {u} ^ {\top} d R ^ {c *} (u, T).\tag{16.50}
$$

Lemma 16.17 also implies that by taking ψ given by (16.49) we obtain a $D _ { - }$ financing portfolio which replicates $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ . Equation (16.44) and representation (16.48) imply that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S _ {t} ^ {c *} = V _ {0} (\phi) + \int_ {\left\| 0, t \right\|} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \varphi_ {u} ^ {l}   d Y _ {u} ^ {l *} + \int_ {\left\| 0, t \right\|} \gamma_ {u} ^ {\top} \big (\alpha_ {u} ^ {\top}   d \mathbf {m} _ {u} \big) ^ {\top} + \int_ {\left\| 0, t \right\|} \gamma_ {u} ^ {\top} \boldsymbol {\Theta} _ {u} ^ {\top}   d M _ {u} \\ = V _ {0} (\phi) + \int_ {\left\| 0, t \right\|} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \big (\varphi_ {u} ^ {l} + \big (\alpha_ {u} ^ {\top}   \mu_ {u} ^ {(l)} \gamma_ {u} \big) ^ {\top} \big)   d Y _ {u} ^ {l *} + \int_ {\left\| 0, t \right\|} (\boldsymbol {\Theta} _ {u} \gamma_ {u}) ^ {\top}   d M _ {u}. \end{array}\tag{16.51}
$$

Moreover, by (16.38) and representation (16.43), 

$$
S _ {t} ^ {c *} = S _ {0} ^ {c} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {n} \alpha_ {u} ^ {\top} \mu_ {u} ^ {S, l} d Y _ {u} ^ {*, l} + \int_ {\llbracket 0, t \rrbracket} \beta_ {u} ^ {\top} d M _ {u}.\tag{16.52}
$$

Comparing coefficients in (16.51) and (16.52), we see that (16.50) holds, provided that $\gamma , \varphi$ satisfies the system of linear equations 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \boldsymbol {\Theta} _ {t} \gamma_ {t} = \beta_ {t}, \\ \varphi_ {t} ^ {l} + \alpha_ {t} ^ {\top} \mu_ {t} ^ {(l)} \gamma_ {t} = \alpha_ {t} ^ {\top} \mu_ {t} ^ {S, l} \quad \text { for } l = 1, \ldots , n, \end{array}
$$

where $\beta$ and α are given by (16.40). The proof is complete. 

Remark 16.70 We assume that primary rating-sensitive instruments have the same maturity $T > 0$ as the rating-sensitive claim we want to replicate. This assumption can be easily relaxed. We could allow the primary rating-sensitive instruments to have different maturities $T _ { i }$ but greater or equal to $T$ , the maturity of the ratingsensitive claim we want to replicate. 

Remark 16.71 If the number of primary rating-sensitive assets is large, then system of equations 

$$
\Theta_ {t} \gamma_ {t} = \beta_ {t}
$$

can have infinitely many solutions. One can ask the question whether we can choose $\gamma$ in such a way that additional n constrains will be satisfied? More precisely, can we choose $\gamma$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {t} ^ {(l)} \gamma_ {t} = \mu_ {t} ^ {S, l}
$$

for $l = 1 , \ldots , n ?$ The positive answer implies that we do not need nondefaultable primary assets in the portfolio, i.e., $\varphi ^ { l } = 0$ for each $l = 1 , \ldots , n$ . A sufficient condition for this to hold is that the matrix 

$$
G _ {t} := \left[ \begin{array}{c} \boldsymbol {\Theta} _ {t} \\ \mu_ {t} ^ {(1)} \\ \vdots \\ \mu_ {t} ^ {(n)} \end{array} \right]
$$

of dimensions $( K - 1 ) ( n + 1 ) \times m$ has the rank equal to $( K - 1 ) ( n + 1 )$ . In this case, for an arbitrary rating-sensitive claim $( X , A , Z , C , \tau )$ ), we can solve the system of equations 

$$
G _ {t} \gamma_ {t} = \left[ \beta_ {t}, \mu_ {t} ^ {S, 1}, \dots , \mu_ {t} ^ {S, n} \right] ^ {\top}
$$

and obtain portfolio with $\varphi = 0$ . A necessary condition for this gives trivially that the number of primary rating-sensitive assets m should satisfy $m \geq ( K - 1 ) ( n + 1 )$ ). This condition can be viewed as a nonsingularity condition for the volatility matrix.
