\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \bigg [ \frac {1}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} \bigg \{\int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma (Z _ {s}) ^ {2} d s + \sum_ {i \in E ^ {0}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} I _ {\{Z _ {s} = i \}} d \widetilde {J _ {s} ^ {i}} \bigg \} \bigg ] \\ = \sum_ {j \in E ^ {0}} \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \bigg [ \frac {1}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} I _ {\{Z _ {s} = j \}} d s \bigg ] w (j), \end{array}
$$

where $w ( j ) : = \sigma ^ { 2 } ( j ) + \mathbb { E } [ \widetilde { J } _ { 1 } ^ { j } ]$ . From the definition of $\widetilde J ^ { j }$ it is easily checked that $\mathbb { E } [ \widetilde { J } _ { 1 } ^ { j } ]$ is equal to $\lambda _ { j }$ times the second moment of the density $f _ { i }$ . One verifies by a straightforward calculation that $w ( j )$ is equal to $V ( j )$ given in (17.57). Furthermore, the Markov property of $Z$ applied at time t yields that 

$$
\mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \left[ \frac {1}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} \int_ {0} ^ {T} I _ {\{Z _ {s} = j \}} d s \right] = e _ {i} ^ {\prime} \exp \bigl (t (Q - \Lambda_ {D}) \bigr) e _ {j} ^ {\prime} e _ {j} \exp \bigl ((T - t) (Q - \Lambda_ {D}) \bigr) \mathbf {1}.
$$

Equation (17.55) follows then by an application of Fubini’s theorem. Furthermore, (17.56) follows by noting that the expectation $\mathbb { E } _ { x , i } [ \mathcal { Z } _ { T } / B _ { T } ^ { D } ]$ can also be obtained by calculating the negative of the derivative of the Laplace transform at zero: 

$$
\mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \bigg [ \frac {\Sigma_ {T}}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} \bigg ] = - \frac {d}{d u} \big \{\big [ \exp \big (T \big (K _ {\Sigma} (u) - \varLambda_ {D} \big) \big) \mathbf {1} \big ] (i) \big \} \bigg | _ {u = 0}.
$$

## 17.5 First Passage Times for Regime-Switching Processes

## 17.5.1 Three Key Matrices

The characteristics of the process $( X , Z )$ can be summarised in terms of three matrices $Q _ { 0 } , \Sigma$ and V that will shortly be specified. Given those three matrices, we will show how to reconstruct (X, Z) in Sect. 17.7. 

The matrices $Q _ { 0 } , \Sigma$ and V will be specified in nine-block matrices using block notation; the middle block of $Q _ { 0 } , \Sigma$ and V describes the rates of regime-switches, and the volatility and drift of the process in the different regimes, while the upper left and lower right blocks of $Q _ { 0 }$ specify the distribution of up-ward and downward jumps in the different regimes, in terms of the (phase-type) generators. More precisely, we define the three key matrices $Q _ { 0 } , \Sigma$ and V, in block notation, by 

$$
Q _ {0} := \left( \begin{array}{c c c} B ^ {+} & b ^ {+} & O \\ A ^ {+} & Q - \varLambda_ {\lambda} & A ^ {-} \\ O & b ^ {-} & B ^ {-} \end{array} \right),\tag{17.61}
$$

$$
\Sigma := \left( \begin{array}{c c c} O & O & O \\ O & \Lambda_ {S} & O \\ O & O & O \end{array} \right), \qquad V := \left( \begin{array}{c c c} I & O & O \\ O & \Lambda_ {M} & O \\ O & O & - I \end{array} \right).\tag{17.62}
$$

Here $Q$ is the generator matrix of the chain $Z$ , and $A _ { \lambda } , A _ { S } , A _ { M }$ denote the $N _ { 0 } \times N _ { 0 }$ diagonal matrices with elements 

$$
\Lambda_ {\lambda} (i, i) := \lambda_ {i}, \quad \Lambda_ {S} (i, i) := \sigma (i) \quad \text { and } \quad \Lambda_ {M} (i, i) := \mu (i).\tag{17.63}
$$

Further, O and I are zero and identity matrices of appropriate sizes such that $Q _ { 0 }$ $\varSigma$ and V are square matrices of the same dimension. In block notation $A ^ { \pm } , B ^ { \pm }$ and $b ^ { \pm }$ are given by 

$$
A ^ {\pm} := \left( \begin{array}{c c c} \lambda_ {1} ^ {\pm} \beta_ {1} ^ {\pm \prime} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & \lambda_ {N} ^ {\pm} \beta_ {N} ^ {\pm \prime} \end{array} \right), \qquad B ^ {\pm} := \left( \begin{array}{c c c} B _ {1} ^ {\pm} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & B _ {N} ^ {\pm} \end{array} \right),
$$

$$
b ^ {\pm} := \left( \begin{array}{c c c} - B _ {1} ^ {\pm} \mathbf {1} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & - B _ {N} ^ {\pm} \mathbf {1} \end{array} \right),\tag{17.64}
$$

where $\lambda _ { i } ^ { + } : = \lambda _ { i } p _ { i }$ and $\lambda _ { i } ^ { - } : = \lambda _ { i } ( 1 - p _ { i } )$ 

Remark The matrix $Q _ { 0 }$ is in fact the generator matrix of a Markov chain, as it has nonnegative off-diagonal elements and zero row sums. We denote the state space of this Markov chain by E. In the sequel we will frequently use the following partition of the set $E$ : 

$$
E ^ {\pm} = \{i \in E: \Sigma_ {i i} \neq 0 \}, \qquad E ^ {+} = \{i \in E: \Sigma_ {i i} = 0, V _ {i i} > 0 \},
$$

$$
E ^ {-} = \{i \in E: \Sigma_ {i i} = 0, V _ {i i} <   0 \}.\tag{17.65}
$$

Note further that $E ^ { \pm }$ can and will be identified with the state space $E ^ { 0 }$ of the chain Z. See Sect. 17.7 for further properties of the Markov chain defined by the generator $Q _ { 0 }$ 

## 17.5.2 Matrix Wiener–Hopf Factorisation

For a given vector of discount rates $h : E \to \mathbb { C }$ , the matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation associates to the matrix 

$$
Q _ {h} := Q _ {0} - \Lambda_ {h},
$$

where $\varLambda _ { h }$ is a diagonal matrix with ith diagonal element $A _ { h } ( i , i ) = h ( i )$ , a quadruple of matrices which, as we will show below, characterises the distributions of the running maximum and minimum of X. 

Let us briefly describe the sets of matrices of which this quadruple are elements. Denote by $\mathbb { D } ( n )$ the set of $n \times n$ square matrices whose eigenvalues all have nonpositive real part. Note that by Lemma 17.2, D(n) includes the set $\mathbb { G } ( n )$ of $n \times n$ subgenerator matrices (i.e. matrices with nonnegative off-diagonal elements and nonpositive rows). Recall that $\mathbb { C } ^ { n \times m }$ denotes the set of $n \times m$ matrices with complex entries. Denote by $\mathbb { H } ( n , m )$ the set of $n \times m$ subprobability matrices (i.e. matrices with nonnegative elements and row sums smaller or equal to one). 

Denote by $N , ~ N ^ { + } , ~ { \underline { { N } } } ^ { + } , ~ N ^ { - }$ and $\underline { { N } } ^ { - }$ the number of elements of the sets $E _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ $E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { + } , E ^ { \overset { . } { + } } , E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { - }$ and $E ^ { - }$ , respectively. Also, let H denote the set 

$$
\mathcal {H} = \Big \{h: E \to \mathbb {C}: \min _ {i \in E} \Re \big (h (i) \big) \geq 0, \min _ {i \in E ^ {0}} \Re \big (h (i) \big) > 0 \Big \}.
$$

Definition 17.20 Let $h \in { \mathcal { H } } ,$ , and let $W ^ { + } , G ^ { + } , W ^ { - }$ and $G ^ { - }$ be elements of the sets $C ^ { N \times N ^ { + } }$ $\mathbb { D } ( N ^ { + } ) , \mathbb { C } ^ { N \times N ^ { - } }$ and $\mathbb { D } ( N ^ { - } )$ , respectively. A quadruple $( W ^ { + } , G ^ { + }$ $W ^ { - } , G ^ { - } )$ is called a matrix Wiener–Hopffactorisation of $Q _ { h }$ if the following matrix equations are satisfied: 

$$
\frac {1}{2} \Sigma^ {2} W ^ {+} (G ^ {+}) ^ {2} - V W ^ {+} G ^ {+} + Q _ {h} W ^ {+} = O ^ {+},\tag{17.66}
$$

$$
\frac {1}{2} \Sigma^ {2} W ^ {-} (G ^ {-}) ^ {2} + V W ^ {-} G ^ {-} + Q _ {h} W ^ {-} = O ^ {-},\tag{17.67}
$$

where $O ^ { + }$ and $O ^ { - }$ are zero matrices of sizes $N \times N ^ { + }$ and $N \times N ^ { - }$ 

## Theorem 17.21

(i) For any $h \in { \mathcal { H } } .$ , there exists a unique matrix Wiener–Hopffactorisation of $Q _ { h }$ , denoted by $( \eta _ { h } ^ { + } , Q _ { h } ^ { + } , \eta _ { h } ^ { - } , Q _ { h } ^ { - } )$ 

(ii) If $h = \Re ( h )$ , then $Q _ { h } ^ { + } \in \mathbb { G } ( N ^ { + } )$ and $Q _ { h } ^ { - } \in \mathbb { G } ( N ^ { - } )$ are subgenerator matrices, and $\eta _ { h } ^ { + } \in \mathbb { H } ( N , N ^ { + } )$ and $\eta _ { h } ^ { - } \in \mathbb { H } ( N , N ^ { - } )$ are in block notation given by 

$$
\eta_ {h} ^ {+} = \binom{I _ {+}}{\underline {{\eta}} _ {h} ^ {+}} \quad a n d \quad \eta_ {h} ^ {-} = \binom{\underline {{\eta}} _ {h} ^ {-}}{I _ {-}}\tag{17.68}
$$

for some matrices $\underline { { \eta } } _ { h } ^ { + } \in \mathbb { H } ( \underline { { N } } ^ { - } , N ^ { + } )$ and $\underline { { \eta } } _ { h } ^ { - } \in \mathbb { H } ( \underline { { N } } ^ { + } , N ^ { - } )$ , and identity matrices $I _ { + }$ and I ofsizes $N ^ { + } \times N ^ { + }$ and $N ^ { - } \times N ^ { - }$ 

Remarks 

(i) For h given by $h ( i ) = q I _ { E ^ { 0 } } ( i )$ ) with $q > 0$ , we will also write $( \eta _ { q } ^ { + } , Q _ { q } ^ { + } , \eta _ { q } ^ { - } , Q _ { q } ^ { - } )$ The proof of Theorem 17.21 will be given in Sect. 17.8. 

(ii) We allow the vector h to take complex values to be able to deal with a Laplace inversion using a Browmich integral, which involves the integration of the resulting first-passage quantities over a curve in the complex plane. Note that, for any real-valued $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ , i.e. $h = \Re ( h )$ , the matrix $Q _ { h }$ is a transient generator matrix, since the off-diagonal elements of $Q _ { h }$ are nonnegative and $Q _ { h } \mathbf { 1 } \neq 0$ 

## 17.5.3 First-Passage into a Half-Line

The marginal distributions of the maximum and minimum as well as the distributions of the first-passage times into a half-line can be described explicitly in terms of the matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation. Denote by $\overline { { X } } _ { t } = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { 0 \leq s \leq t } X _ { s }$ the running maximum of X at time t and by $\underline { { X } } _ { t } = \operatorname* { i n f } _ { 0 \leq s \leq t } X _ { s }$ the corresponding running minimum, and let $T _ { a } ^ { + }$ and $T _ { a } ^ { - }$ be the first passage times of X into a half-line, 

$$
T _ {a} ^ {+} = \inf \left\{t \geq 0: X _ {t} \in (a, \infty) \right\}, \quad T _ {a} ^ {-} = \inf \left\{t \geq 0: X _ {t} \in (- \infty , a) \right\}.
$$

The distributions of those random variables are related via 

$$
\Gamma^ {+} (t) = \mathbb {P} _ {x, i} \left(T _ {a} ^ {+} <   t\right) = \mathbb {P} _ {x, i} (\overline {{X}} _ {t} > a),
$$

$$
\Gamma^ {-} (t) = \mathbb {P} _ {x, i} \left(T _ {a} ^ {-} <   t\right) = \mathbb {P} _ {x, i} (- \underline {{X}} _ {t} > a).
$$

If $\mathbf { e } _ { q }$ denotes a random time that is exponentially distributed with parameter $q > 0$ and that is independent of $( X , Z )$ , then the running maximum and minimum at time $\mathbf { e } _ { q }$ follow a phase-type distribution, with parameters explicitly given in terms of the matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation $( \eta _ { q } ^ { + } , Q _ { q } ^ { + } , \eta _ { q } ^ { - } , Q _ { q } ^ { - } )$ 

For any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ , define the $N \times N ^ { + }$ and $N \times N ^ { - }$ matrices $\phi _ { h , a } ^ { + } ( x )$ and $\Phi _ { h , a } ^ { - } ( x )$ by 

$$
\Phi_ {h, a} ^ {+} (x, i, j) = \left[ \eta_ {h} ^ {+} \exp \bigl ((a - x) Q _ {h} ^ {+} \bigr) \right] (i, j) I _ {(- \infty , a ]} (x) + \delta_ {i j} I _ {(a, \infty)} (x),
$$

$$
i \in E, j \in E ^ {+} \cup E ^ {0},\tag{17.69}
$$

$$
\varPhi_ {h, a} ^ {-} (x, i, j) = \big [ \eta_ {h} ^ {-} \exp \big ((x - a) Q _ {h} ^ {-} \big) \big ] (i, j) I _ {[ a, \infty)} (x) + \delta_ {i j} I _ {(- \infty , a)} (x),
$$

$$
i \in E, j \in E ^ {-} \cup E ^ {0},\tag{17.70}
$$

where $\delta _ { i j }$ is the Kronecker delta $( \mathrm { i . e . } \ \delta _ { i j } = I _ { \{ i \} } ( j ) )$ . For h given by $h ( i ) = q I _ { E ^ { 0 } } ( i )$ with $q > 0$ , we will also denote $\Phi _ { h , a } ^ { \pm } ( x )$ by $\Phi _ { q , a } ^ { \pm } ( x )$ 

Proposition 17.22 For $q > 0$ , it holds that under $\mathbb { P } _ { x , i }$ 

$$
\overline {{X}} _ {\mathbf {e} _ {q}} - x \sim \mathrm{PH} \bigl (\eta_ {q} ^ {+} (i), Q _ {q} ^ {+} \bigr), \quad x \in \mathbb {R}, i \in E ^ {0},
$$

$$
- \underline {{X}} _ {\mathbf {e} _ {q}} + x \sim \mathrm{PH} \big (\eta_ {q} ^ {-} (i), Q _ {q} ^ {-} \big), \quad x \in \mathbb {R}, i \in E ^ {0},
$$

where $\eta _ { q } ^ { + } ( i )$ and $\eta _ { q } ^ { - } ( i )$ are the ith rows of $\eta _ { q } ^ { + }$ and $\eta _ { q } ^ { - }$ . In particular the Laplace transforms $\begin{array} { r } { \widehat { \Gamma } ^ { \pm } ( q ) : = \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } e ^ { - q t } \Gamma ^ { \pm } ( t ) } \end{array}$ dt,for $q > 0$ , are given by theformulae 

$$
\widehat {\Gamma} ^ {+} (q) = \frac {1}{q} \sum_ {j \in E ^ {0}} \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \left[ e ^ {- q T _ {a} ^ {+}} I _ {\{Z _ {T _ {a} ^ {+}} = j \}} \right] = \frac {1}{q} \sum_ {j \in E ^ {0}} \Phi_ {q, a} ^ {+} (x, i, j), \quad x, a \in \mathbb {R}, i \in E ^ {0},
$$

$$
\widehat {\Gamma} ^ {-} (q) = \frac {1}{q} \sum_ {j \in E ^ {0}} \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \left[ e ^ {- q T _ {a} ^ {-}} I _ {\{Z _ {T _ {a} ^ {-}} = j \}} \right] = \frac {1}{q} \sum_ {j \in E ^ {0}} \Phi_ {q, a} ^ {-} (x, i, j), \quad x, a \in \mathbb {R}, i \in E ^ {0}.
$$

Remarks 

(i) The proof of Proposition 17.22 will be given in Sect. 17.8. 

(ii) Denote by $\Phi _ { q , \upsilon } ^ { + } ( x , i )$ and $\Phi _ { q , \ell } ^ { - } ( x , i )$ the $N ^ { + }$ -dimensional and $N ^ { - }$ -dimensional row vectors with jth elements $\Phi _ { q , \upsilon } ^ { + } ( x , i , j )$ and $\Phi _ { q , \ell } ^ { - } ( x , i , j )$ , respectively. Then Proposition 17.22 implies that, under the probability measure $\mathbb { P } _ { x , i } , x \in \mathbb { R }$ $i \in E ^ { 0 }$ , the processes $M ^ { + } = \{ M _ { t } ^ { + } \} _ { t \geq 0 }$ and $M ^ { - } = \{ M _ { t } ^ { - } \} _ { t \ge 0 }$ , defined by 

$$
M _ {t} ^ {+} = e ^ {- q (t \wedge T _ {\upsilon} ^ {+})} \varPhi_ {q, \upsilon} ^ {+} (X _ {t \wedge T _ {\upsilon} ^ {+}}, Z _ {t \wedge T _ {\upsilon} ^ {+}}),
$$

$$
M _ {t} ^ {-} = e ^ {- q (t \wedge T _ {\ell} ^ {-})} \varPhi_ {q, \ell} ^ {-} (X _ {t \wedge T _ {\ell} ^ {-}}, Z _ {t \wedge T _ {\ell} ^ {-}}),
$$

are row-vectors of bounded martingales. Indeed, the Markov property of $( X , Z )$ implies that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \left[ e ^ {- q T _ {v} ^ {+}} I _ {\{Z _ {T _ {v} ^ {+}} = j \}} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t} ^ {(X, Z)} \right]} \\ & {\quad = I _ {\{t <   T _ {v} ^ {+} \}} e ^ {- q t} \mathbb {E} _ {X _ {t}, Z _ {t}} \left[ e ^ {- q T _ {v} ^ {+}} I _ {\{Z _ {T _ {v} ^ {+}} = j \}} \right] + I _ {\{t \geq T _ {v} ^ {+} \}} e ^ {- q T _ {v} ^ {+}} I _ {\{Z _ {T _ {v} ^ {+}} = j \}}} \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {= I _ {\{t <   T _ {v} ^ {+} \}} e ^ {- q t} \mathbb {E} _ {X _ {t}, Z _ {t}} \big [ e ^ {- q T _ {v} ^ {+}} I _ {\{Z _ {T _ {v} ^ {+}} = j \}} \big ]} \\ & {\qquad + I _ {\{t \geq T _ {v} ^ {+} \}} e ^ {- q T _ {v} ^ {+}} \mathbb {E} _ {X _ {T _ {v} ^ {+}}, Z _ {T _ {v} ^ {+}}} \big [ e ^ {- q T _ {v} ^ {+}} I _ {\{Z _ {T _ {v} ^ {+}} = j \}} \big ]} \\ & {= e ^ {- q (t \wedge T _ {v} ^ {+})} \mathbb {E} _ {X _ {t \wedge T _ {v} ^ {+}}, Z _ {t \wedge T _ {v} ^ {+}}} \big [ e ^ {- q T _ {v} ^ {+}} I _ {\{Z _ {T _ {v} ^ {+}} = j \}} \big ]} \\ & {= e ^ {- q (t \wedge T _ {v} ^ {+})} \varPhi_ {q, v} ^ {+} (X _ {t \wedge T _ {v} ^ {+}}, Z _ {t \wedge T _ {v} ^ {+}}) e _ {j} ^ {+} = M _ {t} ^ {+} e _ {j} ^ {+},} \end{array}
$$

where $e _ { j } ^ { + }$ denotes the jth standard basis vector in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N ^ { + } }$ , and we used that $\mathbb { E } _ { x , i } [ e ^ { - q T _ { \upsilon } ^ { + } } I _ { \{ Z _ { T } , + } = j \} ] = e _ { j } ^ { + } ( i ) \mathrm { i f } x \geq \upsilon$ and $i \in E ^ { 0 }$ , which directly follows from the definition (17.69). 

(iii) Suppose that $Q _ { 0 } = O$ . This corresponds to a model in which there are no jumps and no switches between the regimes (i.e. with probability one the process stays in the starting regime and evolves as a Brownian motion with drift). In this case we can identify the matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation in closed form. Note that we have $N ^ { + } = N ^ { - } = N$ , and hence the matrices $G ^ { \pm }$ and $W ^ { \pm }$ are of dimension $N \times N$ . If we take $W ^ { \pm }$ to be equal to the identity matrix and $h ( i ) = R _ { D } ( i ) + q$ the matrix equations (17.66)–(17.67) reduce to 

$$
\frac {1}{2} \Sigma^ {2} (G ^ {+}) ^ {2} - V G ^ {+} = (\Lambda_ {D} + q I) = \frac {1}{2} \Sigma^ {2} (G ^ {-}) ^ {2} + V G ^ {-},
$$

where I is the $N \times N$ identity matrix (recall that the discount rate matrix $\varLambda _ { D }$ is diagonal and satisfies $A _ { D } ( i , i ) = R _ { D } ( i )$ for all $i \in E ^ { 0 } )$ . These equations are satisfied by the diagonal matrices 

$$
G ^ {+} = \operatorname{diag} \left(- \omega_ {i} ^ {+}, i = 1, \dots , N\right), \quad G ^ {-} = \operatorname{diag} \left(- \omega_ {i} ^ {-}, i = 1, \dots , N\right),\tag{17.71}
$$

where 

$$
\omega_ {i} ^ {\pm} = \mp \frac {\mu_ {i}}{\sigma_ {i} ^ {2}} + \sqrt {\left(\frac {\mu_ {i}}{\sigma_ {i} ^ {2}}\right) ^ {2} + \frac {2 (q + r _ {i})}{\sigma_ {i} ^ {2}}} \quad \text { and } \quad r _ {i} := R _ {D} (i).\tag{17.72}
$$

In particular, we obtain the well-known fact that the maximum of a Brownian motion with drift at an independent exponential time is exponentially distributed: 

$$
\mathbb {P} _ {x, i} (\overline {{X}} _ {\mathbf {e} _ {q + r _ {i}}} > a) = e ^ {- \omega_ {i} ^ {+} (a - x)} \quad \text { for } x <   a.
$$

## 17.5.4 Joint Distribution ofthe Maximum and Minimum

In the previous section we have shown how the marginal distribution of the maximum and of the minimum can be explicitly expressed in terms of the matrix Wiener– 

Hopf factorisation. Also the joint distribution of the running maximum and minimum, 

$$
\psi_ {x, i} (t) = \mathbb {P} _ {x} (\underline {{X}} _ {t} > \ell , \overline {{X}} _ {t} <   \upsilon),
$$

can be explicitly identified in terms of the matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation, by considering appropriate linear combinations of the functions $\varPhi ^ { + }$ and $\phi ^ { - }$ defined in (17.69). 

To formulate the result, introduce the matrices $Z ^ { + } \in \mathbb { C } ^ { N ^ { - } \times N ^ { + } }$ and $Z ^ { - } \in$ $\mathbb { C } ^ { N ^ { + } \times N ^ { - } }$ by 

$$
Z ^ {+} (i, j) = \big [ \eta_ {h} ^ {+} e ^ {Q _ {h} ^ {+} (\upsilon - \ell)} \big ] (i, j), \quad i \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {-}, j \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {+},
$$

$$
Z ^ {-} (i, j) = \big [ \eta_ {h} ^ {-} e ^ {Q _ {h} ^ {-} (\upsilon - \ell)} \big ] (i, j), \quad i \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {+}, j \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {-},
$$

and define, for any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ and any $x \in \mathbb { R }$ , the $N \times N ^ { + }$ and $N \times N ^ { - }$ matrices $\psi _ { h , \ell , \upsilon } ^ { + } ( x )$ and ${ \Psi } _ { h , \ell , \upsilon } ^ { - } ( x )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Psi_ {h, \ell , v} ^ {+} (x) = \left(\eta_ {h} ^ {+} e ^ {Q _ {h} ^ {+} (v - x)} - \eta_ {h} ^ {-} e ^ {Q _ {h} ^ {-} (x - \ell)} Z ^ {+}\right) \left(I - Z ^ {-} Z ^ {+}\right) ^ {- 1} I _ {[ \ell , v ]} (x) \\ + \Delta^ {+} I _ {(v, \infty)} (x), \end{array}\tag{17.73}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Psi_ {h, \ell , v} ^ {-} (x) = \left(\eta_ {h} ^ {-} e ^ {Q _ {h} ^ {-} (x - \ell)} - \eta_ {h} ^ {+} e ^ {Q _ {h} ^ {+} (v - x)} Z ^ {-}\right) \left(I - Z ^ {+} Z ^ {-}\right) ^ {- 1} I _ {[ \ell , v ]} (x) \\ + \Delta^ {-} I _ {(- \infty , \ell)} (x), \end{array}\tag{17.74}
$$

where $\varDelta ^ { + }$ and $\varDelta ^ { - }$ are the $N \times N ^ { + }$ and $N \times N ^ { - }$ matrices with elements 

$$
\varDelta^ {+} (i, j) = \delta_ {i j}, \quad \varDelta^ {-} (i, k) = \delta_ {i k}, \quad i \in E, j \in E ^ {+} \cup E ^ {0}, k \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {-}.
$$

For h given by $h ( i ) = q I _ { E ^ { 0 } } ( i )$ with $q > 0$ , we will also write $\psi _ { h , \ell , \upsilon } ^ { \pm } ( x ) = \psi _ { q , \ell , \upsilon } ^ { \pm } ( x )$ 

Proposition 17.23 $L e t i \in E ^ { 0 }$ and 

$$
\psi_ {x, i} ^ {+} (t) = \mathbb {P} _ {x, i} (T _ {\ell , \upsilon} <   t, X _ {T _ {\ell , \upsilon}} \geq \upsilon), \quad \psi_ {x, i} ^ {-} (t) = \mathbb {P} _ {x, i} (T _ {\ell , \upsilon} <   t, X _ {T _ {\ell , \upsilon}} \leq \ell),
$$

where 

$$
T _ {\ell , \upsilon} := \inf \left\{t \geq 0: X _ {t} \notin [ \ell , \upsilon ] \right\} = T _ {\ell} ^ {-} \wedge T _ {\upsilon} ^ {+}.
$$

For any $q > 0$ , the Laplace transforms in t of $\psi _ { x , i } ^ { + }$ and ${ \psi } _ { x , i } ^ { - }$ are given by 

$$
\widehat {\psi} _ {x, i} ^ {+} (q) = \frac {1}{q} \big (\Psi_ {q, x} ^ {+} \mathbf {1} \big) (i), \quad \widehat {\psi} _ {x, i} ^ {-} (q) = \frac {1}{q} \big (\Psi_ {q, x} ^ {-} \mathbf {1} \big) (i).
$$

The Laplace transform of $\psi _ { x , i } ( t ) = \mathbb { P } _ { x , i } ( \underline { { X } } _ { t } > \ell , \overline { { X } } _ { t } < \upsilon )$ is hence oftheform 

$$
\widehat {\psi} _ {x, i} (q) = \widehat {\psi} _ {x, i} ^ {+} (q) + \widehat {\psi} _ {x, i} ^ {-} (q).\tag{17.75}
$$

Remarks 

(i) If $Q _ { 0 } = O$ , then $\eta _ { q } ^ { \pm }$ are identity matrices, and the following identities hold: 

$$
\Psi_ {q, x} ^ {+} = \big (e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {+} (\upsilon - x)} - e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {-} (x - \ell)} e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {+} (\upsilon - \ell)} \big) \big (I - e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {-} (\upsilon - \ell)} e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {+} (\upsilon - \ell)} \big) ^ {- 1},
$$

$$
\Psi_ {q, x} ^ {-} = \big (e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {+} (\upsilon - x)} - e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {+} (x - \ell)} e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {-} (\upsilon - \ell)} \big) \big (I - e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {+} (\upsilon - \ell)} e ^ {Q _ {q} ^ {-} (\upsilon - \ell)} \big) ^ {- 1},
$$

where $Q _ { q } ^ { \pm }$ are diagonal matrices given in (17.71). In particular, we find the well-known two-sided exit identity for Brownian motion with drift: 

$$
\widehat {\psi} _ {x, i} (q) = \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \big [ e ^ {- q \tau_ {\ell , v}} I _ {\{\tau_ {v} <   \tau_ {\ell} \}} \big ] = \frac {e ^ {\omega_ {i} ^ {+} (x - \ell)} - e ^ {\omega_ {i} ^ {-} (x - \ell)}}{e ^ {\omega_ {i} ^ {+} (v - \ell)} - e ^ {\omega_ {i} ^ {-} (v - \ell)}},
$$

where $\omega _ { i } ^ { \pm }$ is given in (17.72) with $r _ { i } = 0$ 

(ii) In the case that no volatility is present $( \Sigma \equiv 0 )$ the identities simplify, and we find the expressions in [5]. 

(iii) Under $\mathbb { P } _ { x , i } , x \in \mathbb { R } , i \in E ^ { 0 }$ , the process $\widetilde M ^ { + } = \{ \widetilde M _ { t } ^ { + } \} _ { t \geq 0 }$ defined by 

$$
\widetilde {M} _ {t} ^ {+} = e ^ {- q (t \wedge T _ {\ell , v})} \Psi_ {q, \ell , v} ^ {+} (X _ {t \wedge T _ {\ell , v}}, Z _ {t \wedge T _ {\ell , v}})
$$

is a row-vector of bounded martingales, where we denoted by $\psi _ { q , \ell , \upsilon } ^ { + } ( x , i )$ the $N ^ { + }$ -dimensional row vector with jth element $\psi _ { q , \ell , \upsilon } ^ { + } ( x , i , j )$ 

Proof Let $q > 0$ and define 

$$
g ^ {+} (x, i) = \Psi_ {q, \ell , \upsilon} ^ {+} (x, i).
$$

In view of the fact that $\widetilde { M } ^ { + }$ is a bounded martingale, it holds that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} g ^ {+} (x, i) = \sum_ {j \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {+}} \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \big [ e ^ {- q \tau} \Psi_ {q, \ell , \upsilon} ^ {+} (X _ {\tau}, Z _ {\tau}, j) I _ {\{\tau <   \infty \}} \big ] \\ = \sum_ {j \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {+}} \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \big [ e ^ {- q \tau} I _ {\{X _ {\tau} \geq \upsilon , Z _ {\tau} = j \}} \big ] \\ = q \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- q t} \mathbb {P} _ {x, i} (\tau <   t, X _ {\tau} \geq \upsilon)   d t = q \widehat {\psi} _ {x, i} ^ {+} (q). \end{array}
$$

Here we used that, in view of the definitions (17.73) and (17.68) of $\psi _ { q , \ell , \upsilon } ^ { + }$ and $\eta _ { q } ^ { + }$ , the function $g ^ { + }$ satisfies: 

$$
g ^ {+} (x, i) = 1 \quad \text { if } x \geq v, i \in E ^ {0},
$$

$$
g ^ {+} (x, i) = 0 \quad \text { if } x \leq \ell , i \in E ^ {0}.
$$

The expression for $\widehat { \psi } _ { x , i } ^ { - }$ can be derived by a similar reasoning. 

## 17.5.5 Valuing a Double-Barrier Rebate Option

A double-barrier rebate option pays a constant rebate L at the moment τ one of the barrier levels is crossed, if this happens before maturity $T$ . By standard arbitrage pricing arguments the Laplace transform $\widehat { v } _ { \mathrm { r e b } }$ in maturity of the price of $v _ { \mathrm { r e b } }$ of such an option is given by 

$$
\widehat {v} _ {\mathrm{reb}} (q) = \frac {1}{q} \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \left[ \left(B _ {\tau} ^ {D}\right) ^ {- 1} \exp (- q \tau) \right].\tag{17.76}
$$

We will find below the following more general quantity, which will also be employed in the sequel: 

$$
H ^ {x, i} (q, u, j) := \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \left[ \left(B _ {\tau} ^ {D}\right) ^ {- 1} \exp (\mathrm{i} u X _ {\tau} - q \tau) I _ {\{Z _ {\tau} = j \}} \right] \quad \text { for } j = 1, \dots , N.\tag{17.77}
$$

In the following result an explicit expression is given for the quantity $H _ { j } ^ { x , i }$ in terms of the matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation, which is an extension of identity (17.75). 

We denote by $E _ { i } ^ { + }$ and $E _ { i } ^ { - }$ , for $i \in E ^ { 0 } = \{ 1 , . . . , N \}$ , the parts of the state space $E$ corresponding to the blocks $B _ { i } ^ { + }$ and $B _ { i } ^ { - }$ in the matrix $Q _ { 0 }$ in (17.61). Recall that the definition of $\alpha _ { i } ^ { \pm }$ was given in (17.21). 

Theorem 17.24 For any $h \in { \mathcal { H } } , ~ i , j \in E ^ { 0 }$ and $u \in \mathbb { C }$ that satisfies $\Im ( u ) \in$ $( - \alpha _ { j } ^ { + } , \alpha _ { j } ^ { - } )$ , it holds that 

$$
H _ {j} ^ {x, i} (h, u) = \left(\Psi_ {h, x} ^ {+} k _ {j, u} ^ {+}\right) (i) + \left(\Psi_ {h, x} ^ {-} k _ {j, u} ^ {-}\right) (i),\tag{17.78}
$$

where the column vectors $k _ { j , u } ^ { + } = ( k _ { j , u } ^ { + } ( i ) , i \in E ^ { + } \cup E ^ { 0 } )$ and $k _ { j , u } ^ { - } = ( k _ { j , u } ^ { - } ( i ) , i \in$ $E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { - } )$ are given by 

$$
k _ {j, u} ^ {+} (i) = e ^ {u v} \cdot \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text {   if   } i = j \in E ^ {0}, \\ ((- u I _ {j} ^ {+} - B _ {j} ^ {+}) ^ {- 1} (- B _ {j} ^ {+}) \mathbf {1}) (i) & \text {   if   } i \in E _ {j} ^ {+}, \\ 0 & \text {   otherwise }, \end{array} \right.
$$

$$
k _ {j, u} ^ {-} (i) = e ^ {u \ell} \cdot \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text { if   } i = j \in E ^ {0}, \\ ((u I _ {j} ^ {-} - B _ {j} ^ {-}) ^ {- 1} (- B _ {j} ^ {-}) \mathbf {1}) (i) & \text { if   } i \in E _ {j} ^ {-}, \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }, \end{array} \right.
$$

where $I _ { j } ^ { + }$ and $I _ { j } ^ { - }$ are $| E _ { j } ^ { + } | \times | E _ { j } ^ { + } |$ and $| E _ { j } ^ { - } | \times | E _ { j } ^ { - } |$ identity matrices. 

The proof is given in Sect. 17.8. 

## 17.6 Double-No-Touch and Other Barrier Options

In this section we show how the prices of double-no-touch and double knock-out call options can be expressed in terms characteristic function H of the process at the corresponding first passage time, which was identified in Theorem 17.24. 

A double-no-touch is a derivative security that pays one unit of the underlying asset at expiry T if the underlying asset price does not leave the interval [exp(), exp(υ)] during the time period [0, T], where $\ell < \upsilon$ . Similarly a double knock-out call option struck at $K$ delivers the payoff $( S _ { T } - K ) ^ { + } : = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ S _ { T } -$ $K , 0 \}$ if throughout the life of the option the asset price stays within the interval [exp(), exp(υ)]. The arbitrage-free prices for a double-no-touch and a double knock-out call options are respectively given by 

$$
D _ {x, i} (T) = \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \bigg [ \frac {I _ {\{\tau > T \}}}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} \bigg ],\tag{17.79}
$$

$$
C _ {x, i} (k, T) = \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \bigg [ \frac {I _ {\{\tau > T \}}}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} (S _ {T} - K) ^ {+} \bigg ],\tag{17.80}
$$

where k = log K is the log-strike, and τ is the first time the process S leaves the interval [exp(), exp(υ)] or equivalently 

$$
\tau := \inf \left\{t \geq 0: X _ {t} \notin [ \ell , v ] \right\}.\tag{17.81}
$$

We will find it more convenient to consider the double-touch-in and the knock-in call options whose values $v _ { \mathrm { d t i } }$ and $v _ { \mathrm { k i c } }$ , as functions of maturity $T$ and log strike $k = \log K$ , are given by 

$$
v _ {\mathrm{dti}} (T) := \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \left[ \frac {I _ {\{\tau \leq T \}}}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} \right] = \mathbb {E} _ {i} \left[ \left(B _ {T} ^ {D}\right) ^ {- 1} \right] - D _ {x, i} (T),\tag{17.82}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} v _ {\mathrm{kic}} (T, k) := \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \bigg [ \frac {I _ {\{\tau \leq T \}}}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} (S _ {T} - K) ^ {+} \bigg ] \\ = \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \big [ \big (B _ {T} ^ {D} \big) ^ {- 1} \big (S _ {T} - e ^ {k} \big) ^ {+} \big ] - C _ {x, i} (k, T). \end{array}\tag{17.83}
$$

Since the zero-coupon bond price and the call option price have already been identified, the problem of calculating the double-no-touch and knock-out call prices thus reduces to identifying $v _ { \mathrm { d t i } }$ and $v _ { \mathrm { k i c } }$ . In general, no closed-form expressions are known for these functions in terms of elementary functions. Below we show that the Laplace transform in $T$ of $v _ { \mathrm { d t i } } ( T )$ as well as the joint Fourier–Laplace transform in (k, T) of $v _ { \mathrm { k i c } }$ can be identified explicitly in terms of the parameters that define the log-price process X. Both transforms will be identified in terms of the Laplace transform $\widehat { F } _ { x , i } ( u , q )$ in T of the function $T \mapsto F _ { x , i } ( u , T )$ given by 

$$
F _ {x, i} (u, T) := \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \bigg [ \frac {I _ {\{\tau \leq T \}}}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} \exp (\mathrm{i} u X _ {T}) \bigg ].\tag{17.84}
$$

The Laplace transform $\widehat { F } _ { x , i } ( u , q )$ in turn will be given in terms of the N -vector $H ^ { x , i } ( q , u )$ whose coordinates are given by 

$$
H _ {j} ^ {x, i} (q, u) := \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \left[ \exp \left(\mathrm{i} u X _ {\tau} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \left(R _ {D} \left(Z _ {s}\right) + q\right) d s\right) I _ {\{Z _ {\tau} = j \}} \right]
$$

for j = 1, . . . , N<sub>0</sub>. 

Theorem 17.25 For any $q > 0$ and $\xi$ with $\Im ( \xi ) < 0$ , it holds that 

$$
\widehat {v} _ {\mathrm{dti}} (q) = \widehat {F} _ {x, i} (0, q),\tag{17.85}
$$

$$
\widehat {v} _ {\mathrm{kic}} ^ {*} (q, \xi) = \frac {1}{\mathrm{i} \xi - \xi^ {2}} \widehat {F} _ {x, i} (\xi - \mathrm{i}, q).\tag{17.86}
$$

Here, $\widehat { F } _ { x , i } ( u , q )$ is given by 

$$
\widehat {F} _ {x, i} (u, q) = \left(H ^ {x, i} (q, u)\right) ^ {\prime} \left(q I + \Lambda_ {D} - K (u)\right) ^ {- 1} \mathbf {1}\tag{17.87}
$$

for all $q \in \mathbb { C }$ such that $\mathfrak { R } ( q ) > q ^ { * } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ \mathfrak { R } ( \psi _ { i } ( u ) ) - R _ { D } ( i ) : i = 1 , \ldots , N _ { 0 } \} .$ 

Remarks 

(i) Note that if $u = 0$ , then $q ^ { * } \leq 0$ , as the interest rates $R _ { D } ( i )$ are assumed to be nonnegative. 

(ii) The Laplace transform in (17.87) can be inverted by evaluating the Bromwich integral 

$$
F _ {x, i} (u, t) = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {c - \mathrm{i} \infty} ^ {c + \mathrm{i} \infty} e ^ {t q} \bigl (H ^ {x, i} (q, u) \bigr) ^ {\prime} \bigl (q I + \varLambda_ {D} - K (u) \bigr) ^ {- 1} \mathbf {1} d q\tag{17.88}
$$

for any $c > q ^ { * }$ . An efficient algorithm to approximate this integral can e.g. be found in Abate and Whitt [1]. 

Proof First note that by a calculation similar to the one in the proof of Proposition 17.15 we find that the Fourier transform in log-strike k of $e ^ { \alpha k } v _ { \mathrm { k i c } } ( T , k )$ can be expressed in terms of $F$ by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} e ^ {(\mathrm{i} v + \alpha) k} v _ {\mathrm{kic}} (T, k)   d k \\ = \frac {1}{(\alpha + \mathrm{i} v) (1 + \alpha + \mathrm{i} v)} \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \bigg [ \frac {I _ {\{\tau \leq T \}}}{B _ {T} ^ {D}} \exp \bigl \{(1 + \alpha + \mathrm{i} v) X _ {T} \bigr \} \bigg ] \end{array}
$$

for any $\alpha > 0$ 

Assume next that $q > 0$ is real with $q > q ^ { * }$ . The Laplace transform $\widehat { F } _ { x , i } ( u , q )$ has the following well-known equivalent probabilistic representation 

$$
\widehat {F} _ {x, i} (u, q) = \mathbb {E} \big [ F _ {x, i} (u, e _ {q}) \big ] / q,\tag{17.89}
$$

where $e _ { q }$ is an exponential random variable with parameter q which is independen of the process $( X , Z )$ 

By conditioning on $\mathcal { F } _ { \tau }$ and applying strong Markov property at τ of the process (X, Z) together with Lemma 17.6, we find that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} \big [ F _ {x, i} (u, e _ {q}) \big ] = \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \Bigg [ \frac {\exp (\mathrm{i} u X _ {\tau})}{B _ {\tau} ^ {D}} \mathbb {E} \Bigg [ I _ {\{\tau \leq e _ {q} \}} \exp \Bigg (- \int_ {\tau} ^ {e _ {q}} R _ {D} (Z _ {s})   d s \\ \qquad + \mathrm{i} u (X _ {e _ {q}} - X _ {\tau}) \Bigg) \Bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \Bigg ] \Bigg ] \\ = \mathbb {E} _ {x, i} \Bigg [ \frac {\exp (\mathrm{i} u X _ {\tau})}{B _ {\tau} ^ {D}} h (Z _ {\tau}, q, u) e ^ {- q \tau} \Bigg ] \\ = \sum_ {j} H _ {j} ^ {x, i} (q, u) h (j, q, u), \end{array}\tag{17.90}
$$

where the value $h ( j , q , u )$ for each state $j \in E ^ { 0 }$ of the Markov chain Z is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{c} h (j, q, u) := \mathbb {E} _ {0, j} \bigg [ \exp \bigg (- \int_ {0} ^ {e _ {q} ^ {\prime}} R _ {D} (Z _ {s})   d s + \mathrm{i} u X _ {e _ {q} ^ {\prime}} \bigg) \bigg ] \\ = \big [ \big (q I + \varLambda_ {D} - K (u) \big) ^ {- 1} \mathbf {1} \big ] (j) \end{array}\tag{17.91}
$$

for some exponential random variable $e _ { q } ^ { \prime }$ with parameter $q$ that is independent of the Markov process $( X , Z )$ , where the second equality follows from Lemma 17.3 and Theorem 17.7. 

A key observation that follows from the representation (17.90) is that the function 

$$
q \mapsto \mathbb {E} \left[ F _ {x, i} (u, e _ {q}) \right] / q
$$

has a holomorphic extension to the complex half-plane $\{ q \in \mathbb { C } : \Re ( q ) > q ^ { * } \}$ which therefore<sup>14</sup> coincides on this domain with the Laplace transform. Thus, (17.90) holds for $q$ in this domain, and the proof is complete. - 

## 17.7 Embedding of the Process $( X , Z )$

In this section and the next we will provide a proof of the matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation and its corollaries derived in previous sections. We will proceed in two steps: 

(i) Reduction of the first-passage problems of X over constant levels, which will involve overshoots and undershoots due to the jumps of X, to the first-hitting problem of a constant level by a regime-switching Brownian motion, employing a classical argument for the embedding of phase-type jumps (see Asmussen [2]), which we review in this section. 

(ii) Solution of the first-passage problem of regime-switching Brownian motion via a characterisation of the dynamics of the ladder processes, which is carried out in Sect. 17.8. 

Let Y be a continuous-time Markov chain with finite state space $E \cup \partial$ and generator restricted to E given by $Q _ { 0 }$ , where $\partial$ is an absorbing cemetery state, and E and $Q _ { 0 }$ will be specified shortly, and denote by $\xi = \{ \xi _ { t } , t \ge 0 \}$ the Markov-modulated Brownian motion given by 

$$
\xi_ {t} = x + \int_ {0} ^ {t} s (Y _ {s}) d W _ {s} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} m (Y _ {s}) d s,\tag{17.92}
$$

where $x \in \mathbb { R }$ is the starting point of $\xi$ , and s and m are functions from $E \cup \partial$ to R also to be specified shortly. The couple $( \xi , Y )$ defined as such is a two-dimensional strong Markov process. In the sequel we will denote by $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } _ { x , i }$ and $\widetilde { \mathbb { E } } _ { x , i }$ the conditiona probability $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } _ { x , i } = \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } [ \cdot | \xi _ { 0 } = x , Y _ { 0 } = i ]$ and conditional expectation $\widetilde { \mathbb { E } } _ { x , i } = \widetilde { \mathbb { E } } [ \cdot | \xi _ { 0 } =$ $x , Y _ { 0 } = i ]$ , respectively. 

Let the state space $E$ be as in Sect. 17.5. In other words, $E = E ^ { - } \cup E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { + }$ where $E ^ { 0 }$ is the state space of the chain Z, and $E ^ { + }$ and $E ^ { - }$ are given in (17.65). The generator $Q _ { 0 }$ is given in (17.61), and $m ( i ) : = A _ { V } ( i , i ) , s ( i ) : = A _ { \Sigma } ( i , i )$ for all $i \in E$ , where the matrices $A _ { V } , A _ { \Sigma }$ are defined in (17.62). Thus, while the chain Y is in state $j \in E ^ { 0 }$ , ξ evolves as a Brownian motion with drift m $( j )$ and volatility $s ( j )$ , and while Y takes values in $E ^ { + }$ and $E ^ { - }$ , the path of $\xi$ is linear with slope $+ 1 \ \mathrm { o r \ - } 1$ . Informally, a path of X can be obtained from a path of $\xi$ by replacing these stretches of unit slope by jumps of the same length, as is illustrated in Fig. 1. These linear increasing and decreasing stretches of path of $\xi$ thus correspond to the positive and negative jumps of $X$ , respectively. 

More formally, by appropriately time-changing $( \xi , Y )$ a stochastic process can be constructed that has the same law as $( X , Z )$ . Denote by 

$$
T _ {0} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} I _ {\{Y _ {s} \in E ^ {0} \}} d s \quad \text { and } \quad T _ {0} ^ {- 1} (u) = \inf \bigl \{t \geq 0: T _ {0} (t) > u \bigr \},
$$

the time before t spent by the chain Y in $E ^ { 0 }$ and its right-continuous inverse respectively. It is clear from the definition of the generator $Q _ { 0 }$ in (17.61) that when the chain $Y$ jumps from any of the states in $E ^ { + } \cup E ^ { - }$ to a state $j \in E ^ { 0 }$ , it must have been in the state j just before it had left $E ^ { 0 }$ . Therefore the form of the matrix (17.61) implies that the process $Y \circ T _ { 0 } ^ { - 1 }$ , which simply ignores all excursions of Y into $E ^ { + } \cup E ^ { - }$ , is a Markov chain with the same generator as $Z .$ . Furthermore it is straightforward to verify that $\xi \circ T _ { 0 } ^ { - 1 }$ is a regime-switching jump-diffusion and the law of the process $( \xi \circ T _ { 0 } ^ { - 1 } , Y \circ T _ { 0 } ^ { - 1 } )$ under $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } _ { x , i }$ is equal to that of (X, Z) under $\mathbb { P } _ { x , i }$ for all $x \in \mathbb { R }$ and $i \in E ^ { 0 }$ 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/badad6ab-6270-4621-ad4a-91cddcb58301/22a013401b81cef188c01208be96af07d857a0eb63d99d1a47073c89b3a10e20.jpg)



Fig. 1 Shown is a sample path of X until the first time τ that X exits the interval $[ \ell , \upsilon ]$ . The process $\xi$ has no positive jumps and always hits a level at first-passage


If we define the first-passage time 

$$
\tau^ {\xi} = \inf \left\{t \geq 0: \xi_ {t} \notin [ \ell , v ] \text {   and   } Y _ {t} \in E ^ {0} \right\},\tag{17.93}
$$

it follows that random variables $T _ { 0 } ( \tau ^ { \xi } )$ and the stopping time $\tau$ defined in (17.81) have the same distribution. In particular, with the extension of $h$ to $E$ that puts $h ( i ) = 0$ for $i \notin E ^ { 0 }$ and that we will also denote by $h$ , it holds that 

$$
\left(\xi_ {\tau^ {\xi}}, \int_ {0} ^ {\tau^ {\xi}} h (Y _ {s}) d s, Y _ {\tau^ {\xi}}\right) \text {   under   } \widetilde {\mathbb {P}} _ {x, i} \text {   has   the   same   distribution   as   }
$$

$$
\left(X _ {\tau}, \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} h (Z _ {s}) d s, Z _ {\tau}\right) \text { under } \mathbb {P} _ {x, i}
$$

for $x \in \mathbb { R }$ and $i \in E ^ { 0 }$ . The function $H _ { i } ^ { x , i }$ defined in (17.77) can thus be expressed in terms of the embedding (ξ, Y) as follows: 

$$
H _ {j} ^ {x, i} (h, u) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \bigg [ \exp \bigg (u \xi_ {\tau^ {\xi}} - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau^ {\xi}} h (Y _ {s}) d s \bigg) I _ {\{Y _ {\tau^ {\xi}} = j \}} \bigg ], \quad i, j \in E ^ {0}.\tag{17.94}
$$

## 17.8 Ladder Processes

This section is devoted to the proof of existence and uniqueness of the h-matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation for any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ . For real $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ , the vector h has the probabilistic interpretation of a vector of state-dependent rates of discounting, and in this case the matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation has a probabilistic interpretation in terms of ladder processes. The existence and uniqueness results are extended to the case of general complex $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ by analytical continuation arguments. It is of interest to consider the case of complex entries, as the Laplace transforms of barrier option prices are expressed in terms of the matrix Wiener–Hopf factorisation as we saw above, and some widely used Laplace transform inversion algorithms are based on the Bromwich (complex) integral representation. 

A classical probabilistic approach to characterisation of the joint distribution of $\tau _ { a } ^ { + }$ and the position of Y at $\tau _ { a } ^ { + }$ is to consider the up-crossing ladder process of $( \xi , Y )$ , defined as follows: 

Definition 17.26 The up-crossing ladder process $Y ^ { + } = \{ Y _ { t } ^ { + } \} _ { t \geq 0 }$ of $( \xi , Y )$ is given by 

$$
Y _ {a} ^ {+} := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} Y (\tau_ {a} ^ {+}) & \text { if } \tau_ {a} ^ {+} <   \infty , \\ \partial & \text { otherwise }, \end{array} \right.\tag{17.95}
$$

where ∂ is a graveyard state, and 

$$
\tau_ {a} ^ {+} = \inf \{s \geq 0: \xi_ {s} > a \}
$$

with inf $\varnothing = \infty$ 

Remark In the case that the original chain is killed at (state-dependent, real-valued) rate h, the up-crossing ladder process can be defined as follows. Recall from Markov chain theory that the chain $Y ^ { h }$ with state space $E \cup \{ \partial \}$ and generator matrix 

$$
\left( \begin{array}{c c} Q _ {h} & - \Lambda_ {h} \mathbf {1} \\ \mathbf {0} & 0 \end{array} \right), \quad \text { where } Q _ {h} := Q _ {0} - \Lambda_ {h}, \text { and } \Lambda_ {h} \text { is   the   diagonal   matrix }
$$

$$
\text { with } (\Lambda_ {h}) _ {i i} = h _ {i},
$$

has the same distribution as the chain Y killed (i.e. sent to the graveyard state ∂) independently at rate $h ( i )$ when $Y _ { t } = i$ . In particular, for i, $j \in E$ and $t \geq 0$ , it holds that 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {i} \left[ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {t} = j \}} \right] = \widetilde {\mathbb {P}} \left(Y _ {t} ^ {h} = j \mid Y _ {0} ^ {h} = i\right) = \exp (Q _ {h} t) (i, j).\tag{17.96}
$$

If we denote by $\xi ^ { h } = \{ \xi _ { t } ^ { h } \} _ { t \geq 0 }$ the process defined by (17.92) driven by the “killed” chain $Y ^ { h }$ instead of Y, then the up-crossing ladder process $Y ^ { h + }$ is given by 

$$
Y _ {t} ^ {h +} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} Y _ {\tau_ {t} ^ {h +}} ^ {h} & \text { if } \tau_ {t} ^ {h +} <   \infty , \\ \partial & \text { otherwise }, \end{array} \right.
$$

where $\tau _ { a } ^ { h + }$ is the stopping time defined by 

$$
\tau_ {a} ^ {h +} = \inf \left\{s \geq 0: \xi_ {s} ^ {h} > a \right\}
$$

with inf $\varnothing = \infty$ 

Proposition 17.27 The process $Y ^ { + }$ is a Markov chain with state space $E ^ { 0 } \cup$ $E ^ { + } \cup \{ \partial \}$ 

Remarks 

(i) We denote by $Q _ { 0 } ^ { + }$ the generator of $Y ^ { + }$ restricted to $E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { + }$ , and by $\eta _ { 0 } ^ { + }$ the initial distribution given by 

$$
\eta_ {0} ^ {+} (i, j) = \widetilde {\mathbb {P}} _ {0, i} \left[ Y _ {0} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {0} ^ {+} <   \infty \right] \quad \text { for } i \in E, j \in E ^ {+} \cup E ^ {0}.\tag{17.97}
$$

(ii) More generally, for any real-valued $h \in { \mathcal { H } } ,$ , it holds that $Y ^ { h + }$ is a Markov chain with generator restricted to $E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { + }$ , denoted by $\boldsymbol { Q } _ { h } ^ { + }$ , and initial (sub)probability distribution by $\eta _ { h } ^ { + } = ( \eta _ { h } ^ { + } ( i , j ) , i \in E , j \in E ^ { + } \overset { \cdot } { \cup } E ^ { 0 } )$ with 

$$
\eta_ {h} ^ {+} (i, j) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \left[ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {0} ^ {+}} h \left(Y _ {s}\right) d s} I _ {\left\{Y _ {0} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {0} ^ {+} <   \infty \right\}} \right] \quad \text { for } i \in E, j \in E ^ {+} \cup E ^ {0}.\tag{17.98}
$$

We have the following identities analogous to (17.96): 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} = j, \tau_ {t} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big | Y _ {0} = i \big ] \\ = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {\tau_ {0} ^ {+}} ^ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} = j, \tau_ {t} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big | Y _ {\tau_ {0} ^ {+}} = i \big ] \\ = \widetilde {\mathbb {P}} \big (Y _ {\tau_ {t} ^ {h +}} ^ {h} = j, \tau_ {t} ^ {h +} <   \infty \big | Y _ {\tau_ {0} ^ {h +}} ^ {h} = i \big) \\ = \widetilde {\mathbb {P}} \big (Y _ {t} ^ {h +} = j \big | Y _ {0} ^ {h +} = i \big) \\ = \exp \big (Q _ {h} ^ {+} t \big) (i, j), \quad i, j \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {+}, \end{array}\tag{17.99}
$$

where we wrote ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } [ \cdot | A ] : = { \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } } [ \cdot | A \cap \{ \xi _ { 0 } = 0 \} ]$ and $\widetilde { \mathbb { E } } [ \cdot | A ] : = \widetilde { \mathbb { E } } [ \cdot | A \cap \{ \xi _ { 0 } = 0 \} ]$ to simplify the notation. Note that the first equality holds since $\tau _ { 0 } ^ { + } = 0$ if the chain $Y$ starts at $i \in E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { + }$ . In particular, from (17.99) we find that, for $i , j \in E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { + }$ 

$$
Q _ {h} ^ {+} (i, j) = \lim _ {t \downarrow 0} \frac {1}{t} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} = j, \tau_ {t} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ], \quad i \neq j,\tag{17.100}
$$

$$
Q _ {h} ^ {+} (i, i) = \lim _ {t \downarrow 0} \frac {1}{t} \left\{\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \left[ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} h \left(Y _ {s}\right) d s} I _ {\left\{Y _ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} = i, \tau_ {t} ^ {+} <   \infty \right\}} \right] - 1 \right\}.\tag{17.101}
$$

Proof Let f be any bounded real-valued Borel function, and let $b < a$ . Denote by $\mathcal { F } _ { a } = \sigma \{ Y _ { u } ^ { + } \} _ { u \leq a }$ and $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \sigma \{ Y _ { s } \} _ { s \leq t }$ the sigma algebras generated by $Y _ { u } ^ { + }$ up to time a and by $Y _ { s }$ up to time t. Observing that $\mathcal { F } _ { b } \subset \mathcal { G } _ { \tau _ { b } }$ and using the spatial homogeneity and continuity of $\xi$ and the strong Markov property of $( \xi , Y )$ , we find that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ f (Y _ {a} ^ {+}) | \mathcal {F} _ {b} \big ] = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ f (Y _ {\tau_ {a} ^ {+}}) | \mathcal {G} _ {\tau_ {b}} \big ] | \mathcal {F} _ {b} \big ]} \\ & {\qquad = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {b, Y _ {\tau_ {b} ^ {+}}} \big [ f (Y _ {\tau_ {a} ^ {+}}) \big ] | \mathcal {F} _ {b} \big ]} \\ & {\qquad = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {Y _ {b} ^ {+}} \big [ f (Y _ {a - b} ^ {+}) \big ] | \mathcal {F} _ {b} \big ] = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {Y _ {b} ^ {+}} \big [ f (Y _ {a - b} ^ {+}) \big ],} \end{array}
$$

where we wrote $\widetilde { \mathbb { E } } _ { j } = \widetilde { \mathbb { E } } _ { 0 , j }$ 

For any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ , we define the square-matrix (resolvent) functions $u \mapsto R _ { h } ^ { + } ( u )$ of dimension $N ^ { + }$ on the complex half-plane $\mathbb { C } _ { > 0 }$ by 

$$
R _ {h} ^ {+} (u) (i, j) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- u y - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {y} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {y} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {y} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} d y \right]
$$

for i, $j \in E ^ { + } \cup E ^ { 0 }$ and $u \in \mathbb { C } _ { > 0 }$ 

(17.102) 

The matrix $\boldsymbol { Q } _ { h } ^ { + }$ can then be defined for any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ as follows: 

Lemma 17.28 Let $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ and $a \geq 0$ and define the matrix $Q _ { h } ^ { + } \in \mathbb { D } ( N ^ { + } )$ by 

$$
Q _ {h} ^ {+} (i, j) = - \omega_ {i} ^ {+} I _ {\{i = j \}} + \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {2}{\sigma_ {i} ^ {2}} (\widetilde {Q} \eta_ {h} ^ {+} R _ {h} ^ {+} (\omega_ {i} ^ {-})) (i, j) & i f i \in E ^ {0}, \\ (\widetilde {Q} \eta_ {h} ^ {+}) (i, j) & i f i \in E ^ {+}, \end{array} \right.\tag{17.103}
$$

where $q _ { i } = - Q _ { 0 } ( i , i ) , h _ { i } = h ( i ) , \widetilde { \mathcal { Q } } = Q _ { 0 } + \mathrm { d i a g } \{ q _ { i } : i \in E \}$ , and 

$$
\omega_ {i} ^ {+} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} F (\frac {\mu_ {i}}{\sigma_ {i} ^ {2}}, \frac {q _ {i} + h _ {i}}{\sigma_ {i} ^ {2}}) & i f i \in E ^ {0}, \\ q _ {i} + h _ {i} & i f i \in E ^ {\pm}, \end{array} \right.\tag{17.104}
$$

where 

$$
F (\nu , \theta) := - \nu + \sqrt {\nu^ {2} + 2 \theta}, \quad \nu \in \mathbb {R},   \theta \in \mathbb {C} _ {> 0}.\tag{17.105}
$$

Then it holds that 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {a} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {a} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {a} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ] = \exp \big (Q _ {h} ^ {+} a \big) (i, j), \quad i, j \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {+}.\tag{17.106}
$$

Remarks 

(i) Note that Proposition 17.22 follows as a direct consequence of (17.106) since 

$$
\mathbb {P} _ {x, i} (\overline {{X}} _ {\mathbf {e} _ {q}} > a) = \mathbb {P} _ {x, i} \big (Y _ {\zeta} ^ {q +} > a \big),
$$

where $\zeta$ is the life time of the killed up-crossing ladder process. 

(ii) Equation (17.106) yields in particular the joint Laplace transform of the vector 

$$
\mathbf {Z} _ {a} ^ {+} = \left(\int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {a} ^ {+}} I _ {\{Y _ {s} = i \}} d s, i \in E\right),\tag{17.107}
$$

whose components record the length of time spent by Y in each of the states in $E$ , until the moment $\tau _ { a } ^ { + }$ of first-passage. 

(iii) The down-crossing ladder process $Y ^ { - }$ , defined as the up-crossing ladder process of $( - \xi , Y )$ , is a Markov chain with generator restricted to $E _ { 0 } \cup E ^ { - }$ denoted by $Q _ { 0 } ^ { - }$ . Analogously to (17.103), for any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ , a matrix ${ Q } _ { h } ^ { - }$ can be defined, which satisfies 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \left[ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {a} ^ {-}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {a} ^ {-} = j, \tau_ {a} ^ {-} <   \infty \}} \right] = \exp \left(Q _ {h} ^ {-} a\right) (i, j), \quad i, j \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {-}.\tag{17.108}
$$

## 17.8.1 Proof ofLemma 17.28

We will show that the limits in (17.100)–(17.101) in fact exist for any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ , and identify these. Let 

$$
\rho = \inf \{t \geq 0: Y _ {t} \neq Y _ {0} \}
$$

be the first time that the chain Y jumps, and $\tau _ { a } ^ { i } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \geq 0 : X _ { t } ^ { i } > a \}$ the firstpassage time of $X _ { t } ^ { i } : = \mu _ { i } t + \sigma _ { i } W _ { t }$ (recall that if $i \in E ^ { \pm }$ , then $\mu _ { i } = \pm 1$ and $\sigma _ { i } = 0 )$ over the level $a _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , and let $\mathbf { e } _ { i }$ be an exponential random time with mean $1 / q _ { i }$ (with $q _ { i } = - Q _ { 0 } ( i , i ) )$ that is independent of $X ^ { i }$ . In view of the definition of $\xi$ (i.e. the first jump time $\rho$ of Y is independent of $X ^ { i } )$ , it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \Big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {t} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {t} ^ {+} <   \infty , \tau_ {t} ^ {+} <   \rho \}} \Big ] \\ = I _ {\{i = j \}} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- \tau_ {t} ^ {i} h (i)} I _ {\{\tau_ {t} ^ {i} <   \mathbf {e} _ {i} \}} \big ] = I _ {\{i = j \}} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- \tau_ {t} ^ {i} (h _ {i} + q _ {i})} \big ] \\ = I _ {\{i = j, i \in E ^ {+} \}} \exp \big (- t (h _ {i} + q _ {i}) \big) \\ \qquad + I _ {\{i = j, i \in E ^ {0} \}} \exp \big (- t \sigma_ {i} ^ {- 2} \big (- \mu_ {i} + \sqrt {\mu_ {i} ^ {2} + 2 (q _ {i} + h _ {i}) \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}} \big) \big) \\ = I _ {\{i = j \}} \big [ 1 - \omega_ {i} ^ {+} t + o (t) \big ] \quad \text {as} t \downarrow 0, \end{array}
$$

where $\omega _ { i } ^ { + }$ was defined in Lemma 17.28, and we used the fact that the Laplace transform of $\tau _ { a } ^ { i }$ is given by 

$$
\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- q \tau_ {a} ^ {i}} \big ] = \exp \bigl (- a \sigma_ {i} ^ {- 2} \bigl (- \mu_ {i} + \sqrt {\mu_ {i} ^ {2} + 2 q \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}} \bigr) \bigr), \quad a > 0, q \in \mathbb {C} _ {> 0}.
$$

For every $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ , we can define the following matrices: 

$$
\widetilde {P} _ {t} ^ {h +} (i, j) := \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \left[ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} h \left(Y _ {s}\right) d s} I _ {\left\{Y _ {t} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {t} ^ {+} <   \infty \right\}} \right] \quad \text { for } i, j \in E ^ {+} \cup E ^ {0}.\tag{17.109}
$$

Note that the definition in (17.102) implies that the identity $R _ { h } ^ { + } ( u ) ( i , j ) =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } e ^ { - u y } \widetilde { P } _ { y } ^ { h + } ( i , j ) d y } \end{array}$ holds for all $u \in \mathbb { C } _ { > 0 }$ . For every $h \in \mathcal { H } , x \in ( - \infty , t ]$ and $m \in E$ , we have the following identity: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, m} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {t} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {t} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ] \\ \qquad = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, m} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t - x} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {t - x} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {t - x} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ] \\ \qquad = \big (\eta_ {h} ^ {+} \widetilde {P} _ {t - x} ^ {h +} \big) (m, j) \quad \text { for } j \in E ^ {+} \cup E ^ {0}, \end{array}\tag{17.110}
$$

where $\eta _ { h } ^ { + }$ is defined in (17.98). The first equality in (17.110) is a consequence of the spacial homogeneity of the process $\xi$ . 

Let $\overline { { { \xi } } } _ { u } = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { s \leq u } \xi _ { s }$ denote the running supremum of the stochastic process $\xi$ . The strong Markov property applied at the first jump time $\rho$ of the chain Y and (17.110) imply that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {t} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {t} ^ {+} <   \infty , \tau_ {t} ^ {+} \geq \rho \}} \big ] \\ = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \big [ e ^ {- h (i) \rho} I _ {\{\overline {{\xi}} _ {\rho} \leq t \}} \big (\eta_ {h} ^ {+} \widetilde {P} _ {t - \xi_ {\rho}} ^ {h +} \big) (Y _ {\rho}, j) \big ] \\ = \sum_ {m \in E \setminus \{i \}} \frac {Q _ {0} (i , m)}{q _ {i}} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \big [ e ^ {- h (i) \rho} I _ {\{\overline {{\xi}} _ {\rho} \leq t \}} \big (\eta_ {h} ^ {+} \widetilde {P} _ {t - \xi_ {\rho}} ^ {h +} \big) (m, j) \big ]. \end{array}\tag{17.111}
$$

The last equality is a consequence of the fact that $Y _ { \rho }$ is independent of the random vector $( \rho , \xi _ { \rho } , \overline { { \xi } } _ { \rho } )$ and takes values in the set $E \backslash \{ i \}$ with $\widetilde { \mathbb { P } } _ { 0 , i } ( Y _ { \rho } = m ) =$ $Q _ { 0 } ( i , m ) / q _ { i }$ . Since $\rho$ is the first jump time of the chain $Y$ , the vector $( \rho , \xi _ { \rho } , \overline { { \xi } } _ { \rho } )$ has the same distribution as the vector $( \mathbf { e } _ { i } , X _ { \mathbf { e } _ { i } } ^ { i } , \overline { { X } } _ { \mathbf { e } _ { i } } ^ { i } )$ , where, as above, $\mathbf { e } _ { i }$ is an exponential random variable with mean $1 / q _ { i }$ , independent of the Brownian motion with drift $X _ { t } ^ { i } = \mu _ { i } t + \sigma _ { i } W _ { t }$ . The symbol $\overline { { \boldsymbol X } } _ { \mathbf { e } _ { i } } ^ { i }$ denotes the maximum of $X ^ { i }$ at the independent exponential time $\mathbf { e } _ { i }$ . Note that if $i \in E ^ { + }$ , then $\overline { { { X } } } _ { t } ^ { i } = X _ { t } ^ { i } = t$ for all $t \in \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ and the expectation in (17.111) is very easy to compute. 

Assume now that $i \in E ^ { 0 }$ . Then the Wiener–Hopf factorisation implies that the random variables $\overline { { \boldsymbol X } } _ { \mathbf e _ { u } } ^ { i }$ and $\overline { { \boldsymbol X } } _ { \mathbf e _ { u } } ^ { i } - \boldsymbol X _ { \mathbf e _ { u } } ^ { i }$ are exponentially distributed with parameters 

$$
\sigma_ {i} ^ {- 2} \left(- \mu_ {i} + \sqrt {\mu_ {i} ^ {2} + 2 u \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}}\right) \quad \text { and } \quad \sigma_ {i} ^ {- 2} \left(\mu_ {i} + \sqrt {\mu_ {i} ^ {2} + 2 u \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}}\right)
$$

respectively and independent for any exponential random variable $\mathbf { e } _ { u }$ with parameter $u > 0$ , which is independent of $X ^ { i }$ . Therefore the joint density $f _ { \overline { { X } } _ { t } ^ { i } , \overline { { X } } _ { t } ^ { i } - X _ { t } ^ { i } }$ satisfies the following identity for any x, $y \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} u e ^ {- u t} f _ {\overline {{{X}}} _ {t} ^ {i}, \overline {{{X}}} _ {t} ^ {i} - X _ {t} ^ {i}} (x, y) d t = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} u e ^ {- u t} f _ {\overline {{{X}}} _ {t}} (x) d t \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} u e ^ {- u t} f _ {\overline {{{X}}} _ {t} ^ {i} - X _ {t} ^ {i}} (y) d t \\ \text { for   all } u > 0, \end{array} \tag {17.11}
$$

where $f _ { \overline { { X } } _ { t } ^ { i } - X _ { t } ^ { i } }$ and $f _ { \overline { { X } } _ { t } ^ { i } }$ are the densities of the corresponding random variables. It is clear that there exists a unique extension to the complex half-plane $\mathbb { C } _ { > 0 }$ of both sides of the formula in (17.112) and that the following formulae hold: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- u t} f _ {\overline {{X}} _ {t}} (x) d t = \frac {\sigma_ {i} ^ {- 2} (- \mu_ {i} + \sqrt {\mu_ {i} ^ {2} + 2 u \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}})}{u} e ^ {- x \sigma_ {i} ^ {- 2} (- \mu_ {i} + \sqrt {\mu_ {i} ^ {2} + 2 u \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}})}, \\ x > 0, u \in \mathbb {C} _ {> 0}, \\ \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- u t} f _ {\overline {{X}} _ {t} ^ {i} - X _ {t} ^ {i}} (y) d t = \frac {\sigma_ {i} ^ {- 2} (\mu_ {i} + \sqrt {\mu_ {i} ^ {2} + 2 u \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}})}{u} e ^ {- y \sigma_ {i} ^ {- 2} (\mu_ {i} + \sqrt {\mu_ {i} ^ {2} + 2 u \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}})}, \\ y > 0, u \in \mathbb {C} _ {> 0}. \end{array} \tag {17.}\tag{17.113}
$$

(17.114) 

By substituting identity (17.112) into the expectation (17.111), applying the formulae in (17.113) and (17.114) and taking the limit as t tends to zero, we see that the limits in (17.100) and (17.101) are as stated for any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ . Furthermore the formula in (17.103) holds. 

The strong Markov property of $( \xi , Y )$ next implies that for any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ and any $t > 0$ , the matrices $\widetilde { P } _ { t } ^ { h + } = ( \widetilde { P } _ { t } ^ { h + } ( i , j ) _ { t } , i , j \in E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { + } )$ with $\widetilde { P } _ { t } ^ { h + } ( i , j )$ ) defined by (17.109) satisfy the system of ordinary differential equations 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \widetilde {P} _ {t} ^ {h +} = \widetilde {P} _ {t} ^ {h +} Q _ {h} ^ {+}, \quad t > 0, \qquad P _ {0} ^ {h +} = \mathbb {I},
$$

where I denotes the $N ^ { + } \times N ^ { + }$ identity matrix, the unique solution of which is given by 

$$
\widetilde {P} _ {t} ^ {h +} = \exp \bigl (Q _ {h} ^ {+} t \bigr).
$$

This proves that the matrix $\boldsymbol { Q } _ { h } ^ { + }$ identified above satisfies (17.106). Since $\widetilde { P } _ { t } ^ { h + } ( i , j )$ $ 0$ for all $i , j \in E ^ { 0 } \cup E ^ { + }$ as $t \to \infty$ , it follows that all eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol { Q } _ { h } ^ { + }$ must have nonpositive real parts and therefore $Q _ { h } ^ { + } \in \mathbb { D } ( N ^ { + } )$ . The proof of the existence of a matrix $Q _ { h } ^ { - } \in \mathbb { D } ( N ^ { - } )$ satisfying (17.108) is similar and omitted. 

## 17.8.2 Proof of Theorem 17.21

(Existence) For any $h \in { \mathcal { H } }$ and $x , \ell \in \mathbb { R }$ , define the matrices $\Phi _ { \ell } ^ { \pm } ( x )$ ) by 

$$
\Phi_ {\ell} ^ {+} (x) = \eta_ {h} ^ {+} \exp \bigl (Q _ {h} ^ {+} (\ell - x) \bigr), \quad \Phi_ {\ell} ^ {-} (x) = \eta_ {h} ^ {-} \exp \bigl (Q _ {h} ^ {-} (x - \ell) \bigr).\tag{17.115}
$$

The proof of existence rests on the martingale property of $M ^ { + } = \{ M _ { t } ^ { + } \} _ { t \geq 0 }$ and $M ^ { - } = \{ M _ { t } ^ { - } \} _ { t \ge 0 }$ given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} M _ {t} ^ {+} = e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} f _ {+} (Y _ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}}, \xi_ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}}) \quad \text { and } \\ M _ {t} ^ {-} = e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {-}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} f _ {-} (Y _ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {-}}, \xi_ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {-}}) \end{array}\tag{17.116}
$$

with 

$$
f _ {+} (i, x) := e _ {i} ^ {\prime} \varPhi_ {\ell} ^ {+} (x) k _ {+}, \qquad f _ {-} (i, x) := e _ {i} ^ {\prime} \varPhi_ {\ell} ^ {-} (x) k _ {-},\tag{17.117}
$$

where $k _ { + }$ and $k _ { - }$ are $N ^ { + }$ - and $N ^ { - }$ -column vectors, respectively. 

The martingale property of $M ^ { + }$ follows from the equality 

$$
M _ {t} ^ {+} = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \left[ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} k _ {+} \left(Y _ {\ell} ^ {+}\right) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {t} \right],
$$

where $\{ \mathcal { G } _ { t } \} _ { t \ge 0 }$ denotes the filtration generated by $( \xi , Y )$ . To verify this identity, observe first that the Markov property of $( \xi , Y )$ yields that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} k _ {+} \big (Y _ {\ell} ^ {+} \big) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big | \mathcal {G} _ {t} \big ] \\ = e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} k _ {+} \big (Y _ {\ell} ^ {+} \big) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ] \big | _ {(x, i) = (\xi_ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}}, Y _ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}})}. \end{array}
$$

Further, in view of the strong Markov property and spatial homogeneity of $\xi$ , the expectation on the right-hand side of the previous display is for $x \leq \ell$ given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} k _ {+} \big (Y _ {\ell} ^ {+} \big) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ] \\ = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {\ell - x} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} k _ {+} \big (Y _ {\ell - x} ^ {+} \big) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell - x} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ] \\ = \sum_ {j \in E ^ {0} \cup E ^ {+}} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {0, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {0} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {0} ^ {+} = j, \tau_ {0} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ] \\ \times \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {\ell - x} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} k _ {+} \big (Y _ {\ell - x} ^ {+} \big) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell - x} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} | Y _ {0} = j, \xi_ {0} = 0 \big ] \\ = e _ {i} ^ {\prime} \eta_ {h} ^ {+} \exp \big (Q _ {h} ^ {+} (\ell - x) \big) = e _ {i} ^ {\prime} \varPhi_ {\ell} ^ {+} (x) k _ {+} = f _ {+} (i, x), \end{array}\tag{17.118}
$$

where the last line follows by definitions (17.106) and (17.98) of $\boldsymbol { Q } _ { h } ^ { + }$ and $\eta _ { h } ^ { + }$ . 

As $M ^ { + }$ is a martingale, an application of Itô’s lemma shows that $f _ { + } =$ $( f _ { + } ( i , u ) , i \in E )$ satisfies, for all $u < \ell$ 

$$
\frac {1}{2} s (i) ^ {2} f _ {+} ^ {\prime \prime} (i, u) + m (i) f _ {+} ^ {\prime} (i, u) + \sum_ {j} q _ {i j} \left(f _ {+} (j, u) - f _ {+} (i, u)\right) = 0,\tag{17.119}
$$

where $f _ { + } ^ { \prime }$ and $f _ { + } ^ { \prime \prime }$ denote the first and second derivatives of $f _ { + }$ with respect to u. By substituting the expressions (17.115)–(17.117) into (17.119) we find, since $k ^ { + }$ was arbitrary, that $\boldsymbol { Q } _ { h } ^ { + }$ and $\eta _ { h } ^ { + }$ satisfy the first set of equations of system (17.66). The proof for ${ Q } _ { h } ^ { - }$ and $\eta _ { h } ^ { - }$ is analogous and omitted. 

(Uniqueness) Now we turn to the proof of the uniqueness of the Wiener–Hopf factorization. To this end, let $( W ^ { + } , G ^ { + } , W ^ { - } , G ^ { - } )$ be a complex matrix Wiener– Hopf factorization and define the function $\widetilde { f }$ as $f _ { + }$ in (17.117), but replacing $\eta ^ { + }$ and $Q ^ { + }$ by $W ^ { + }$ and $G ^ { + }$ , respectively. An application of Doob’s optional stopping theorem then yields that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {f} (j, x) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, j} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} \widetilde {f} (Y _ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}}, \xi_ {t \wedge \tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}}) \big ] \\ = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, j} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} \widetilde {f} \big (Y _ {\ell} ^ {+}, \xi_ {\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} \big) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ] \\ + \lim _ {t \to \infty} \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, j} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {t} h (Y _ {s}) d s} \widetilde {f} (Y _ {t}, \xi_ {t}) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+} = \infty \}} \big ]. \end{array}\tag{17.120}
$$

By the definition of ${ \widetilde { f } } ,$ the absence of positive jumps of $\xi$ and (17.118), the first expectation in (17.120) is equal to 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, j} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} \widetilde {f} (Y _ {\ell} ^ {+}, \ell) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ]} \\ & {\qquad = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, j} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} k _ {+} (Y _ {\ell} ^ {+}) I _ {\{\tau_ {\ell} ^ {+} <   \infty \}} \big ] = f _ {+} (j, x)} \end{array}
$$

for $x \leq \ell$ . The second term in (17.120) is zero, since $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } I _ { \{ Y _ { s } \in E _ { 0 } \} } d s  \infty \widetilde { \mathbb { P } } _ { x , j } } \end{array}$ almost surely on the event $\{ \tau _ { \ell } ^ { + } = \infty \}$ for all $j \in E$ and $x \in \mathbb { R }$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { m i n } _ { i \in E _ { 0 } } \Re ( h ( i ) ) > } \end{array}$ $0 .$ . Thus $f _ { + } = \widetilde { f }$ for all $N ^ { + }$ -column vectors $k _ { + }$ , and we deduce that $G ^ { + } = Q _ { h } ^ { + }$ and $W ^ { + } = \eta _ { h } ^ { + }$ . Similarly, one can show that $G ^ { - } =  { Q _ { h } } ^ { - }$ and $W ^ { - } = \eta _ { h } ^ { - }$ , and the uniqueness is proved. 

## 17.8.3 Proof of Theorem 17.24

Applying the strong Markov property at $\bar { \tau }$ and noting that $\bar { \tau } \leq \tau ^ { \xi }$ yields, in view of the representation (17.94), that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} H _ {j} ^ {x, i} (h, u) = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\bar {\tau}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {\bar {\tau}} = j \}} F (\xi_ {\bar {\tau}}, Y _ {\bar {\tau}}) \big ] \\ = \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\bar {\tau}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {\bar {\tau}} = j, \tau_ {\upsilon} ^ {+} <   \tau_ {\ell} ^ {-} \}} F (\upsilon , Y _ {\bar {\tau}}) \big ] \end{array}

$$
+ \widetilde {\mathbb {E}} _ {x, i} \Big [ e ^ {- \int_ {0} ^ {\bar {\tau}} h (Y _ {s}) d s} I _ {\{Y _ {\bar {\tau}} = j, \tau_ {\upsilon} ^ {+} > \tau_ {\ell} ^ {-} \}} F (\ell , Y _ {\bar {\tau}}) \Big ],

where

since $\widetilde { h } ( i ) = h ( i ) I _ { \{ i \in E ^ { 0 } \} }$ , by the definition of $\widetilde { h } .$ . From the definition of $\tau ^ { \xi }$ it is straightforward to check that 

$$

$$

so that $F ( \upsilon , i ) = e ^ { u \upsilon } \delta _ { i j }$ and $F ( \ell , i ) = e ^ { u \ell } \delta _ { i j }$ if $i \in E ^ { 0 }$ , where $\delta _ { i j }$ denotes the Kronecker delta. 

Moreover, in view of the form (17.61)–(17.62) of $Q _ { h }$ and the definition of phasetype distribution, it is clear that, conditionally on $Y _ { 0 } = i \in E _ { i } ^ { + }$ and $\xi _ { 0 } = \upsilon , Y _ { \tau ^ { \xi } } = j$ and $\tau ^ { \xi } \sim \mathrm { P H } ( \delta _ { i } , B _ { i } ^ { + } )$ ), where $\delta _ { i }$ is the vector with elements $\delta _ { i } = ( \delta _ { i k } )$ .
